title: 8.1 Nutrition in Plants

mdxBody:
You have learnt that plants absorb nutrients from the soil which are then utilized in the leaves to prepare organic nutrients by photosynthetic activity. These organic solutes are also to be moved to different parts of the plant body. When organic solutes are utilized in plant body, some waste compounds are also produced which are then removed out of the plant body. All these movements of materials are generally referred to as transport in plants.

## Need of Transport

In a plant body, transport occurs at three different levels:
At $1^{\text {st }}$ level, the materials are moved from outside to inside the plant body because plant needs mineral nutrients and water to maintain its live activities which are to be absorbed from the soil, however, gases like $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ are obtained from air.

At $2^{\text {nd }}$ level, the materials are transported within the plant body from one place to another because the inorganic nutrients must be transported to the leaves so that they can be used to prepare organic solutes by photosynthetic activity. These organic solutes are also to be moved to different parts of the plant body so that they can be used in plant growth and metabolism.
At $3^{\text {rd }}$ level, the materials are moved from inside to outside the plant body because when organic solutes are utilized in plant body, some waste compounds are also produced which are then removed out of the plant body. These are the reasons why transport in plants occurs at three different levels.

## Structure of root and root hairs

Root is an underground part of the plant, which serves as the organ of uptake of mineral nutrients and water. It possesses large surface area due to extensive branching system and root hairs which make them favourable for organ of uptake.

Dicot plants have tap root which consists of a thick primary root that bears several

<CaptionedImage src="kg20h6g5n16pkatsjg4zh0vtt18cr9w0" alt="Biological diagram" caption="" />

secondary roots. Each secondary root further consists of large number of tertiary roots. On the other hand, monocot plants have fibrous adventitious roots that show no differentiation of primary, secondary, and tertiary roots.
## Internal structure of root and root hairs

In both monocot and dicot roots, the outermost layer is called epidermis. Many cells of the epidermis have extensions that penetrate the spaces among soil particles. These extensions of the root epidermal cells are called root hairs, which increase approximately $67 \%$ surface area of the root. Inner to the epidermis is a ground tissue, the cortex. The

<CaptionedImage src="kg2b9hgp3xwz800ghmfepjtjs98csset" alt="Biological diagram" caption="" />

inner lining of the cortex is called the endodermis. The endodermal cells have deposition of a wax, the suberin in their radial walls. These depositions are in the form of strips called the Casparian Strips. Inner to the endodermis is the pericycle which surrounds the innermost vascular bundles. The vascular bundle consists of xylem and phloem which are arranged in the form of ring in monocot root with central ground tissue called pith. Whereas, in the dicot roots, the vascular bundles are present in the form of star shape in the centre of the root without the presence of pith.
## Uptake of mineral salts and water by active and passive transport

Plant roots serve two vital functions: anchoring the plant in soil and absorbing essential minerals and water. To support the process of photosynthesis, plants require three key nutrients: carbon dioxide, water, minerals, and light. To obtain these nutrients, roots develop an extensive branching system and are covered by root hairs. These root hairs are the primary sites for the absorption of water and minerals.

<CaptionedImage src="kg23y20hm66k0yxbtr1d5afj8d8cr81g" alt="Biological diagram" caption="" />

With these raw materials (minerals and water from the soil, carbon dioxide from the air, and light energy), plants synthesize all the compounds they need. While most minerals enter the root hairs or epidermal cells of the roots through bulk flow with water, some are absorbed through diffusion, facilitated diffusion, or active transport.
## Mechanism of mineral absorption by root

Plants absorb minerals from water in the soil. When minerals are stuck to soil particles and not dissolved in water, plants can't use them. Only those minerals can be absorbed that are dissolved in soil water. Plants take in minerals through root cells using both passive and active processes that require energy, specifically ATP.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2a3j94h5bedrn8nt9wet8fz58dm83k" alt="Biological diagram" caption="Schematic representation of shoot- and root-level interactions, detailing gas exchange and active/passive mineral ion transport." />

Passive uptake happens through diffusion, as minerals move along their concentration gradient through plasmodesmata to cells in the root's cortex, endodermis, and pericycle before reaching the xylem cells. They are then pulled up by transpiration.

Certain nutrients are transported from the soil into the epidermal cells of roots through their cell membranes by a process called facilitated diffusion. In facilitated diffusion, proteins within the cell membrane act as carrier molecules to help move nutrients across the membrane. These carrier proteins are found in the cell membranes of epidermal and other root cells.

Active transport, on the other hand, requires energy and allows plants to take in minerals even when their concentration inside the root cells is higher than in the soil. This is against the natural concentration gradient, and it involves the use of ATP. Active transport is selective and relies on respiration. Some ions can also move through passive transport.
## Mechanism of water absorption by root

Absorption of water by roots occurs by means of a passive transport mechanism called osmosis. This is the movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane from an area where they are more concentrated to an area where they are less

<SideActivity title="Science Tidbit">
One crucial nutrient, nitrogen (N), is often scarce in both rock particles and soil water. Many plants have developed beneficial partnerships with other organisms to obtain these limited nutrients. For example, mycorrhizal fungi and nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the root nodules of legumes are examples of such partnerships. Fungal associations with the roots of higher plants enhance the plant's ability to absorb minerals like phosphorus and trace metals such as zinc and copper. A root infected with mycorrhizal fungi can absorb phosphate at a faster rate than an uninfected root. In exchange for their services, mycorrhizal fungi receive sugars and protection from the plant, ultimately increasing the plant's efficiency in acquiring mineral nutrients. Mycorrhizae form associations with plants from a wide range of plant families, covering approximately $90 \%$ of flowering plants.
</SideActivity>

concentrated. If water moves into a cell through osmosis, it's called endosmosis, and if it moves out of the cell, it's called exosmosis.

In the epidermal cells of roots, the cell wall allows water and minerals to pass through freely. However, the cell membrane is selectively permeable, meaning it only allows certain substances from the solution to pass through. Water entering the epidermal cells follows the concentration gradient, moving through the cortex, endodermis, pericycle, and finally into the xylem cells.

<CaptionedImage src="kg24qgz1366cm56epfdhhb5sj18cs5xh" alt="Add Root hair absorbing water and air from soil particles to Biology 9 Ch8 note" />
## Transpiration

<CaptionedImage src="kg2374s9z8wxtpv8shfh4wpbtn8csk8g" alt="Biological diagram" caption="" />

You have learnt that plants absorb water from the soil by the roots. This absorbed water moves in the aerial parts of the plant from where the most of this water (approx. $99 \%$) has been lost in the form of

> Critical Thinking
> Does a submerged aquatic plant perform transpiration.

vapours into the atmosphere. This loss is called transpiration. $90 \%$ of this loss occurs through the stomata present mainly in the leaves and some other aerial parts of the plant. This is called stomatal transpiration. Some other amount of this absorbed water $(7-9 \%)$ is lost from general body surface through the cuticle, called cuticular transpiration. A very little amount of water (less than $3 \%$ ) is also lost through lenticels which are scar-like regions (with ruptured epidermis and loosely packed underlying cortical cells) present in the stem. This is called lenticular transpiration.

Transpiration is a vital process for the plant as it not only provides cooling to the plant but also helps to absorb the water and dissolved minerals and to move them in upward direction to the leaves. Therefore,

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Why transpiration is sometimes called necessary evil. Without transpiration plants are unable to survive. On the other hand, transpiration is generally regarded as disadvantageous as it shows great loss of absorbed water so, an unchecked excessive transpiration can lead to the wilting (loss of turgor) and ultimately death of the plant.
</SideActivity>
## Relation of transpiration with leaf surface area and Stomatal opening and closing

As you have learnt that transpiration mainly occurs through the stomata, which are present on the leaf surface. So, the plants having large surface area of the leaves having more stomata show greater rate of transpiration as compared to the plants having narrow and reduced surfaces of the leaves having less

> Critical Thinking
> Can you think that the shape and the size of the leaves would be an adaptation of the plants in different habitats such as aquatic and terrestrial.

stomata.

Similarly, more transpiration is generally observed in date time than night as the stomata are widely open during day and nearly close at night.

## Factors affecting the rate of transpiration

The rate of transpiration is influenced by several environmental factors like temperature, wind, and humidity etc. The rate of transpiration can be measured by using a simple apparatus called the potometer which is shown in the diagram. Students under the guidance of their teachers should plan simple

<CaptionedImage src="kg21f2g86q6ah2n5fgfa53m0hs8dm8t4" alt="Biological diagram" caption="Factors affecting the rate of transpiration" />

experimental activities to investigate the effect of these factors on the rate of transpiration using the potometer.
## Effect of temperature

On a sunny day with strong sunlight, the air temperature rises, and this increase in temperature lowers the humidity in the air. As a result, more water evaporates from the surfaces of plant mesophyll cells, which leads to a higher rate of transpiration. For every $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ increase in temperature, the rate of transpiration roughly doubles. However, when the environmental temperature becomes very high, around $40-45^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, it causes the stomata on plant leaves to close. This closure helps the plant conserve its muchneeded water because excessive loss can be detrimental.

If these higher temperatures persist for an extended period and the soil doesn't have enough water, the plants may start to wilt and could eventually die.

## Effect of Wind

Wind is moving air, and it speeds up the diffusion of water molecules. This leads to a higher rate of evaporation from the surfaces of mesophyll cells. In contrast, when the air is calm and still, the movement of water molecules (diffusion) slows down, resulting in a decreased rate of transpiration.

<SideActivity title="Scientific Enquiry">
To instigate the effect of temperature on rate of transpiration, set the apparatus as shown in the figure 8.6, observe the movement of bubble in potometer and record the readings with appropriate intervals. Perform the experiment in different temperatures in a growth room. Remember that other conditions like sun light, wind and humidity should be constant. Take the mean reading of every experiment and plot a graph to show the relationship of rate of transpiration against temperature. Interpret your results and make conclusion.
To instigate the effect of wind on the rate of transpiration, set the apparatus as shown in the figure 8.6, observe the movement of bubble in potometer and record the readings with appropriate intervals. Perform the several experiments by putting the potometer at different distances in front of pedestal fan so that different velocities of wind can be investigated. Remember that other conditions like sun light, temperature and humidity should be constant. Take the mean reading of every experiment and plot a graph to show the relationship of rate of transpiration against different velocities of wind. Interpret your results and make conclusion.
Similarly, plan an activity to instigate the effect of humidity on the rate of transpiration.
</SideActivity>

## Effect of Humidity

Humidity is the percentage of water vapours in the air. In dry air (low humidity), water molecules diffuse more rapidly from the surfaces of mesophyll cells, air spaces, and through stomata to the outside of the leaf. This results in more water being lost, which increases the rate of transpiration. Conversely, in humid air, the diffusion rate slows down, leading to a significant decrease in the rate of transpiration.
Similarly, can you predict the effect of other factors like sun light, $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ concentration and availability of soil water on the rate of transpiration.

## Transport of water and salts within plant body (Ascent of Sap)

Root epidermal cells absorb water and minerals from the soil. These substances are then transported from the roots to the leaves. This upward movement of water and dissolved minerals through the xylem tissue is known as the "ascent of sap." This process requires a passage and a significant amount of force because it occurs against the force of gravity, especially in tall plants. It is now quite evident that passage of ascent of sap is the xylem tissue and the most widely accepted theory that explains the force responsible for ascent of sap is called the "TACT theory."

## Passage of Ascent of Sap

Xylem is a complex and permanent tissue which act as passage for ascent of sap. Two types of xylem cells: Tracheids and Vessels are very important. Tracheids are long, dead cells with pointed ends and Xylem vessels are long, dead, and thick-walled tube-like structures formed by the fusion of vessel cells (vessel elements) placed end to end. Both are essential for water and mineral transport as well as structural support.

## TACT Theory

According to the TACT theory, four factors work together to make a force that moves water and minerals up a plant. These factors are Transpiration pull, Adhesion, Cohesion, and Tension, forming the acronym TACT.

<CaptionedImage src="kg27vxw4g8hp75pqp55p2kkwkd8dnya3" alt="Biological diagram" caption="Fig. 8.8: Movement of water in xylem through TACT Mechanism" />

### i) Transpiration Pull

When stomata (tiny openings) on leaves are open, water evaporates from the leaves into the air, creating a pulling force known as transpiration. This pull makes water move from the roots to the leaves through the xylem tissue.

### ii) Adhesion

Adhesion is the attraction between water molecules and other substances. Water is strongly attracted to the walls of the xylem cells because both water and cellulose (in cell walls) are polar molecules. This adhesion helps water move upward in the plant against gravity. It also keeps water in the xylem when transpiration is not happening.

### iii) Cohesion and Tension

Cohesion is the attraction between nearby water molecules, which is possible because water is a polar molecule. Tension refers to the tension created in the water column. These forces help hold the water molecules together in a continuous column within the xylem.
## How TACT Force Works

Imagine the column of water in the xylem as strong as a steel wire. Hydrogen bonds among water molecules create cohesion, holding the water molecules together like a string. As long as transpiration continues (water evaporating from leaves), the string of water remains tense and is pulled upward as a single unit. This bulk flow of water to the top of the plant is driven by solar energy, as it's the evaporation from leaves that causes the transpiration pull.

<CaptionedImage src="kg24cqa39h21azf9j2f50xft6x8csmdk" alt="Add Fig 8.8: Movement of water in xylem through the TACT mechanism to Biology 9 Ch8 note" />
## Transport of organic solute within plant body

The transport of prepared food (organic solutes) to different parts of the plant through the phloem tissue is translocation.

## Passage of Translocation

It is evident that translocation occurs through phloem tissues which are complex and permanent plant tissue. Sieve tube elements and companion cells are important components of phloem.

<CaptionedImage src="kg20rk7abj78gme3jqh712yj358dnvx7" alt="Biological diagram" caption="Pressure-flow hypothesis (or bulk flow mechanism) for translocation in plant phloem." />

Sieve Tubes are long tube-like structures that transport organic solutes (like sucrose) throughout the plant. Since sieve tube elements lack nuclei, companion cells next to them control their functions. Together, sieve elements and companion cells act as conducting channels for moving organic solutes.
## Direction of Translocation

This movement is not just up or down; it goes in various directions. We usually say that translocation goes from a "source" to a "sink." A "source" supplies food (like leaves making food), and a "sink" uses food (like roots or storage organs). Leaves are sources, fruits are sinks, and stems and roots can act as both.

## Composition of Translocating Fluid (Phloem Sap)

Phloem sap contains about $10-25 \%$ dry matter. Most of this dry matter is sucrose (a kind of sugar), with some other organic compounds.

## Mechanism of Translocation (Pressure Flow or Mass Flow Theory)

The most accepted idea for how organic solutes move in plants is the "pressure flow" or "mass flow" theory. Here's how it works:

1. Sugars produced in source regions, like leaves or storage areas, are loaded into the phloem's sieve tube elements by companion cells.
2. This active transport raises the sugar concentration and reduces the water concentration in the phloem. This makes the phloem cells more "sweet."
3. Water moves into the phloem through osmosis from nearby xylem cells, increasing hydrostatic pressure (pressure from water) in the phloem cells. This pressure pushes the sugary solution away from the source (usually a leaf).
4. The pressure difference, from the high-pressure source to the lower-pressure sink, causes translocation. It's like water being pushed through a hose.
5. When the solution reaches a sink, like the roots, root cells actively absorb the organic solutes. This makes the phloem sap less "sweet."
6. The loss of solutes in phloem sap increases solute potential and water potential, causing water to flow back into the xylem tubes.
So, it's like a system of moving food and water around the plant, driven by differences in pressure and the needs of different plant parts.

<CaptionedImage src="kg249af3a9ekya2p2aaa7rn34x8csvf3" alt="Add Phloem translocation: source-to-sink sucrose transport to Biology 9 Ch8 note" />

title: 8.2 Transport in Plants

mdxBody:
Gas exchange is the type of respiration that occurs at the organismic level. Gas exchange is when the entire organism exchanges gases with the environment. The goal is to ensure the organism is provided with oxygen, needed for cellular respiration (where complex organic compounds are broken down and carbon dioxide is produced), which must then be removed to the outer environment. Every cell in a plant does its own gas exchange, depending on what it needs. This exchange mainly happens through two openings: stomata (tiny openings in leaves) and lenticels (small openings in stems), through a process called diffusion.

## Pattern of gas exchange in leaves (Photosynthetic parts)

Plants, being photosynthetic autotrophs, show different patterns of gas exchange in day and night through the leaves.

| Table: 8.1 Pattern of gas exchange between plant and environment |  |  |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  | In daytime | In nighttime |
| Inhale | Carbon dioxide (CO2) | Oxygen (O2) |
| Exhale | Oxygen (O2) | Carbon dioxide (CO2) |

During the day, plants are busy with both photosynthesis (making food) and respiration. The rate of photosynthesis varies throughout the day, mainly depending on light intensity. Generally, the rate of photosynthesis is greater than the rate of respiration, so photosynthesis needs more carbon dioxide than respiration produces, and plants bring in extra carbon dioxide from the environment. On the other hand, photosynthesis produces more oxygen than respiration needs, so plants release excess oxygen.

<CaptionedImage src="kg20fxqqjst5txvkqwyhsq3fax8csert" alt="Diagram showing gas exchange in a leaf during daytime, taking in CO2 and releasing O2." caption="Fig. 8.10: Daytime gas exchange in a leaf." />

At night, plants act more like animals: they absorb oxygen and release carbon dioxide, because there is no photosynthesis happening in the dark.

During dawn and dusk, when light intensity is low, the rates of photosynthesis and respiration become equal. The carbon dioxide produced by respiration is enough for photosynthesis, and the oxygen released by photosynthesis is used in respiration. At this point, there is no net exchange of gases with the environment; this is called the compensation point of photosynthesis.
## Pattern of gas exchange in roots (non-photosynthetic parts)

Roots also exchange gases with soil air through root epidermal cells, absorbing oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide, because there is no photosynthesis happening in the roots; this pattern remains the same day and night.

<SideActivity title="Lab Activity: Green Breathing - Plant Respiratory Patterns in Day and Night">
To recognize how a plant's exposure to light and darkness impacts its gas exchange.

The increase or decrease in carbon dioxide concentration will be tested in this inquiry using hydrogen carbonate indicator. It goes from pink or red to yellow when carbon dioxide builds up, and becomes purple when carbon dioxide concentrations fall.

1. Take three test tubes of 50 ml volume and wash them properly with tap water, then rinse with distilled water and finally with hydrogen carbonate indicator (the indicator will change colour if the boiling tube is not clean).
2. Add 30 ml hydrogen carbonate indicator solution to each of the three boiling tubes.
3. Place equal-sized pieces of Canadian pondweed (Elodea) or Hydrilla or any other locally available aquatic plant in tubes 1 and 2, then stopper all three tubes.
4. Use a bench lamp to expose tubes 1 and 3 to light, then cover tube 2 with aluminum foil or put it in a dark cabinet or black box.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2bqvg40zpsn2dstamt20f3kd8dnrpq" alt="Diagram of the three-test-tube setup for the hydrogen carbonate indicator gas exchange activity." caption="Photosynthesis and respiration in pond weed using a hydrogencarbonate indicator." />

5. Note the colour of each tube's hydrogen carbonate indicator after a period of 24 hours.

The indicator in tube 2 (plant in the dark) should turn yellow, the indicator in tube 1 (plant in the light) should turn purple, and the indicator in tube 3 (the control, no plant), initially pink/red, should not change colour.

Hydrogen carbonate indicator helps show changes in acidity caused by carbon dioxide: more carbon dioxide turns it yellow, less carbon dioxide turns it purple. This experiment shows that in light, plants use more carbon dioxide in photosynthesis than they produce in respiration; in the dark, plants produce carbon dioxide through respiration, since there is no photosynthesis to consume it. A control tube without a plant confirms the plant caused the colour change. Note that the indicator can react to any change in acidity or alkalinity, not just carbon dioxide, but changes in carbon dioxide from leaf activity are the most likely explanation here.
</SideActivity>

title: 8.3 Gas Exchange in Plants

mdxBody:
Homeostasis in plants refers to the adjustment or adaptation of plants to varying degrees of environmental temperatures and availability of water and salts in the soil.

## Importance of Homeostasis

Homeostasis in plants is essential for their survival, growth, and reproduction. Homeostatic mechanisms help plants respond to temperature changes, allowing them to survive in various climates. Homeostasis ensures that plants maintain adequate hydration levels. Homeostasis allows plants to respond to various stressors, such as drought, salinity, pathogens, and herbivores. Plants can activate specific defense mechanisms to mitigate damage. It enables them to adapt to changing environmental conditions and maintain internal stability, ultimately contributing to their ecological success.

## Excretion in plants

Unlike animals, excretion in plants is a very broad term, which encompasses the removal of anything from plant body. Plants have a different way of getting rid of waste compared to animals. Plants make various organic and inorganic compounds that they store for different reasons and remove when needed. Following are different ways of excretion in plants.

## Excretion of carbon dioxide and oxygen

Carbon dioxide is the waste of respiration which is excreted from plant body at night during gas exchange process. Similarly, oxygen is the waste of photosynthesis which is excreted in day during the same gas exchange process.

## Excretion of water

Water is produced as waste of both photosynthesis and respiration and it is also absorbed from soil. The excretion of water occurs through the plant body during the process of transpiration.

## Excretion through leaves

Plant cells have large vacuoles that can store useful stuff or waste. Sometimes, these stored substances can build up and form crystals in the vacuoles. Leaves are key players in this process. When the leaves are loaded with large amounts of pigmented compounds, they turn yellow. Remember, this yellowing

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Can you differentiate between chlorotic leaves and excretophores?
</SideActivity>

is not due to lack of chlorophyll as happens in chlorosis. Such leaves generally fall from plants in autumn season. In this way leaves act as organ of excretion, therefore, such leaves are also called excretophores. This is why gardeners like using decomposed autumn leaves as a mineral-rich source for plants.

## Excretion through stem and branches

Some trees deposit unusual chemicals in their branches and trunks, especially in old xylem that's no longer used for water transport. Ebony trees, for instance, produce very dark wood in their centres. Plant scientists consider these deposits as waste materials. Although, these wastes are not removed but are dumped in one part of the body as we put the trash in waste bin however, it is still present in the home.

## Excretion through roots

Some plants actively release waste compounds into the soil, almost like using them as chemical weapons against other plants competing for resources. Conifer trees are known for this tactic.

## Osmotic adjustment (Osmoregulation) in plants

Osmotic adjustment, also known as osmoregulation, is like a plant's way of maintaining the right balance of water and solutes in its body. This balance creates three different situations: hypotonic, hypertonic, and isotonic.

## Hypotonic Situation

When a cell is in a watery environment with more water and less stuff dissolved in it (solute), water moves into the cell, making it swell up and firm (we call this "turgid").

## Hypertonic Situation

If a cell is in an environment with less water and more dissolved stuff than it has inside (cell sap), water moves out of the cell, causing it to shrink and become limp (we call this "flaccid").
Both of these situations, hypotonic and hypertonic, require the plant to make adjustments to keep things in balance.

## Ideal Situation (Isotonic)

The best scenario for a cell is when the water and solute balance inside and outside the cell is just right. In this "isotonic" situation, there's no net movement of water in or out of the cell. However, this balance is rarely found in a plant's natural environment.

## Osmotic adjustment in different plants groups

Plants are categorized into three groups based on their water availability: hydrophytes (live in water-rich environments), mesophytes (thrive where water is moderately available), and xerophytes (adapted to extreme dry conditions). These groups have distinct adaptations:

1. Transpiration rates vary, with hydrophytes having the highest and xerophytes the lowest.
2. Stomatal placement differs, hydrophytes have them on the upper leaf surface, mesophytes on the lower surface, and xerophytes have sunken stomata.
3. Stomatal behaviour varies, hydrophytes keep stomata open day and night, mesophytes open them during the day, and xerophytes open them at night.
4. Cuticle thickness on leaves differs, with xerophytes having the thickest, mesophytes a thinner cuticle, and hydrophytes almost none.
5. Water storage capacity varies, with xerophytes, known as succulents, storing ample water.

title: 8.4 Homeostasis in Plants

mdxBody:
Asexual reproduction is a straightforward method of creating new plant life. In this process, only one parent plant is involved, and it gives rise to offspring that are essentially clones, sharing the exact genetic makeup of the parent. What makes asexual reproduction distinct is that it doesn't rely on the formation of specialized reproductive cells called gametes or the complex process of meiosis, which shuffles genetic material to produce variation. Instead, asexual reproduction relies on simpler methods, such as cell division or the growth of specialized structures. This simplicity and genetic uniformity make asexual reproduction a reliable and efficient way for some plants to propagate and expand their population. Asexual reproduction includes binary fission, budding, spore formation and vegetative propagation.

## Binary Fission

Binary fission is a simple way of making more of something: it's like splitting something into two equal parts. This method is commonly used for making more of certain tiny living things, like bacteria, some one-celled creatures called protozoa, and some small invertebrates, but no true plant is known to use this process.

In bacteria, first, a copy of their DNA is formed so that there are two identical sets. Then, these sets move to opposite ends of the bacterium. Next, the middle part of the bacterium starts to fold in, dividing the contents into two parts. A new wall forms between these two parts. This whole process ends with two new bacteria, which will keep growing and eventually split into more.

<CaptionedImage src="kg222gk30patgbpmr9hssck6058dqbt6" alt="Diagram showing the steps of binary fission in a bacterium." caption="Fig. 9.1: Binary fission." />
## Budding

In this kind of asexual reproduction, a tiny outgrowth called a bud emerges on the parent's body, like a small bulge. In yeast, a single-celled fungus, this outgrowth forms on one side of the cell. Inside the cell, the nucleus splits into two by mitosis, and one of these new nuclei goes into the outgrowth. Sometimes the parent cell can have more than one outgrowth growing at the same time. Each outgrowth gets bigger and becomes more like the parent. Eventually, the outgrowth can break away from the parent; in other cases, the outgrowths stay attached, leading to groups of individuals living close together, almost like a little community.

<CaptionedImage src="kg21z3m34cw6knzr5zw6vghgtn8dnt01" alt="Diagram of budding in yeast, showing an outgrowth forming on the parent cell." caption="Budding in yeast, a form of asexual reproduction where a new organism develops from an outgrowth or bud due to cell division at one particular site." />

In higher plants, the outgrowths that develop are often of two types: vegetative buds and floral buds. Vegetative buds give rise to new branches and leaves, and floral buds give rise to new flowers.
## Spore Formation

Spores are very small, unicellular, non-motile, thick-walled resistant asexual reproductive bodies. In many fungi, like Rhizopus, when ready to reproduce, body cells create strong, protective sacs called sporangia on the tip of a stalk called a sporangiophore. Inside these sacs, cells divide repeatedly to make many tiny spores. Each spore has a tough shell called a cyst that helps it survive unfavourable conditions. When the sporangia mature, they burst open and release the spores; when conditions become favourable, the spores grow into new Rhizopus.

In unfavourable conditions, some filamentous bacteria, such as actinomycetes, also make spores. These bacterial spores are also thick-walled, and form outside the bacterial cells, so they are called exospores. Upon germination, each spore from a parental filament gives rise to several new bacterial filaments.

It is important to note that the microspores and megaspores of seed-producing plants, and the spores of bryophytes and pteridophytes that give rise to a gametophyte body, are not considered part of asexual reproduction, because meiosis is generally involved in their formation.

<CaptionedImage src="kg21yrqqma722dk8qxtqnzqwjn8dmvn3" alt="Diagram of sporangia forming spores in Rhizopus." caption="Rhizopus (commonly known as black bread mold), depicting its asexual reproductive cycle through spore formation." />

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Under unfavourable conditions, some species of bacteria reproduce by forming spores, e.g. Clostridium and Bacillus species. These bacterial spores are also thick-walled. They are formed inside bacterial cells, so are called endospores. This way, these bacteria can survive unfavourable periods. When conditions are good, each endospore germinates and resumes normal life. Do you think endospore formation is a reproductive process?
</SideActivity>
## Parthenogenesis

Parthenogenesis is the development of an offspring directly from an unfertilized egg. In flowering plants, it is defined as the asexual formation of a seed from the maternal tissues of the ovule, avoiding the processes of meiosis and fertilization, leading directly to embryo development. This can happen due to various triggers, such as changes in environmental conditions or hormonal signals. Parthenogenesis in plants is also known as apomixis. Since it involves creating offspring without the fusion of genetic material from two parents, it is considered a form of asexual reproduction.

## Vegetative Propagation

Flowering plants generally reproduce sexually by means of their flowers, but some also reproduce without flowers, which we call vegetative propagation. There are two kinds: natural vegetative propagation, which plants do on their own, and artificial vegetative propagation, in which people intervene.

## Natural Vegetative Propagation

Natural vegetative propagation in plants refers to the process by which plants reproduce asexually using their own natural mechanisms, without any human intervention. New plants are generated from various vegetative structures of the parent plant, such as roots, stems, leaves, or specialized structures like runners or bulbs. These structures develop into independent plants, and since they originate from the same parent, they often have identical genetic characteristics.

## Bulbs

Bulbs are compact, thickened, vertically growing, underground stems enveloped by thick, succulent (fleshy) leaves, serving as reservoirs of stored nutrients. Beneath the bulb's base, adventitious roots sprout, while shoots emerge from its upper region. Each shoot can develop into a new plant. Species like tulips, onions, and lilies use bulbs to reproduce.

<CaptionedImage src="kg224p3xb037tgm6rtrtxbrysd8dm8cw" alt="Diagram of a bulb's internal structure." caption="Structural anatomy of an onion bulb." />

The next illustration continues this visual sequence.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2b1cjr9ss6e5b32zjtr4wkah8dnhd6" alt="Diagram of a bulb sprouting a new plant." caption="The structure of a corm, which is an underground modified stem (commonly seen in plants like Colocasia / taro or Gladiolus) adapted for food storage and vegetative propagation." />
## Corms

Corms are compact, thickened, vertically growing underground stems that store food, but are not enveloped by fleshy leaves. Buds at the top of a corm give rise to shoots, which then develop into new plants. Examples of plants that reproduce using corms include dasheen and garlic.

## Rhizomes

Rhizomes are flat, horizontal underground stems that have small scale-like leaves. Along the rhizome are distinct nodes and internodes; buds form at these nodes. Buds on the upper side of the rhizome grow into shoots, while the lower side produces adventitious roots. These shoots can develop into new plants. Plants like ginger, ferns, and water lilies use rhizomes to reproduce.

<CaptionedImage src="kg28hetsvngqaatg5frmh70pqx8dmtck" alt="Diagram of a rhizome showing nodes with shoots and roots." caption="Rhizome, which is a horizontal underground modified stem (such as in ginger or turmeric)" />
## Stem Tubers

Stem tubers are swollen tips of underground stems that primarily serve as storage structures in certain plants. Stem tubers often have "eyes" or bud clusters on their surface, from which new shoots can grow when conditions are suitable. Examples include potatoes and yams; these structures serve both as a food source and a means of propagation.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2cjrsx21bzx86k0w49v72ay18dn384" alt="Diagram of a potato stem tuber showing eyes/buds." caption="vegetative propagation in a potato plant using underground stem tubers." />
## Stolons or Runners

The above-ground parts of plants like strawberries and creeping buttercups are typically very short, with most of their structure below ground; these short stems are called rootstocks, and carry leaves and flowers. After the main shoot has bloomed, side buds create long shoots that grow horizontally along the ground, called stolons or runners. These runners have small scale-like leaves at specific points (nodes), with long internodes between them. At each node there is a bud that can grow into both a shoot and roots, so a whole new plant can develop there, getting nourishment from the parent plant through the runner for a while. Eventually the runner dries up and withers away, leaving a new independent plant growing a short distance from the parent. This is how a strawberry plant, for example, can make many new plants without using seeds.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2dhspgpvv4k70g5jw5acqn998dn8xk" alt="Diagram of a strawberry plant producing runners." caption="Asexual reproduction in a strawberry plant using horizontal stems called runners (or stolons)." />

The next illustration continues this visual sequence.

<CaptionedImage src="kg273bx2wp560fdq42vhah921s8dnc3q" alt="Diagram of a new plantlet forming at a runner's node." caption="Vegetative propagation by suckers (or root shoots) in a blackberry plant." />
## Suckers

Suckers typically emerge as small shoots from the underground parts of a plant, such as the root system or near the base of the main stem. These shoots can develop into new plants; as suckers grow, they form their own stems, leaves, and roots, essentially becoming self-sustaining plants while remaining connected to the parent plant for a period. Suckers may receive nutrients and water from the parent plant, helping them establish themselves, which is especially beneficial in adverse conditions. Over time, suckers develop their own root system and become less dependent on the parent plant, eventually thriving independently. Suckers are a common method of natural vegetative propagation in various ground cover plants such as lawn grass.

## Vegetative Propagation by Leaves

In Bryophyllum, new plantlets are created along the edges of its leaves. These plantlets are like tiny versions of the parent plant. When they detach from the parent plant and fall onto the soil below, they can grow and develop into separate, self-sustaining plants.

## Methods of Artificial Vegetative Propagation

Artificial vegetative propagation is adapted when people purposely grow plants to meet specific needs. The part of the plant used for this is called a "vegetative propagule." These methods help preserve the good qualities of plants, like taste, colour, and disease resistance. Two common methods of artificial vegetative propagation are stem cuttings and grafting.

## Stem Cuttings

Stem cuttings are small segments or cut pieces of stem having at least one node. New plants can be grown from some plants by placing a cut piece of stem in water or damp soil: roots start growing from the bottom of the stem into the soil, while the top part keeps growing and making leaves. If a cutting does not start growth, the cut ends can be treated with a plant hormone called auxin to stimulate growth. Sometimes the top part of the cutting is covered with plastic or a glass jar to reduce water loss. This method is often used to propagate roses, ivy, grapevines, and chrysanthemums.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2b6h58pd3b3g573nr15akr698dmvcq" alt="Diagram of a stem cutting rooting in soil." caption="vegetative propagation using stem cuttings" />
## Grafting

This method involves joining two plant parts together to create a single, new plant. It is commonly used to reproduce desirable plant varieties, like fruit trees or ornamental plants, and it's a skilled practice often performed by gardeners and farmers.

Two plant parts are involved in grafting: the scion and the rootstock. The scion is the upper part of the plant, carrying the desired characteristics, such as specific fruit or flower traits. The rootstock is the lower part, which provides the root system and stem support. A skilled gardener makes precise cuts on both the scion and rootstock, usually at specific angles to maximize contact between the two parts. The scion is carefully attached to the rootstock; this connection is crucial for the transport of water, nutrients, and other substances between the two parts. To ensure a secure connection, the graft is typically bound with grafting tape, rubber bands, or other materials, which helps hold the scion in place until the graft heals. Once the graft has healed, the plant begins to grow, producing leaves, flowers, and fruit based on the characteristics of the scion.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2450hb7wn6sw6pq5q7dvq7ah8dm6jf" alt="Diagram showing the scion and rootstock being joined in grafting." caption="Selected image illustrates grafting, an artificial method of vegetative (asexual) plant propagation." />

The next illustration continues this visual sequence.

<CaptionedImage src="kg25pxzs1kjhpc7b41p5v1344s8dncts" alt="Diagram of a healed graft union." caption="Plant tissue culture (micropropagation) using a carrot to grow new plants from a small tissue sample." />
## Cloning (Tissue Culturing)

Cloning is a method of producing genetically identical individuals from a single parental cell. In plants, the term "cloning" refers to tissue culturing, in which a single plant cell or piece of tissue is grown on artificial nutrient medium under aseptic (microbe-free) conditions to develop a genetically identical copy (clone) of the parent plant. This method of artificial vegetative propagation is also called micropropagation. The first cell or tiny piece of the parent plant used in tissue culture is called an "explant." This explant is placed on a special nutrient medium to grow into an undifferentiated mass of cells known as "callus." The callus is then treated with different substances to make it produce shoots and later roots, resulting in a young plant called a "plantlet." These plantlets are carefully moved into soil in their natural surroundings to continue growing.

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Sweet potato is an enlarged root. Farmers place it in moist sand or soil until it produces several plantlets. Then the plantlets are removed and planted. This process is used to produce many plants from a single plant. Is it artificial or natural vegetative propagation, and which type does it belong to?
</SideActivity>

title: 9.1 Asexual Reproduction

mdxBody:
## Sexual Reproduction Across Plant Groups

Sexual reproduction in plants, like in animals, involves the fertilization of gametes (egg and sperm) and formation of a zygote and embryo. Different groups of plants, like bryophytes, pteridophytes, and seed plants (spermatophytes), have different mechanisms of gamete formation and fertilization. In bryophytes and pteridophytes, the sperms are like little swimmers: they can move around and find the egg cells, so they need water to do this (it could be dew or rain). Seed-producing plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms), on the other hand, don't rely on water to get their sperm to the egg cells; they have their own special techniques, covered further in this chapter.

One of the prominent features of plants is the haplo-diplontic lifecycle, i.e. a haploid gametophyte (gamete-producing plant body) generation and a diploid sporophyte (spore-producing plant body) generation that regularly alternate with each other during the lifecycle. In some plants like bryophytes, the gametophyte generation is more prominent (dominant) while the sporophyte is much reduced. In the rest of the plant kingdom, the sporophyte is the dominant generation, while the gametophyte is a very small structure.

## Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants (Angiosperms)

In flowering plants (angiosperms), the major plant body is the sporophyte, which may be a herb, shrub, or tree. Flowers are the reproductive parts of these plants.

## Structure of a Flower

A flower is like a plant's special tool for making new plants: a part of the plant changed and adapted for reproduction. A flower generally consists of a stalk called the pedicel, like the flower's stem, holding it up. At the top of the pedicel is a swollen part called the thalamus, like the flower's platform. The thalamus generally bears four kinds of parts called floral leaves, arranged in whorls (circles) on its upper surface.

The outermost circle is the calyx, made up of green leaves called sepals, a protective cover for the inside parts of the flower. Just inside the calyx is another circle, the corolla, consisting of variously coloured floral leaves called petals. Deeper inside is the androecium, the male parts of the flower, called stamens, important for making pollen. Right in the centre is the gynoecium, where the female parts are, in something called the carpel or pistil, where new seeds start to form.

<CaptionedImage src="kg23y4yqrfkqs5s3dn5yth8e518dnwy1" alt="Diagram of a flower's structure showing calyx, corolla, androecium, and gynoecium." caption="anatomy of a typical bisexual flower" />

The calyx and corolla, the outer two circles, are like the flower's protectors: they keep everything safe inside but do not take part in reproduction directly, so they are called accessory whorls. The androecium and gynoecium, the inner two circles, are the ones that actually make the flower's reproduction happen, so they are called necessary whorls.
## Formation of Microspores and Megaspores

Each stamen consists of a long stalk, the filament, and a bilobed swollen tip called the anther. In the anther lobes, four pollen sacs (microsporangia) are present, which produce haploid pollen grains (microspores) by meiosis.

Each carpel or pistil consists of a sac-like structure at the bottom called the ovary, a long tubular structure above the ovary called the style, and a swollen tip on the style called the stigma. The ovary contains one to numerous ovules (megasporangia). Each ovule possesses one spore mother cell that undergoes meiosis to produce four megaspores; of these four, only one is capable of surviving further and becomes the functional megaspore.

## Pollination

When microspores are formed, the wall of the pollen sacs bursts and the microspores are liberated. The microspores are transferred from the anther of the stamen to the stigma of the carpel by wind, insects, or other animals; this event is called pollination, and the microspores during pollination are called pollen grains. If pollination occurs within the same flower or between two flowers of the same plant, it is called self-pollination; if it occurs between two flowers of separate plants, it is called cross pollination, which ensures more genetic variability in coming generations.

| Table 9.1: Adaptations in insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers |  |  |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Feature | Insect Pollinated Flowers | Wind Pollinated Flowers |
| Size | Generally large | Generally small |
| Colour | Petals brightly coloured | Petals green or dull in colour |
| Nectar | Produce nectar | Do not produce nectar |
| Floral arrangement | Flowers face upwards | Flowers hang down for easy shaking |
| Stamens and stigmas | Enclosed inside ring of petals | Hang out of ring of petals |
| Pollen grains | Small number produced, heavy and sticky | Large number produced, light with smooth surface |
| Stigma | Pinhead shaped with no branches | Feathery branches for catching pollen |

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Sometimes pesticides are used to control the attack of insect pests on crops. Although pesticides are quite effective at preventing loss from insect pests, farmers sometimes still get a lower yield than normal. Why is this so?
</SideActivity>

## Development of Male Gametophyte

After pollination, the microspores (pollen grains) germinate on the surface of the stigma to produce a male gametophyte. In this process, the microspore nucleus first divides by mitosis to form two nuclei, the tube nucleus and the generative nucleus, which divides further to form two sperm nuclei. The tube nucleus controls the formation of the pollen tube, which passes down through the style and ultimately penetrates the ovule. This whole structure, comprising the microspore body, pollen tube, tube nucleus, and the two sperm nuclei, is referred to as the male gametophyte.

## Development of Female Gametophyte

Meanwhile, the nucleus of the functional megaspore at the centre of the ovule divides three times by mitosis to make 8 nuclei. Three of these eight nuclei migrate to one end of the ovule; the central one becomes the egg, and the two flanking it are called synergids. Three other nuclei migrate to the other end of the ovule, and act as antipodals. The remaining two daughter nuclei rest at the centre of the ovule and are called polar nuclei, which in some cases fuse together to become a diploid secondary nucleus before the sperm enters. This whole structure, comprising the body of the megaspore, three antipodals, two synergids, two polar nuclei (or the secondary nucleus), and an egg, is referred to as the female gametophyte, or embryo sac.

## Fertilization and the Formation of Zygote and Endosperm Nucleus

When the pollen tube penetrates the ovule, one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote, and the other sperm nucleus fuses with the polar nuclei (or secondary nucleus) to make a triploid endosperm nucleus. Since one male gametophyte contributes two sperm nuclei for fertilization, this event is called double fertilization. It is assumed that the rest of the nuclei in the embryo sac, such as the synergids and antipodals, control the process of fertilization.

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Why is fertilization in angiosperms called double fertilization?
</SideActivity>

## Seed and Fruit Formation

After fertilization, the ovule is transformed into a seed, so it is defined as a "ripened ovule", while the surrounding wall of the ovary is transformed into fruit, so it is defined as a "ripened ovary".

<CaptionedImage src="kg28dw8vvmpyrc91n98fzwbeys88x9nr" alt="Diagram showing an ovule ripening into a seed and the ovary wall ripening into fruit." caption="Fig. 9.15: Seed and fruit formation." />

## Structure of Seed

Angiosperm seeds are made up of three important parts:

1. **Embryo**: This part comes from the union of male and female cells (zygote): a baby plant that's not yet fully grown.
2. **Endosperm**: A storage space for food, formed from a special cell inside the seed.
3. **Seed Coat**: The seed's protective jacket, developing from the outer layer that used to wrap around the seed when it was part of the plant.

The seed coat can be thin like paper (as in peanuts) or thick and tough (as in coconuts). It keeps the baby plant safe from harm and stops it from drying out. There's a mark on the seed coat called the hilum, where the seed used to be connected to the plant. Nearby is the micropyle, a small opening the seed uses to take in water.

Inside the seed, the embryo is an immature plant, consisting of a radicle, a plumule, and one or two cotyledons (seed leaves). The radicle of the embryo grows into the new root, while the plumule grows into the new shoot upon germination; radicle and plumule are therefore called the embryonic root and embryonic stem respectively. The embryonic stem above the point of attachment of the cotyledon(s) is called the epicotyl; the embryonic stem below that point is the hypocotyl. Within the seed there is a store of nutrients for the growing seedling; in angiosperms, this stored food is derived from the endosperm tissue, rich in oil or starch and protein. In many seeds, the food of the endosperm is absorbed and stored by the cotyledons.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2cktfw0mfht752t32vb3ebb188w99x" alt="Diagram of seed structure showing embryo, endosperm, and seed coat." caption="Fig. 9.16: Structure of a seed." />

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Why are angiosperms called closed-seeded plants?
</SideActivity>

<SideActivity title="Science Tidbit">
Based on the number of cotyledons and some other features, angiosperms are classified into two classes: monocots and dicots.
</SideActivity>

## Seed Germination

For seeds to start growing, they need to be in the right place at the right time; this process is called seed germination, the start of a plant's life. The seed absorbs water, which makes it swell and breaks open the seed coat. First, a root pops out from the radicle; this root grows quickly and starts taking in water and nutrients from the soil. Then a tiny shoot called the plumule begins to grow, stretching up and out of the soil. There are two main ways seeds can start growing:

<SideActivity title="STEAM Activity 9.1">
Take a few seeds of commonly growing plants in your vicinity, plant them together in a pot, and observe the germination process day by day, picking one germinating seed to examine every day.
</SideActivity>

## Epigeal Germination

In this type, the hypocotyl stretches out and forms a hook, pulling the seed leaves (cotyledons) above the ground. Beans, cotton, and papaya are examples of seeds that germinate this way.

## Hypogeal Germination

Here, it's the epicotyl that stretches and forms a hook, but the seed leaves (cotyledons) stay underground. Peas, maize, and coconuts are examples of seeds that germinate this way.

## Conditions for Seed Germination

For seeds to start growing, they need the right conditions, both inside and outside. Inside, the seed must have a living baby plant (embryo) and enough stored food.

Outside, there are three key conditions:

1. **Water (Moisture)**: Most seeds have very little water inside them; they can't start growing until they soak up water from the environment, which is used to break down stored food and help the baby plant's parts grow.
2. **Oxygen**: Just as we need oxygen to breathe, the cells in the baby plant need it too, to carry out their functions.
3. **Temperature**: Different seeds prefer different temperatures to start growing; for most plants, the best temperature is between 25-30°C.

<CaptionedImage src="kg21dh8v94jjbt3mdw5fr6j4r98dmh65" alt="Diagram of conditions needed for seed germination: water, oxygen, and temperature." caption="the two main types of seed germination: Epigeal and Hypogeal." />

When a seed gets these conditions right, it's like a green light for the baby plant to begin its journey.

<SideActivity title="Lab Activity: Flower Encounters - Secrets of Plant Reproduction">
Investigate the structure of flowers and gain insights into the reproductive mechanisms of plants.

**Materials:** Assorted flowers (various species), scalpels or small knives, disposable gloves, magnifying glasses, petri dishes or small trays, notebooks and pens, camera or smartphones for documentation.

**Procedure:**

1. Begin by discussing the significance of flowers in plant reproduction and the different parts of a typical flower (petals, sepals, stamens, pistil).
2. Distribute various types of flowers to students, ensuring a diverse selection.
3. Provide disposable gloves and scalpels or small knives for flower dissection, emphasizing safety precautions during handling of cutting tools.
4. Instruct students to carefully dissect the flowers, identifying and observing each part, focusing on the arrangement of reproductive structures within the pistil and stamens.
5. Encourage students to use magnifying glasses or take photos for closer examination, sketch the dissected flowers in their notebooks, and paste the floral parts on a hard chart to make herbarium sheets.

Ask students to identify specific adaptations related to attracting pollinators and achieving successful fertilization, compare their findings, and discuss similarities and differences in flower anatomy. Discuss observed variations in flower structure among different species and how these variations contribute to successful pollination, linking observed structures to the process of seed and fruit formation. Discuss the relation between overuse of insecticide by farmers and insect pollinators in plant reproduction. Conclude by reinforcing the role of flowers as essential components of the plant life cycle.
</SideActivity>

mdxBody:
## Variation

The term variation refers to the differences in traits displayed by members of the same species. For instance, although all domestic cats are members of the same species, they differ greatly in terms of size, coat colour, eye colour, hair length, and other characteristics. Variations are beneficial for living organisms, as they help increase the chances of survival of the particular organisms; these are desirable variations, as they help organisms be more advanced and resilient. Variations can sometimes lead to a genetic defect, becoming a harmful, undesirable variation.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2fcpwb1mwe4pvn8y6skv1x798dpvmq" alt="Photographs showing variation in size, coat colour, and hair length among domestic cats." caption="Figure 10.1: Variations in domestic cats" />

Meiosis, along with other factors, serves as a main source of variation. These are:

1. Genetic recombination, resulting from crossing over during gamete development.
2. Different chromosome combinations in gametes, formed by independent assortment of chromosomes.
3. The process of fertilization, in which one of countless sperm fuses with an egg.
4. Mutation in the gamete-forming germ cells.
5. Gene flow, the transfer of genes from one population of a species to another.
## Evolution

According to scientists, the Earth is more than four billion years old. New life forms developed from unicellular organisms; all current living things developed gradually from earlier ones. Evolution is the gradual alteration of a population's or species' traits over time in response to environmental conditions. Evolutionary changes can always be passed on to the next generation.

## How Variation Promotes Evolution

Some individuals of a population may have an advantage over other members as a result of population variations. These individuals will be able to have more offspring; consequently, the population will gradually see more instances of that specific variant. With these variations, they will have a better chance of surviving and reproducing. That's evolution.

An inherited trait or group of traits that increases an organism's chances of survival in specific environmental conditions is known as an adaptation. Members of a species' population compete with one another for resources. Only the healthiest, fittest, and strongest will survive and reproduce; if food or water is in short supply, there is little room for sharing, and there aren't many available partners.

## Theory of Natural Selection

Natural selection is the process through which organisms that possess traits helpful for reproduction in a certain environment produce more offspring in the following generation, gradually expanding those traits' presence in the population's genetic diversity. Natural selection theory is based on:

1. **Overproduction:** All living creatures are very fertile, so their populations could grow quickly to produce a large number of offspring.
2. **Competition:** Population sizes do not rise to very high levels even after overproduction; numbers largely stay constant because food supplies and other resources are scarce, so there is competition for resources and food.
3. **Variations:** No two organisms are the same; they will not have the same opportunities to survive and reproduce as others. A large portion of this diversity is heritable, inherited from parents through the genes of the offspring.
4. **Natural selection:** Only organisms that live and reproduce can give rise to the next generation, and only organisms with desirable variations will live to reproductive age. The population will have more advantageous genetic variations and fewer harmful ones after many generations. Natural selection is essentially an elimination process: only the fittest organisms will survive.

After a five-year voyage around the world on the ship HMS Beagle, Charles Darwin put forth the Theory of Natural Selection in 1838. In 1859, he released a book titled "On the Origin of Species by Natural Selection", recording his observations.

Darwin was able to develop his theory of natural selection partly from his observations on the Galapagos Islands, where he found a number of finch species that varied from island to island; the form of the birds' beaks varied depending on the kind of food they ate. Darwin believed the processes of speciation and adaptation were linked: the overall accumulation of adaptations in different environments, isolated from the original environment by geographic barriers, would lead to the formation of a new species from an ancestral form, as the two groups differ sufficiently over many generations to be classified as two different species. Darwin identified three basic patterns in biological diversity: (1) global, (2) local, and (3) variation over time in species.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2c6v6gpbjak94y7c32z3dny58dnv8h" alt="Diagram showing Darwin's finches with differently shaped beaks adapted to different food sources." caption="Fig 10.2. Darwin's observation of finches at Galapagos islands, showing beak variation across the Galapagos Islands." />

Natural selection causes population-wide changes in gene frequencies over time: individuals with more advantageous traits become more prevalent in the population, and individuals with less advantageous traits become less prevalent.
## Industrial Melanism: A Case Study in Natural Selection

In Britain, the industrial melanism of the peppered moth (Biston betularia) is a strong indicator of natural selection.

<SideActivity title="Case Study: Variation and Natural Selection">
The phrase "changes in the environment can bring about changes in a population by natural selection" is supported by evidence.

All reported variants of the peppered moth in the UK up until 1848 had light colours with dark patches. A dark-coloured moth was discovered in 1848, and by 1895, dark-coloured moths made up 95% of the peppered moth population. This variety's dark colour resulted from a mutation.

The moths fly at night and rest on tree trunks throughout the day. Light-coloured lichens growing on the tree trunks blended in with the colour of the light-coloured moth, giving it excellent concealment from predator birds. As the industrial revolution progressed, sulphur dioxide pollution from coal burning killed off the lichens growing on trees in industrial locations, exposing the darker bark underneath.

Predator birds could now easily locate and consume the light-coloured moths resting on dark-coloured trunks; the dark colour became the adaptive variant that resulted in a selection advantage. 90% of the peppered moth population in England during the industrial era of pollution was black; this specific phenomenon is called "industrial melanism". After the 1950s, England's industrial pollution was reduced, and the number of light-coloured moths increased again.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2dsvdcmr81a4b949xx7791y98e9bg5" alt="Photograph comparing light-coloured and dark-coloured peppered moths on light and dark tree bark." caption="Fig. 10.3 (a) The light and dark coloured forms of the peppered moth are resting on a lichen-covered tree. (b) The light and dark coloured forms of the peppered moth are resting on a lichen free tree trunk, which was darkened by industrial air pollution." />

**Analysis:** (1) The variation (change in bark colour matching) is an illustration of variation subject to selection (by birds) in a changing environment. (2) It demonstrates the reality of evolution. (3) It shows that evolution and natural selection operate on the basis of genetic change within a population.
</SideActivity>

title: 10.1 Variation and Evolution

mdxBody:
The evidence for evolution is compelling and extensive. Looking at every level of organization in living systems, biologists see the signature of past and present evolution.

## Evidence from Palaeontology

In addition to offering strong evidence that ancient species were distinct from modern ones, fossils also show the evolution of organisms across time. To determine how long ago an organism lived in relation to another, scientists classify and age fossils from all around the world. The resulting fossil record shows the evolution of form over millions of years and tells the tale of the past. For example, researchers have found extremely comprehensive records demonstrating how humans and horses have evolved.

<CaptionedImage src="kg22y2xsy8fkzpsxga7ykarr7x8dm8bj" alt="Biological diagram" caption="Figure 10.4: Evolution of modern horse" />
## Evidence from Comparative Anatomy

The existence of structures in creatures with the same fundamental shape is another type of evidence supporting evolution. For example, due to their origin in the appendages of a common ancestor, the bones in the limbs of a human, dog, bird, and whale all share the same general structure. The shapes and sizes of these bones have evolved over time in different animals, but their general structure has remained the same. These similar parts are known as homologous structures.

<CaptionedImage src="kg272ccda90gp1vq43h0hc2tp18dnpe5" alt="Biological diagram" caption="Fig 10.5: Homologous structure of bones of limbs of mammals" />

Some organisms possess such organs that don't appear to have any function at all now and are likely just the remains from a previous common ancestor. Vestigial organs are these inactive, non-functional structures that have lost their use over time. Wings on flightless birds, leaves on some cacti, and appendix in humans are a few examples of vestigial organs
## Evidence from Selective Breeding

Artificial selection is the practice of breeding domesticated and genetically enhanced plants and animals to produce offspring with desired genetic features. Selective breeding is the current name for artificial selection. Selective breeding and hybridization are the two techniques used to develop desired features in plants and animals.

## Improving Plants by Selection

Farmers have been using selection to create plants with desired features for ages. They frequently choose varieties that will cause the plants to grow larger, more quickly, be drought-resistant, etc.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2482fkrpm0g3atbkzapkzypd8dntrw" alt="Biological diagram" caption="Figure 10.6 Improving Plants by selection" />

| Artificial selection produces crops with higher yields |  |  |  |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Natural variation occurs in the wild population. | 2. Seeds for the next generation are chosen only from individuals with the most desirable traits. | 3. Repeat this process for several generations. | 4. Over time, the yield of the crop increases. |
## Improving Animals by Selection

Animals have also been the subjected to selection. Cows that generate a lot of milk and high-quality meat are chosen for selective breeding. They serve as parents for the following generation. In this manner, a breed of cow that can produce more milk than the original breed is created.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2bb2gykmp1nca9a217tgk2d58dmr3b" alt="Biological diagram" caption="Fig. 10.7 : Dog breeds produced from wolf by artificial selection" />

| Table 10.1. Comparing Natural Selection and Artificial Selection |  |
| :--- | :--- |
| Natural Selection | Artificial selection |
| Selection occurs when natural environmental condition changes. | It is selected by man. |
| Varieties are produced by mutations. | Varieties are produced by selective breeding. |
| It operates in natural population. | It operates in domesticated population. |
| It is a slow process and takes thousand to millions of years. | It is a fast process and results are immediate (in the next generation). |
| It is responsible for the great biological diversity. | It is responsible for new varieties different from starting generation. |

title: 10.2 Evidences of Evolution

mdxBody:
The evolutionary process by which new biological species arise is called speciation. Two groups that originate from the same ancestor can become very different over time if they live in different places. When a species gets split into two geographical regions, the process of speciation starts. Each adapts to its own environmental conditions. After a while, individuals from one group can no longer reproduce with the other group. Ultimately, two new species have evolved from one.

topicTitle: 1.1 Definition of Chemistry and Its Interaction with Other Matter and Energy:
mdxBody:
Chemistry is defined as the science that investigates the materials of the universe and the changes that these materials undergo. Chemistry deals with the composition, structure, properties, behavior, and changes of matter and energy. Understanding the fundamental concepts of chemistry help to explain natural phenomena and apply them to the formation of new substances, drugs, and technologies.

DO YOU KNOW?

- How green chemistry is helpful in understanding and reducing pollution?
- Green chemistry is the model of chemical products and processes that reduce the use of hazardous substances.
title: 1.1 Definition of Chemistry and Its Interaction with Other Matter and Energy:

mdxBody:
Chemistry is a diverse field of study, surrounding numerous sub-fields and interdisciplinary areas.

1. Organic Chemistry
Organic chemistry is a branch of chemistry that deals with substances containing carbon (except carbonates, bicarbonates, oxides, and carbides).
2. Inorganic Chemistry
Inorganic chemistry is a branch of chemistry that deals with elements and their compounds except organic compounds.
3. Physical Chemistry
Physical chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with laws and theories to understand the structure and changes of matter.
4. Analytical Chemistry
Analytical chemistry is a branch of chemistry that deals with the methods and instruments for determining the composition and properties of matter.
5. Biochemistry
The branch of chemistry that deals with physical and chemical changes that occur in living organisms is called biochemistry.
6. Environmental Chemistry
Environmental chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the study of chemical and toxic substances that pollute the environment and their adverse effects on human beings.

7. Industrial Chemistry
Industrial chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the large-scale production of chemical substances.
8. Medicinal Chemistry
The branch of chemistry that deals with the study of the interaction between drugs and biological targets, as well as the development of new medicinal agents.
9. Polymer Chemistry
The branch of chemistry that focuses on the study of polymers, their types, properties, uses, importance, and types of polymerizations is called polymer chemistry. Examples of synthetic polymers include nylon bearings, plastic bags, polyethylene cups, polyester, Teflon coated cook ware, and epoxy glue etc.
10. Geochemistry
Geochemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the study of chemical composition, distribution, and transformation of elements and compounds in the Earth's crust, such as rocks, minerals, soils, water, and the atmosphere.
11. Nuclear Chemistry
The branch of chemistry that deals with the changes that occur in atomic nuclei is called nuclear chemistry.
12. Astrochemistry
Astrochemistry is a branch of chemistry that deals with the study of chemical processes and reactions that occur in astronomical environments, such as stars, planets, comets, and interstellar space.
title: 1.2 Branches of Chemistry

topicTitle: 1.3 Examples of Essential Questions That Are Important for the Branches of Chemistry
mdxBody:
Some essential questions for various branches of chemistry that can help enhance understanding are as follows:
Physical Chemistry

1. What is the structure of an atom, and how does it influence chemical behavior?
2. How do different types of chemical bonds (ionic, covalent, metallic) form and function?

Organic Chemistry

1. Why carbon is considered the backbone of organic compounds?
2. What are the major functional groups in organic molecules, and how do they affect chemical properties?

Inorganic Chemistry

1. What distinguishes inorganic compounds from organic compounds?
2. How does Periodic table helps to organise elements?

Analytical Chemistry

1. How are analytical methods used to identify and quantify chemical substances?

Biochemistry

1. How do biomolecules such as carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids contribute to the structure and function of living organisms?

Environmental Chemistry

1. How do human activities contribute to air pollution, and what are the consequences for the environment?
2. What role do greenhouse gases play in climate change, and how can we mitigate their effects?

Medicinal Chemistry

1. How are drugs designed and developed for specific therapeutic purposes?

Polymer Chemistry

1. What are polymers, and how do their structures affect their properties?

Geochemistry

1. How do geological processes influence the distribution of elements in the Earth's crust?

Nuclear Chemistry

1. How do nuclear reactions differ from chemical reactions, and what are their applications?
2. What is the role of radioisotopes in medicine and industry?

Astronomy

1. What types of reactions occur in astronomical environments?

These questions can serve as a foundation for exploring the key concepts within each branch of chemistry.
title: 1.3 Examples of Essential Questions That Are Important for the Branches of Chemistry

mdxBody:
Organic Chemistry
To treat diseases, organic chemists synthesize new medicines that interact with specific targets like proteins or enzymes.
<CaptionedImage src="kg2cx20zbx4j984qdmb9dqekms8dncdf" alt="" caption="Pharmaceutical capsules — everyday application of chemistry in medicine" />

## Inorganic Chemistry

Lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries are used as rechargeable batteries for electronics, toys, wireless headphones, handheld power tools, small and large appliances, electrical storage devices, and electric vehicles.

Physical chemistry is a part of our everyday life. The batteries in our vehicles are built on the principle of electrochemistry.
