mdxBody:
Laws of logarithms are closely related to the laws of exponents, since logarithms in nature, are exponents. The laws of exponents are given in unit 1. In this section the laws of exponents are used to develop some laws of logarithms, for solving complicated equations involving exponents and logarithms. Also the complicated questions of multiplication, division and root extraction are converted to handy sums of addition and subtraction.
2.4.1 Product Law of Logarithms
For any real numbers $\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{n}$ and b where $\mathrm{b} \neq 1, \log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{mn}=\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{m}+\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{n}$
Proof: Let $\quad \log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{m}=x$ $\_\_\_\_$ (i) and $\quad \log _{b} \mathrm{n}=y$ $\_\_\_\_$ (ii)
Their respective exponential equations are

$$
\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{b}^{x}
$$

$\_\_\_\_$ (iii) and $\mathrm{n}=\mathrm{b}^{\mathrm{y}}$ $\_\_\_\_$ (iv)
Now product of equations (iii) and (iv) is

$$
\begin{array}{rlr}
\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{n} & =\mathrm{b}^{x} \cdot \mathrm{~b}^{y} & \\
\mathrm{mn} & =\mathrm{b}^{x+y} & \leftarrow \text { using product rule of exponents } \\
\Rightarrow \log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{mn} & =x+y & \leftarrow \text { logarithmic form of above equation }
\end{array}
$$

or

$$
\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{mn}=\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~m}+\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{n} \quad \leftarrow \text { substituting the values of } x \text { and } y
$$

The Product law of logarithms states that:
Logarithm of a product of two (or more) numbers is equal to the sum of their logarithms, provided that all logarithms are defined.

Example 13 (a): Use the product rule to expand $\log _{e}\left(x^{2} y^{3} z\right)$.
Solution $\log _{e}\left(x^{2} y^{3} z\right)=\log _{e} x^{2}+\log _{e} y^{3}+\log _{e} z$
(b) Use product rule to combine $\ln \mathrm{a}+\ln \sqrt{b}+\ln \mathrm{c}^{3}$ in a single logarithmic term.
Solution $\ln \mathrm{a}+\ln \sqrt{b}+\ln \mathrm{c}^{3}=\ln \left(\mathrm{a} \sqrt{b} \mathrm{c}^{3}\right)$
2.4.2 The Quotient Law of Logarithm
For any positive numbers $\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{n}$ and b , where $\mathrm{b} \neq 1$.

$$
\log _{\mathrm{b}} \frac{m}{n}=\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~m}-\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{n}
$$

Proof: Let $\quad \log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{m}=x$ $\_\_\_\_$ (i) and $\log _{b} n=y$ (ii)
Respective exponential forms of above equations are

$$
\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{b}^{x}
$$

(iii) and $\mathrm{n}=\mathrm{b}^{y}$ (iv)
Dividing (iii) by (iv) i.e. $\frac{m}{n}=\frac{b^{x}}{b^{y}}$

$$
\begin{gathered}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{m}{n} & =\mathrm{b}^{x-y} \leftarrow \text { quotient rule of exponents with same base } \\
\Rightarrow \log _{\mathrm{b}} \frac{m}{n} & =x-y \leftarrow \text { conversion to logarithmic form } \\
\log _{\mathrm{b}} \frac{m}{n} & =\log _{\mathrm{b}} m-\log _{\mathrm{b}} n \quad \leftarrow \text { Substituting the value of } x \text { and } y
\end{aligned}
\end{gathered}
$$

The Quotient law of logarithms states that:
Logarithms of quotient of two numbers is equal to the difference of their logarithms provided that all the logarithms are defined.

Example 14 (a): Use quotient law of logarithms to expand log $\frac{13}{7 b}$.
(b) Use quotient law of logarithms to combine $\log 39-\log \mathrm{t}-\log \mathrm{b}$ into single logarithmic term.
Solution (a): $\quad \log \frac{13}{7 b}=\log 13-(\log 7+\log b)=\log 13-\log 7-\log b$
Solution (b): $\log 39-\log t-\log b=\log 39-(\log t+\log b)=\log 39-\log t b=\log \frac{39}{t b}$
Key Fact
$\log (50-5) \neq \log 50-\log 5$
2.4.3 The Power Law of Logarithm
For any real number $\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{n}$ and b , where $\mathrm{m}>0, \mathrm{~b}>0, \mathrm{~b} \neq 1, \log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{m}^{\prime \prime}=\mathrm{n} \log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{m}$
Proof: Let $\quad \log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{m}=x$
Converting into exponential equation i.e $\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{b}^{\mathrm{x}}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m^{n}=\left(b^{x}\right)^{n} \\
& \text { or } \quad m^{n}=b^{n x} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \log _{b} m^{n}=n x \\
& \log _{b} m=n \log _{b} m
\end{aligned}
$$

← taking $\mathrm{n}^{\text {th }}$ power on both sides.

- using power of power rule .
← converting into logarithmic form .
← substituting the value of $x$.
The Power Law of logarithms states that:
Logarithm of power of a number is equal to the power times the logarithm of the number. provided that all logarithms are defined.

Example 15(a): Use power law of logarithms to expand $\log _{2} 100^{-3}$
Solution: $\quad \log _{2} 100^{-3}=-3 \log _{2} 100$
(b) Use power law of logarithms to combine $-\frac{4}{3} \log _{\sqrt{3}} 7$
Solution: $\quad-\frac{4}{3} \log _{\sqrt{3}} 7=\log _{\sqrt{3}} 7^{-\frac{4}{3}}$
2.4.4 Change of Base Law of Logarithms
Although only common logarithms and natural logarithm are programmed into a calculator still the logarithms for other positive real bases can be found by changing that base into some frequently used base that is 'e' or '10'. The law which enables us to change the base is called change of base law which is given below.
If $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}$ and m are positive real numbers and, $\mathrm{a} \neq 1, \mathrm{~b} \neq 1$, then

$$
\log _{a} m=\log _{b} m \cdot \log _{a} b
$$

Proof: Let $\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{m}=x$

$$
\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{m}=\mathrm{b}^{x} \quad \leftarrow \text { converting above equation into exponential equation. }
$$

$\log _{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{m}=\log _{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{b}^{x} \leftarrow$ taking $\log$ on both sides with base ' a '.
$\log _{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{m}=x . \log _{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{b} \leftarrow$ applying power law of logarithm.

$$
\log _{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{~m}=\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~m} \cdot \log _{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{~b} \quad \text { or } \quad \log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~m}=\frac{\log _{\mathrm{a}} m}{\log _{\mathrm{a}} b}
$$

Example 16: Convert the base of $\log _{b} 536$ into 10 .

Solution: $\log _{b} 536=\frac{\log _{10} 536}{\log _{10} b}$ or $\frac{\log 536}{\log b}$

Key Fact
The change of base law and the quotient law of logarithms are often confused. Remember the difference between $\log _{b}\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)$ and $\frac{\log _{a} m}{\log _{a} n}$. These two expressions look alike, however they are totally different.
Example 17(a): Use laws of logarithms to expand $\log \frac{5 p^{2} q^{\frac{1}{2}}}{4 \sqrt{s t^{3}}}$.
Solution: $\log \frac{5 p^{2} q^{\frac{1}{2}}}{4 \sqrt{s t^{3}}}=\log \left(5 p^{2} q^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)-\log \left(4 \sqrt{s} t^{3}\right) \quad \leftarrow$ using quotient law of $\log$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\log 5+\log p^{2}+\log q^{\frac{1}{2}}-\left[\log 4+\log \sqrt{s}+\log t^{3}\right] \leftarrow \text { using product } \operatorname{law} \text { of } \log \\
& =\log 5+2 \log p+\frac{1}{2} \log q-\log 4-\frac{1}{2} \log s-3 \log t \quad \leftarrow \text { using power law of } \log
\end{aligned}
$$

(b) Use laws of logarithms to evaluate
(i) $\log _{2} 5 \sqrt{3}$
(ii) $\log _{2}\left(\log _{2} 8^{2}-\log _{\sqrt{3}} 27+\log _{\sqrt{10}} 10\right)$

Solution: (i) $\log _{2} 5 \sqrt{3}=\frac{\log _{10} 5 \sqrt{3}}{\log _{10} 2} \leftarrow$ change of base law

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{\left[\log 5+\log 3^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]}{\log 2}=\left(\log 5+\frac{1}{2} \log 3\right)+\log 2 \\
& =\left[0.6990+\frac{1}{2}(0.4771)\right] \div(0.3010) \\
& =\frac{0.9376}{3.010}=3.1148
\end{aligned}
$$

(ii) Evaluate $\log _{2}\left(\log _{2} 8^{2}-\log _{\sqrt{3}} 27+\log _{\sqrt{10}} 10\right)$

$$
\log _{2}\left(\log _{2} 8^{2}-\log _{\sqrt{3}} 27+\log _{\sqrt{10}} 10\right)
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\log _{2}\left(\log _{2}\left(2^{3}\right)^{2}-\log _{\sqrt{3}}\left((\sqrt{3})^{2}\right)^{3}+\log _{\sqrt{10}}(\sqrt{10})^{2}\right) \\
& =\log _{2}\left(\log _{2} 2^{6}-\log _{\sqrt{3}}(\sqrt{3})^{6}+\log _{\sqrt{10}}(\sqrt{10})^{2}\right) \\
& =\log _{2}\left(6 \log _{2} 2-6 \log _{\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{3}+2 \log _{\sqrt{10}} \sqrt{10}\right) \\
& =\log _{2}(6-6+2) \quad\left(\because \log _{b} b^{x}=x\right) \\
& =\log _{2} 2=1 \quad\left(\because \log _{b} b=1\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

c. If $\log _{\mathrm{b}} 2=0.3010, \log _{\mathrm{b}} 3=0.4771$ and $\log _{b} 5=0.6990$, then evaluate $\log _{\mathrm{b}} 0.0036$, applying laws of logarithms.

Solution: $\log _{\mathrm{b}} 0.0036=\log _{\mathrm{b}}\left(\frac{36}{10000}\right)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\log _{b}\left(\frac{2^{2} \times 3^{2}}{2^{4} \times 5^{4}}\right) \\
& =\log _{b}\left(\frac{3^{2}}{2^{2} \times 5^{4}}\right) \\
& =2 \log _{b} 3-2 \log _{b} 2-4 \log _{b} 5 \\
& =2(0.4771)-2(0.3010)-4(0.6990) \\
& =-2.4438
\end{aligned}
$$

(which is negative number having both characteristic and mantissa as negative.)
Since mantissa can never be negative, to make the mantissa positive check the next positive integer to the magnitude of the answer. The next integer is ' +3 ' as shown on the number line
<CaptionedImage src="kg2edvqdbvhsg6szpwa1eqqszd8e7yxq" alt="A number line marking the position of the logarithmic value 2.4438 between 2 and 3." caption="A number line marking the position of the logarithmic value 2.4438 between 2 and 3." />

Now 'add 3 to' and 'subtract 3 from' the answer
i.e. $\log _{b} 0.0036=-2.4438+3-3=0.5562-3$.
The positive term is mantissa and negative term is characteristic.
So, $\log _{b} 0.0036=\overline{3} .5562$
Important results deduced from Laws of Logarithms
(i) $\log _{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{a} \times \log _{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{b}=1$
(ii) $\log _{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{a}=\frac{1}{\log _{\mathrm{a}} c}$
(iii) $\log _{b} a \cdot \log _{c} b=\log _{c} a$
(iv) $\log _{\mathrm{s}} \mathrm{r}^{\mathrm{t}} \times \log _{\mathrm{t}} \mathrm{s}^{\mathrm{t}} \times \log _{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{t}}=r s t$
(v) $\log _{x} z \times \log _{y} x \times \frac{1}{\log _{y} z}=1$.
(vi) $\log _{b}$
a. $\log _{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{b} \times \log _{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{c}=1$

1. Use laws of logarithms to expand the followings.
(I) $\log 9$ t
(ii) $\log \frac{59}{s}$
(iii) $\log \frac{\left(5 p q^{2}\right)}{\left(x y^{3}\right)}$
(iv) $\log \sqrt{\frac{53.3}{46.4}}$
(v) $\log \left(\frac{5^{2} \mathrm{t}^{5} \mathrm{a}^{\frac{1}{3}}}{\sqrt[3]{4.4 t \mathrm{~b}^{3}}}\right)$
(vi) $\log \sqrt[5]{\frac{7^{2} t^{3} p}{d^{6} b^{2}}}$
(vii) $\log \left(\frac{\sqrt[3]{5.512} \mathrm{pm}^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\sqrt[4]{5.91} \mathrm{a}^{2} \mathrm{~b}}\right)^{\prime}$
2. Use laws of logarithms to combine the followings into single logarithmic terms.

(i) $3 \log x-5 \log y$
(ii) $\frac{1}{2} \log \mathrm{t}+\frac{1}{3} \log \mathrm{r}-\frac{1}{5} \log \mathrm{~s}$
(iii) $\frac{1}{7}[\log 57.7-3 \log 9.24+4 \log 36.6-2 \log 23.3]$
(iv) $5 \log 6-7 \log 9.42+\frac{1}{3} \log t-\frac{1}{2} \log 32.2+\frac{2}{3} \log a$
(v) $\frac{5}{4} \log 37.74-\frac{1}{4} \log 53.71+\frac{1}{4} \log 28.83$
3. Use laws of logarithms to evaluate the followings.
(i) $\log _{2} 15$
(ii) $\log _{9} \sqrt[3]{9}$
(iii) $\log _{3} 65$
(iv) $\log _{\sqrt{3}} 72.34$
(v) $\log _{\sqrt{7}} 343$
4. If $\log _{\mathrm{b}} 2=0.3010, \log _{\mathrm{b}} 3=0.4771, \log _{\mathrm{b}} 5=0.6990$ then evaluate the followings with laws of logarithms.
(i) $\log _{\mathrm{b}} \frac{6}{5}$
(ii) $\log _{b} \frac{100}{9}$
(iii) $\log _{b} \frac{\sqrt[3]{450}}{\sqrt{27}}$
(iv) $\log _{\mathrm{b}} 0.024$

Common logarithms appear in many scientific formulae.
Richter Scale
Opening of this unit depicts the 2005 earthquake in Pakistan, when thousands of people lost their lives. The Richter Scale used for measuring the magnitude (M) of earthquake is a logarithmic scale. If I is intensity of its shock waves and $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{o}}$ is a constant then
$\mathrm{M}=\log \left(\frac{I}{I_{0}}\right)$

Example 18: An earthquake that occurred in Pakistan in 2005, measured 7.6 on the Richter scale. In 1978, an earthquake in China measured 8.2 on the Richter scale. How many times, the China's carthquake was stronger than the Pakistan's earthquake.
Solution: Let $\mathrm{I}_{1}$ be the intensity of Pakistan's earthquake and $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ be the intensity of China's earthquake.
As, $\quad \mathrm{M}=\log \left(\frac{I}{I_{0}}\right)$
Then, $7.6=\log \left(\frac{I_{1}}{I_{0}}\right)=\log \mathrm{I}_{1}-\log \mathrm{I}_{0}$

$$
\begin{equation*}
8.2=\log \left(\frac{I_{2}}{I_{0}}\right)=\log \mathrm{I}_{2}-\log \mathrm{I}_{0} \tag{i}
\end{equation*}
$$

Subtracting (i) from (ii)

$$
\begin{gathered}
\log I_{2}-\log I_{1}=8.2-7.6 \\
\Rightarrow \quad \log \left(\frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}}\right)=0.6 \\
\text { antilog } \log \left(\frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}}\right)=\operatorname{antilog} 0.6 \\
+\quad \frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}}=3.98 \approx 4
\end{gathered}
$$

∴ China's earthquake is nearly 4 times stronger than Pakistan's earthquake.
Example 19: Use laws of logarithms to evaluate.

$$
\begin{equation*}
\text { (a) } \quad \frac{\sqrt[3]{8.59} \times(55.6)^{2}}{2.51 \times \sqrt{2.12}} \tag{b}
\end{equation*}
$$

$$
\sqrt[3]{5 \frac{1}{3}} \div \sqrt{\frac{22}{7}}
$$

Solution: (a) let $x=\frac{\sqrt[3]{8.59} \times(55.6)^{2}}{2.51 \times \sqrt{2.12}}$
Then, by taking common log on both sides.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log x & =\log \frac{\sqrt[3]{8.59} \times(55.6)^{2}}{2.51 \times \sqrt{2.12}} \\
& =\log (8.59)^{\frac{1}{3}}+\log (55.6)^{2}-\log (2.51)-\log (2.12)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
& =\frac{1}{3} \log 8.59+2 \log 55.6-\log 2.51-\frac{1}{2} \log (2.12) \\
& \approx \frac{1}{3}(0.9340)+2(1.7451)-(0.3997)-\frac{1}{2}(0.3263) \\
& \approx 0.3113+3.4902-0.3997-0.1632 \\
\log x & \approx 3.2386 \\
\log x & \approx \text { antilog } 3.2386 \leftarrow \text { Taking antilog on both sides } \\
x & \approx 1732.21
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\sqrt[3]{8.59} \times(55.6)^{2}}{2.51 \times \sqrt{2.12}} \approx 1732.21
$$

(b) let $x=\sqrt[3]{5 \frac{1}{3}} \div \sqrt{\frac{22}{7}}$
$\log x=\log \sqrt[3]{5 \frac{1}{3}} \div \sqrt{\frac{22}{7}} \quad \leftarrow$ Taking common $\log$ on both sides
$$
\log x=\log \left(\frac{16}{3}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}-\log \left(\frac{22}{7}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{3} \log \left(\frac{16}{3}\right)-\frac{1}{2} \log \left(\frac{22}{7}\right)
$$
$=\frac{1}{3}(\log 16-\log 3)-\frac{1}{2}(\log 22-\log 7)$
$$
\begin{align*}
& =\frac{1}{3} \log 16-\frac{1}{3} \log 3-\frac{1}{2} \log 22+\frac{1}{2} \log 7 \\
& \approx \frac{1}{3}(1.2041)-\frac{1}{3}(0.4771)-\frac{1}{2}(1.3424)+\frac{1}{2} \tag{0.8451}
\end{align*}
$$
Taking antilog on both sides.
antilog $\log x \approx$ antilog 1.9938
$$
x \approx 0.9858
$$
Example 20: Find the number of digits in $5^{50}$.
Solution:
By finding the log of the given whole number, we can find the relevant characteristic. But the number of digits in a whole number is always one more than the characteristic of the log of that number.
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Now } \log 5^{50} & =50 \log 5 \\
& =50 \times(.6990)=34.95
\end{aligned}
$$
Characteristic $=34$
Number of digits in $5^{50}=$ characteristic $+1=34+1=35$

mdxBody:
ALLAH - بحائ، وتعالى created this huge universe and a part of it is exposed to humans but a big part of it is still unknown to humans. It is estimated that there are 200 billions to 2 trillion galaxies in the observable universe. The adjoining figure shows a set of 10 naked eye galaxies.
Definition:
A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects.
The term well-defined, means that the objects follow a given discipline with which presence or absence of some object in the set is checked.
For instance, if we say that we have a collection of lighter stones, then this collection is not well defined. Instead of this, if we say that we have a collection of stones weighing less than 1kg, this collection is well defined.
A set may consist of objects of different types.
e.g. A set of luminous objects may contain a star, a moon, a tube light or a candle.
Similarly, a set of objects present in a library may include books, tables, chairs, newspapers, keys, locks, stock registers etc.
Example 1:

(a) A set of Prime numbers which are also even i.e. \{2\}
(b) A set of Pakistani currency i.e.
$$
\{5,10,20,50,100,500,1000,5000\}
$$
(c) A set of flowers in my garden. i.e. \{Pansy, Lilly, Daisy, Jasmine, Tulip, Rose, Hibiscus\}
(d) A set of Natural numbers less than 1 i.e.
(e) A set of all letters present in the word 'set' $\{\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{e}, \mathrm{t}\}$
(f) A set of Natural numbers among 3, -9, 2, 3, 4, 2 i.e. \{2, 3, 4\}.

The repeating elements are taken once only, since repetition is not allowed in a set.
Mathematics as a Study of Patterns, Structures and Relationships
In mathematics, patterns are more than a beautiful design. Patterns follow a predictable rule and that rule allows us to predict what will come next.
For example:
In the set of even numbers,

$$
\{2,4,6,8, \ldots\}
$$

a pattern exists and one can determine the next number(s) in the set.
If we want to relate the above pattern with some real situation, we can ask the following question to the students:
What will be the number of mangoes in next two boxes?
<CaptionedImage src="kg24gq88vks3w5bxy4p8pzbc2d8bv75s" alt="" caption="" />

Students can easily predict the number of mangoes in the next two boxes.
Obviously, they will say:

| Number of box | Number of mangoes |
| :--- | :--- |
| 5 | 10 |
| 6 | 12 |

In the same way, we can relate the set of square of natural numbers with structural geometry as:

$$
\left\{1^{2}, 2^{2}, 3^{2}, 4^{2}, \ldots\right\}=\{1,4,9,16, \ldots\}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg2evnndcs5hpxkm7xc52xff7s8btqfs" alt="" caption="" />

$$
1^{2}=1
$$

$$
2^{2}=4
$$

$$
3^{2}=9
$$

$$
4^{2}=16
$$

This example relates the patterns in numbers and geometry in the best way where the square numbers represent area of various geometrical shapes.

Key Fact
Mathematicians say that mathematics is the study of patterns in numbers and structure in geometry, and their relationships.

Check Point
Search number patterns in the set of first 100 natural numbers and relate patterns with some kind of geometrical shape or represent pattern in pictorial form.

Set Builder Form (Rule Method)
In set builder form, all the elements of a set are not listed, however we write the set by its defining rule. While writing a set in this method, some variable say $x$ is chosen which represents all the elements of that set according to the defining rule.

e.g. $\mathrm{A}=$ Set of all integers, can be written in set builder form as
$$
A=\{x \mid x \in Z\} \text { and read as }
$$
"A is the set of all elements $x$ such that $x$ belongs to Z"

Example 2: Write the following sets in the set builder form.

(i) $\mathrm{B}=$ Set of Prime numbers less than 17.
$$
\mathrm{B}=\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{P} \wedge x<17\} .
$$
(ii) $\mathrm{C}=$ Set of multiples of 4 greater than or equal to 40.
$$
C=\{4 x \mid x \in N \wedge x \geq 10\} .
$$

(iii) $\mathrm{D}=\{1,2,3,6\}$.
$D=\{x \mid x$ is a factor of 6$\}$.
(iv) $\mathrm{E}=$ Set of squares of $1^{\text {st }}$ three natural multiples of 10.
$\mathrm{E}=\left\{(10 x)^{2} \mid x \in \mathrm{~N} \wedge 1 \leq x \leq 3\right\}$.

Example 3:

(i) The set $\mathrm{G}=\{15 x \mid x \in \mathrm{Z} \wedge x \geq 1\}$, in descriptive form is written as
$\mathrm{G}=$ Set of integral multiples of 15 , greater than or equal to 15 .
(ii) The set $\mathrm{H}=\left\{y \mid y \in \mathrm{~W} \wedge y^{3}-1=7\right\}$, in tabular form is $\mathrm{H}=\{2\}$.
(iii) The set $\mathrm{I}=\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{~W} \wedge-3>x>-5\}$, in tabular form is $\mathrm{I}=\{ \}$.
(iv) The set $\mathrm{J}=\left\{\left.\frac{x}{2} \right\rvert\, x \in \mathrm{E} \wedge x>0\right\}$, in tabular form is $\mathrm{J}=\{1,2,3,4, \ldots\}$.
(v) The set $\mathrm{K}=\left\{y \mid y \in \mathrm{Z} \wedge y^{2}=9\right\}$, in descriptive method is
$\mathrm{K}=$ Set of negative integers containing ' $-3^{\prime}$ only.

Most Commonly used Sets of Numbers

i. $\mathrm{N}=$ Set of Natural numbers $=\{1,2,3,4, \ldots \ldots\}$
ii. $W=$ Set of Whole numbers $=\{0,1,2,3,4, \ldots \ldots\}$
iii. Z = Set of Integers
$$
=\{0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \ldots .\}
$$
iv. $\mathrm{E}=$ Set of Even numbers
$$
=\{0, \pm 2, \pm 4, \pm 6, \ldots .\}
$$

v. $\mathrm{O}=$ Set of Odd numbers
$$
=\{ \pm 1, \pm 3, \pm 5, \pm, \ldots\}
$$
vi. $\mathrm{P}=$ Set of Prime numbers
$$
=\{2,3,5,7,11,13, \ldots \ldots\}
$$
vii. $\mathrm{Q}=$ Set of Rational numbers $=\left\{\frac{\mathrm{p}}{\mathrm{q}} / p, q \in \mathrm{Z} \wedge q \neq 0\right\}$
viii. $Q^{\prime}=$ Set of Irrational numbers $=\left\{x / x \neq \frac{p}{q}, p, q \in Z \wedge q \neq 0\right\}$
ix. $\mathrm{R}=$ Set of Real numbers $=\left\{x / x \in Q \vee x \in Q^{\prime}\right\}$

The above mentioned sets from (i-vi) are first written in descriptive method and then in tabular form (Roster method).
However, the sets from (vii-ix) are first written in descriptive method then in set builder form.
Set Operations
Union of Sets
Let A and B be two given sets. Then union of A and B is the set of all those elements which are taken either from A or from B or from both.

The union of $A$ and $B$ is denoted by ' $A \cup B$ ' and:

$$
\mathrm{A} \cup \mathrm{~B}=\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{~A} \vee x \in \mathrm{~B}\}
$$

e.g. If $\mathrm{A}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ and $\mathrm{B}=\{3,4,1,7,6\}$, then:
$$
A \cup B=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}
$$

Intersection of Sets
Let A and B be given sets then the intersection of A and B is the set of elements which belong to both A and B.
The intersection of A and B is denoted by ' $\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B}$ ' and:

$$
\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{~B}=\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{~A} \wedge x \in \mathrm{~B}\}
$$

e.g. If $\mathrm{A}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ and $\mathrm{B}=\{3,4,1,7,6\}$, then:

$$
A \cap B=\{1,3,4\}
$$

Difference of Sets
Difference of two sets A and B, denoted by A - B is a collection of those elements of A which are not present in B . For the two sets A and B :

$$
\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{B}=\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{~A} \wedge x \notin \mathrm{~B}\}
$$

Let $\mathrm{A}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ and $\mathrm{B}=\{3,4,6,7,8\}$, then:

$$
A-B=\{1,2,3,4,5\}-\{3,4,6,7,8\}=\{1,2,5\}
$$

In general, $\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{B} \neq \mathrm{B}-\mathrm{A}$
Complement of a Set
Let $\mathrm{A} \subset \mathrm{U}$ (i.e. A is proper subset of the universal set). Then the set of all elements of U , which are not in A , is called complement of A .
Complement of A is denoted by $\mathrm{A}^{c}$ or $\mathrm{A}^{\prime}=\mathrm{U}-\mathrm{A}$ and is defined as:

$$
\{x \mid x \in U \wedge x \notin \mathrm{~A}\}
$$

e.g. If $\mathrm{U}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}, \mathrm{A}=\{2,4,6\}$, then:

$$
\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{c}}=U-\mathrm{A}=\{1,3,5,7\}
$$

Key Fact

- The common elements of A and B are written once.
- Two sets A and B are said to be disjoint, if $\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B}=\phi$
- The elements of A are never present in A ${ }^{\mathrm{C}}$ and vice versa.
- Two sets are said to be overlapping, if neither set is subset of the other and their intersection is non-empty.

Union and Intersection of Three Sets

Disjoint Sets
Two sets A and B are said to be disjoint if they have no common elements. i.e. A $\cap \mathrm{B}=\phi$.
For example,
$A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{4,5\}$ are disjoint sets as both sets have no common element. i.e.

$$
A \cap B=\{1,2,3\} \cap\{4,5\}=\varnothing
$$

Overlapping Sets
Two sets A and B are called overlapping if:

(i) There is at least one element common in both the sets.
(ii) Neither of the sets is a subset of other set.

For example, the sets

$$
\begin{aligned}
& A=\{2,3,5,7,9\} \text { and } B=\{0,3,5,8\} \text { are overlapping as } \\
& A \cap B=\{3,5\} \neq \phi \text { and } A \text { and } B \text { are not subsets of each other. }
\end{aligned}
$$

Key Fact
Venn diagrams are used to explain the whole set theory in a very simple way.

Subset
Set A is called subset of a set B if every element of set A is also an element of B.
For example, the set $\mathrm{A}=\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}\}$ is a subset of $\mathrm{B}=\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d}, \ldots\}$ as all elements of set A are also elements of set B.

We use brackets to separate two sets from the third one because these represent different sets. i.e. $(A \cup B) \cap C$ or $A \cup(B \cap C)$

## Veriffeation of Associative Laws Using Venn Diagram

We illustrate the concept with the help of following examples.
Associative Property of Union

$$
(A \cup B) \cup C=A \cup(B \cup C)
$$

Proof:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text { Let } & x \in(\mathrm{~A} \cup \mathrm{~B}) \cup \mathrm{C} \\
\Rightarrow & x \in(\mathrm{~A} \cup \mathrm{~B}) \text { or } x \in \mathrm{C} \\
\Rightarrow & (x \in \mathrm{~A} \text { or } x \in \mathrm{~B}) \text { or } x \in \mathrm{C} \\
\Rightarrow & x \in \mathrm{~A} \text { or }(x \in \mathrm{~B} \text { or } x \in \mathrm{C}) \\
\Rightarrow & x \in \mathrm{~A} \text { or } x \in(\mathrm{~B} \cup \mathrm{C}) \\
\Rightarrow & x \in \mathrm{~A} \cup(\mathrm{~B} \cup \mathrm{C}) \\
\Rightarrow & (\mathrm{A} \cup \mathrm{~B}) \cup \mathrm{C} \subseteq \mathrm{~A} \cup(\mathrm{~B} \cup \mathrm{C}) \tag{a}
\end{array}
$$

Similarly, we can prove that:

$$
\begin{equation*}
A \cup B \cup C) \subseteq(A \cup B) \cup C \tag{b}
\end{equation*}
$$

From (a) and (b), we have:

$$
(A \cup B) \cup C=A \cup(B \cup C)
$$

Example 8:

\text { If } U=\{1,2,3,4,5, \ldots, 15\}, \mathrm{A}=\{2,4,6,8,10\}, \mathrm{B}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\} \text { and }

$$
\mathrm{A} \cup(\mathrm{~B} \cup \mathrm{C})=\square
$$

From both the figures, it is observed that same region is shaded.

i.e. $(\mathrm{A} \cup \mathrm{B}) \cup \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{A} \cup(\mathrm{B} \cup \mathrm{C})$
∴ Associative property of Union is verified.

Associative Property of Intersection
$(A \cap B) \cap C=A \cap(B \cap C)$
Proof:
Let $\quad y \in(\mathrm{~A} \cap \mathrm{~B}) \cap \mathrm{C}$
$\Rightarrow y \in \mathrm{~A} \cap \mathrm{~B}$ and $y \in \mathrm{C}$
$\Rightarrow \quad(y \in \mathrm{~A}$ and $y \in \mathrm{~B})$ and $y \in \mathrm{C}$
$\Rightarrow \quad y \in \mathrm{~A}$ and $(y \in \mathrm{~B}$ and $y \in \mathrm{C})$
$\Rightarrow y \in A$ and $y \in(B \cap C)$
$\Rightarrow \quad y \in \mathrm{~A} \cap(\mathrm{~B} \cap \mathrm{C})$
$\Rightarrow \quad(A \cap B) \cap C \subseteq A \cap(B \cap C)$ (a)
Similarly, we can prove that:
$A \cap(B \cap C) \subseteq(A \cap B) \cap C$ (b)
From (a) and (b), we have:
$(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B}) \cap \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{A} \cap(\mathrm{B} \cap \mathrm{C})$

Example 9:
If $\mathrm{U}=\{1,2,3, \ldots, 11\}, \mathrm{A}=\{1,2,3,5,7,9\}, \mathrm{B}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and $\mathrm{C}=\{5,6,7,8\}$ then verify the associative property of intersection.

Solution:

<CaptionedImage src="kg268x764sggr0w0p1nfmbtkr58bvp4h" alt="" caption="" />
From both the figures it is observed that same regions are shaded.

i.e. $(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B}) \cap \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{A} \cap(\mathrm{B} \cap \mathrm{C})$
∴ Associative property of intersection is verified.

(a) Distributive Property of Union over Intersection
$$
A \cup(B \cap C)=(A \cup B) \cap(A \cup C)
$$

Proof:
Let $\quad x \in A \cup(B \cap C)$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & x \in A \text { or } x \in(B \cap C) \\
\Rightarrow & x \in A \text { or }(x \in B \text { and } x \in C) \\
\Rightarrow & (x \in A \text { or } x \in B) \text { and }(x \in A \text { or } x \in C) \\
\Rightarrow & x \in(A \cup B) \text { and } x \in(A \cup C) \\
\Rightarrow & x \in(A \cup B) \cap(A \cup C) \\
\Rightarrow & A \cup(B \cap C) \subseteq(A \cup B) \cap(A \cup C)
\end{array}
$$

(a)
Again, let $y \in(A \cup B) \cap(A \cup C)$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & y \in(\mathrm{~A} \cup \mathrm{~B}) \text { and } y \in(\mathrm{~A} \cup \mathrm{C}) \\
\Rightarrow & (y \in \mathrm{~A} \text { or } y \in \mathrm{~B}) \text { and }(y \in \mathrm{~A} \text { or } y \in \mathrm{C}) \\
\Rightarrow & y \in \mathrm{~A} \text { or }(y \in \mathrm{~B} \text { and } y \in \mathrm{C}) \\
\Rightarrow & y \in \mathrm{~A} \text { or } y \in(\mathrm{~B} \cap \mathrm{C}) \\
\Rightarrow & y \in \mathrm{~A} \cup(\mathrm{~B} \cap \mathrm{C}) \\
\Rightarrow & (\mathrm{A} \cup \mathrm{~B}) \cap(\mathrm{A} \cup \mathrm{C}) \subseteq \mathrm{A} \cup(\mathrm{~B} \cap \mathrm{C})
\end{array}
$$

(b)
From (a) and (b), we have:

$$
A \cup(B \cap C)=(A \cup B) \cap(A \cup C)
$$

(b) Distributive Property of Intersection over Union
$$
A \cap(B \cup C)=(A \cap B) \cup(A \cap C)
$$

Proof:
Let $\quad x \in A \cap(B \cup C)$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & x \in A \text { and } x \in(B \cup C) \\
\Rightarrow & x \in A \text { and }(x \in B \text { or } x \in C) \\
\Rightarrow & (x \in A \text { and } x \in B) \text { or }(x \in A \text { and } x \in C) \\
\Rightarrow & x \in(A \cap B) \text { or } x \in(A \cap C) \\
\Rightarrow & x \in(A \cap B) \cup(A \cap C) \\
\Rightarrow & A \cap(B \cup C) \subseteq(A \cap B) \cup(A \cap C)
\end{array}
$$

(a)

Again, let $y \in(A \cap B) \cup(A \cap C)$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & y \in(A \cap B) \text { or } y \in(A \cap C) \\
\Rightarrow & (y \in A \text { and } y \in B) \text { or }(y \in A \text { and } y \in C)
\end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & y \in A \text { and }(y \in B \text { or } y \in C) \\
\Rightarrow & y \in A \text { and } y \in(B \cup C) \\
\Rightarrow & y \in A \cap(B \cup C) \\
\Rightarrow & (A \cap B) \cup(A \cap C) \subseteq A \cap(B \cup C) \tag{b}
\end{array}
$$

From (a) and (b), we have:

$$
A \cap(B \cup C)=(A \cap B) \cup(A \cap C)
$$

Ansel Adams (1902-1984) was a famous American photographer known for his style of detailed and focused photos that showed its subjects simply and directly. To take sharp and clear pictures, Adams had to focus the camera precisely. The distance from the object to the lens ' $p$ ' and the distance from the lens to the film ' $q$ ' must be calculated accurately to ensure that sharp image. The focal length of the lens is $f^{\prime}$. The formula that relates these measurements

The process in which an algebraic expression can be expressed as the product of its factors is called its factorization. For example,

$$
15 x^{2} y=(5 x)(3 x y)
$$

Here, $5 x$ and $3 x y$ are the factors of $15 x^{2} y$.
Hence, the factorization process which converts expressions like $15 x^{2} y$ into ( $5 x$ )( $3 x y$ ) is essentially the opposite of the multiplication process.
<CaptionedImage src="kg2ceg03c3xhbgcb679ery3z3x8bty3a" alt="" caption="" />
In the previous grades, we have learnt about the factorization of polynomials of the following types:

(i) $\quad \mathrm{ka}+\mathrm{kb}+\mathrm{kc}=\mathrm{k}(\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}+\mathrm{c})$
(ii) $\quad a c+a d+b c+b d=(c+d)(a+b)$
(iii) $a^{2} \pm 2 a b+b^{2}=(a \quad b)^{2}$
(iv) $\quad \mathrm{a}^{2}-\mathrm{b}^{2}=(\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b})(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{b})$
(v) $\quad a^{2}+2 a b+b^{2}-c^{2}=(a+b+c)(a+b-c)$
(vi) $\quad \mathrm{a}^{2}-2 \mathrm{ab}+\mathrm{b}^{2}-\mathrm{c}^{2}=(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{b}+\mathrm{c})(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{b}-\mathrm{c})$

Let us learn some more about the factorization of polynomials.

## Type-I ⟶ Factorizing Expressions of the Forms

(a) $a^{4}+a^{2} b^{2}+b^{4}$
(b) $a^{4}+4 b^{4}$

(a) To factorize $a^{4}+a^{2} b^{2}+b^{4}$ or $a^{4}+4 b^{4}$, we shall modify it and try to make it in appropriate form to utilize the previous results for its factorization.
Consider: $\quad a^{4}+a^{2} b^{2}+b^{4}=\left(a^{2}\right)^{2}+a^{2} b^{2}+\left(b^{2}\right)^{2}$
Here first and last terms are perfect squares but middle term is not twice the product of the square root of first and last term. So, we shall add and subtract $a^{2} b^{2}$ to make it twice.
i.e.
$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{4}+a^{2} b^{2}+b^{4} & =\left(a^{2}\right)^{2}+a^{2} b^{2}+a^{2} b^{2}+\left(b^{2}\right)^{2}-a^{2} b^{2} \\
& =\left(a^{2}\right)^{2}+2 a^{2} b^{2}+\left(b^{2}\right)^{2}-a^{2} b^{2} \\
& =\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)^{2}-(a b)^{2} \\
& =\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+a b\right)\left(a^{2}+b^{2}-a b\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
So, $\quad a^{4}+a^{2} b^{2}+b^{4}=\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+a b\right)\left(a^{2}+b^{2}-a b\right)$
(b) Similarly, $a^{4}+64 b^{4}=\left(a^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(8 b^{2}\right)^{2}$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\left(a^{2}\right)^{2}+2\left(a^{2}\right)\left(8 b^{2}\right)+\left(8 b^{2}\right)^{2}-2\left(a^{2}\right)\left(8 b^{2}\right) \\
& =\left(a^{2}+8 b^{2}\right)^{2}-16 a^{2} b^{2} \\
& =\left(a^{2}+8 b^{2}\right)^{2}-(4 a b)^{2} \\
& =\left(a^{2}+8 b^{2}+4 a b\right)\left(a^{2}+8 b^{2}-4 a b\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Example 1: Factorize the expression $8 x^{4}-26 x^{2} m^{2}+18 m^{4}$.
Solution: $\quad 8 x^{4}-26 x^{2} m^{2}+18 m^{4}$

$$

& =2\left[\left(2 x^{2}+3 m^{2}\right)^{2}-12 x^{2} m^{2}-13 x^{2} m^{2}\right] \\

& =2\left(2 x^{2}+3 m^{2}+5 x m\right)\left(2 x^{2}+3 m^{2}-5 x m\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Type-II ⟶ Factorization of a Trinomial of the Form

(ii) $x^{2}+\mathrm{p} x+\mathrm{q} \quad$ (ii) $\mathrm{a} x^{2}+\mathrm{bx}+\mathrm{c}$

To factorize a trinomial of this form means to express the trinomial as the product of two binomials. To factorize such trinomials keep in mind the following steps:

(i) Make a list of all possible factors of 'product of extreme coefficients'.
(ii) Select a pair of factors among the list such that:
    - their sum is equal to middle coefficient if extremes terms have same signs.
    - their difference is equal to middle coefficient if extremes terms have opposite signs.

Consider only negative factors when the middle term is negative and the coefficients of last term is positive.

So,

Example 7: Factorize the following expressions.

(ii) $x^{3}+\frac{3}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{3}}-3 x$

Solution:
(i)

$$
27 \mathrm{a}^{3}+1+27 \mathrm{a}^{2}+9 \mathrm{a}
$$

\begin{aligned}
& =(3 a)^{3}+(1)^{3}+3(3 a)^{2}(1)+3(3 a)(1)^{2} \\

a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)\left(a^{2}-a b+b^{2}\right) \text { and } a^{3}-b^{3}=(a-b)\left(a^{2}+a b+b^{2}\right)

Example 8: Factorize: $x^{3}+27 y^{3}$
Solution:
As,

a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b) \quad\left(a^{2}-a b+b^{2}\right)

So,

$$

x^{3}+27 y^{3}=(x)^{3}+(3 y)^{3} & =(x+3 y)\left[(x)^{2}-(x)(3 y)+(3 y)^{2}\right] \\
& =(x+3 y)\left(x^{2}-3 x y+9 y^{2}\right)

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

Example 10: Factorize $8 \mathrm{a}^{3}-125 \mathrm{~b}^{3}-2 \mathrm{a}+5 \mathrm{~b}$

$$

& =(2 a-5 b)\left(4 a^{2}+10 a b+25 b^{2}-1\right) \longleftarrow \text { factor out }(2 a-5 b)
\end{aligned}
$$

4.2 Highest Common Factor of Algebraic Expressions

As algebra is an extension of arithmetic, so we apply almost the same rules for finding HCF of two or more algebraic expressions (polynomials) as used in arithmetic.
4.2.1 Highest Common Factor by Factorization
A factor of a polynomial is an-other polynomial which divides it completely. The common factor of two or more polynomials is a polynomial which divides them exactly.

The highest common factor of two or more than two polynomials is a highest degree polynomial which divides the given polynomials exactly.
(a) HCF of Monomial Expressions

To Find the HCF of Monomials:

I. Determine the HCF of numerical coefficients by prime factorization.
II. Determine the common variables and select their lowest power that appears in all monomials.
This will be the HCF of variables.

Example 11: Find the HCF of $18 a b^{3} c, 30 a^{2} b^{4} c^{3}, 24 b^{2} c^{5}$.
Solution: First we find the HCF of numerical coefficients 18, 30 and 24 as

$$
\begin{aligned}
18 & =2 \times 3^{2} \\
30 & =2 \times 3 \times 5 \\
24 & =2^{3} \times 3
\end{aligned}
$$

∴ HCF of 18, 30 and $24=2 \times 3=6$
HCF of $\mathrm{b}^{2}, \mathrm{~b}^{3}$ and $\mathrm{b}^{4}$ is $\mathrm{b}^{2}$. - least common power of b

What is HCF of $7 x^{2}$ and $5 v^{2}$ ? HCF of $\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{c}^{3}$ and $\mathrm{c}^{5}$ is $\mathrm{c} . \square$ least common power of c
Hence, required $\mathrm{HCF}=6 \mathrm{~b}^{2} \mathrm{c}$
(b) HCF of Compound Polynomial Expressions

To Find the HCF of Compound Expressions:

I. Write each expression in complete factored form. Repeated factors should be expressed as powers.
II. Select the least power of each common factor.
III. The highest common factor (HCF) is the product of results of step-II.

Example 12: Find the HCF of $2 m^{2}-2 m n, 4 m^{4}-4 m^{2} n^{2}$ and $2 m^{3}-4 m^{2} n+2 m n^{2}$.
Solution: First factor each polynomial expression completely as

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 m^{2}-2 m n & =2 m(m-n) \\
4 m^{4}-4 m^{2} n^{2} & =4 m^{2}\left(m^{2}-n^{2}\right) \\
& =2^{2} m^{2}(m+n)(m-n) \\
2 m^{3}-4 m^{2} n+2 m n^{2} & =2 m\left(m^{2}-2 m n+n^{2}\right) \\
& =2 m(m-n)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Common factors with least power are 2, m, m -n
∴ Required $\mathrm{HCF}=2 \mathrm{~m}(\mathrm{~m}-\mathrm{n})$
Example 13: Find the HCF of the following.

$$
a x^{2}+7 a x+12 a, a x^{2}-5 a x-24 a, 2 a x^{2}+5 a x-3 a
$$

Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{ax}^{2}+7 \mathrm{ax}+12 \mathrm{a} & =\mathrm{a}\left(x^{2}+7 x+12\right) \\
& =\mathrm{a}\left(x^{2}+4 x+3 x+12\right) \\
& =\mathrm{a}[x(x+4)+3(x+4)] \\
& =\mathrm{a}(x+3)(x+4)
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a x^{2}-5 a x-24 a & =a\left(x^{2}-5 x-24\right) \\
& =a\left(x^{2}-8 x+3 x-24\right) \\
& =a[x(x-8)+3(x-8)]
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\mathrm{a}(x+3)(x-8) \\
2 \mathrm{ax}^{2}+5 \mathrm{ax}-3 \mathrm{a} & =\mathrm{a}\left(2 x^{2}+5 x-3\right) \\
& =\mathrm{a}\left(2 x^{2}+6 x-x-3\right) \\
& =\mathrm{a}[2 x(x+3)-1(x+3)] \\
& =\mathrm{a}(2 x-1)(x+3)
\end{aligned}
$$

∴ Required HCF = product of all common factors with least power

$$
=a(x+3)
$$

## Highest Common Factor by Division

Sometimes, it is difficult to factorize the given polynomials completely. In such cases, we adopt division method to find the HCF of these polynomials.
We will explain the procedure with the help of the following example.
Example 14: Find the HCF of two polynomials $x^{3}+x^{2}-5 x+3$ and $x^{2}+3 x$.
Solution: The following steps will be followed for finding HCF.

Step-I: Arrange the given polynomials in descending order w.r.t. the variables.
In this case, polynomials are already in descending order.
Step-II: Consider the higher degree polynomial as dividend and lower degree polynomial as divisor and start division process.
Step-III: Since degree of remainder has become smaller than the degree of divisor, so remainder will be taken as divisor and divisor will be considered as dividend.
Continue the same process until we get 0 remainder. As $x+3$ is the last divisor which gives remainder as ' 0 '. Therefore, required $\mathrm{HCF}=x+3$
Example 15: Find the HCF of $12+16 a+7 a^{2}+a^{3}$ and $13 a+5 a^{2}+14+a^{3}$.
Solution: First arrange the given polynomials in descending order w.r.t. the variable.
i.e. $a^{3}+7 a^{2}+16 a+12$ and $a^{3}+5 a^{2}+13 a+14$. Since degree of both the polynomials is same, so any one can be taken as a divisor or dividend.
Key Fact
HCF of two polynomials P and Q will be the same as that of mP and nQ (where m and n are non zero constants). So in the process of finding the HCF, we can multiply or divide any divisor or dividend by any suitable number according to our requirement, but we cannot multiply or divide it by a variable.

mdxBody:
The least common multiple of two or more polynomials is a polynomial of lowest degree that contains the factors of each polynomial.
4.3.1 Least Common Multiple by Factorization
The process of determining the LCM is almost identical to that for determining the HCF. Prime factorization is also useful to determine the LCM of two or more polynomials. The LCM is obtained by taking product of all factors (common and uncommon) with highest power.
(a) LCM of Monomial Expressions
To determine the LCM of two or more monomials, find LCM of the numerical coefficients and LCM of each variable. Then find their product for the required LCM.
To understand this concept, consider the two monomials $45 x^{2} y$ and $60 x^{3} y^{2} z$.
First find the LCM of numerical coefficients 45 and 60 which is 180.
Now consider variables $x, y$ and $z$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { LCM of } x^{2} \text { and } x^{3}=\text { highest power of } x \text { appearing in any monomial }=x^{3} \\
& \text { LCM of } y \text { and } y^{2}=\text { highest power of } y \text { appearing in any monomial }=y^{2} \\
& \text { LCM of } z
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, required LCM = product of LCM of coefficients and LCM of each variable.

$$
=180 x^{3} y^{2} z
$$

Example 16: Find LCM of $18 a^{3} b^{4} c^{5}, 60 a^{3} b^{4} c^{6}$ and $42 a^{4} b^{3}$.
Solution: First we find the LCM of 18, 60 and 42 by prime factorization as

$$
18=2 \times 3^{2}, 60=2^{2} \times 3 \times 5,42=2 \times 3 \times 7
$$

∴ LCM of 18, 60 and $42=$ product of all factors with highest power

$$
=2^{2} \times 3^{2} \times 5 \times 7=1260
$$

Now we find LCM of each variable as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { LCM of } a^{3} \text { and } a^{4}=a^{4} \text { (highest power of } a \text { ) } \\
& \text { LCM of } b^{3} \text { and } b^{4}=b^{4} \text { (highest power of } b \text { ) } \\
& \text { LCM of } c^{5} \text { and } c^{6}=c^{6} \text { (highest power of } c \text { ) } \\
& \therefore \text { Required LCM }=1260 a^{4} b^{4} c^{6}
\end{aligned}
$$

(b) LCM of Compound Polynomial Expressions

To understand the procedure, let us consider the following examples.
Example 17: Find LCM of $x^{4} y^{3}-x^{3} y^{4}$ and $x^{3} y-x y^{3}$
Solution: First we factorize each polynomial completely.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{4} y^{3}-x^{3} y^{4} & =x^{3} y^{3}(x-y) \\
x^{3} y-x y^{3} & =x y\left(x^{2}-y^{2}\right)=x y(x-y)(x+y)
\end{aligned}
$$

We choose every factor with highest power as: $x^{3} y^{3}, x-y$ and $x+y$.
Then their product is $x^{3} y^{3}(x+y)(x-y)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \text { Required LCM } & =x^{3} y^{3}(x+y)(x-y) \\
& =x^{3} y^{3}\left(x^{2}-y^{2}\right) \\
& =x^{5} y^{3}-x^{3} y^{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

To find the LCM of Compound Expressions:

I. Write each polynomial in complete factored form. Repeated factors should be expressed as powers.
II. Select the highest power of every factor that appears.
III. The least common multiple is the product of the results of step II.

Example 18: Find the LCM of $2 x^{2}-12 x y+16 y^{2}, x^{2}-6 x y+8 y^{2}$ and $3 x^{2}-12 y^{2}$.
Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 x^{2}-12 x y+16 y^{2} & =2\left(x^{2}-6 x y+8 y^{2}\right) \\
& =2(x-4 y)(x-2 y) \\
x^{2}-6 x y+8 y^{2} & =(x-4 y)(x-2 y) \\
3 x^{2}-12 y^{2} & =3\left(x^{2}-4 y^{2}\right) \\
& =3(x+2 y)(x-2 y)
\end{aligned}
$$

All factors with highest powers are $2,3, x-4 y, x-2 y, x+2 y$

∴ Required LCM $=2 \times 3 \times(x-4 y)(x-2 y)(x+2 y)$
$$
=6(x-4 y)\left(x^{2}-4 y^{2}\right)
$$

Note: Same pattern will be followed for more than three polynomials.

Key Fact

- The key words in the two processes of HCF and LCM are:
$\mathrm{HCF} \longrightarrow$ lowest power and common factor.
LCM ⟶ highest power and every factor.
- LCM of two or more polynomials is a lowest degree polynomial that is exactly divisible by each of the given polynomials.

4.3.2 Relation between HCF and LCM

Consider two polynomials $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{a}^{2}-\mathrm{b}^{2}$ and $\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{a}^{2}-2 \mathrm{ab}+\mathrm{b}^{2}$. For their LCM and HCF, first factorize them as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P=a^{2}-b^{2}=(a+b)(a-b) \\
& Q=a^{2}-2 a b+b^{2}=(a-b)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

∴ HCF of P and Q = a - b
and LCM of P and $\mathrm{Q}=(\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b})(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{b})^{2}$
Now

$$
\begin{align*}
\text { HCF } \times \text { LCM } & =(a-b)(a+b)(a-b)^{2} \\
& =\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)(a-b)^{2} \\
& =\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)\left(a^{2}-2 a b+b^{2}\right)  \tag{...........}\\
\text { of } \mathrm{P} \text { and } \mathrm{Q} & =\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)\left(a^{2}-2 a b+b^{2}\right) \tag{i}
\end{align*}
$$

Thus, $\mathrm{LCM} \times \mathrm{HCF}=\mathrm{P} \times \mathrm{Q}$
Hence, it can be generalized that:
product of their HCF and LCM = product of given polynomials
4.3.3 Finding of Least Common Multiple by Division

Sometimes, it is much difficult to find the LCM of given polynomials P and Q by factorization method. Then in that case, we can find the LCM by division as follows. From the relation (1) we have,

$$
\mathrm{LCM}=\frac{P \times Q}{H C F}=\frac{P}{H C F} \times Q=\frac{Q}{H C F} \times P
$$

Procedure is illustrated through examples.
Example 19: Find the LCM of $\mathrm{P}=10 x^{4}+3 x^{3}+8$ and $\mathrm{Q}=8 x^{4}+3 x+10$

## 0perations on Algebraic Fractions

In this topic addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of algebraic fractions will be discussed.

## Algebraic Fractions

Algebraic expressions of the type $\frac{x^{2}+2 x+1}{2 x^{2}-5 x-3}, \frac{-1-\mathrm{t}}{\frac{1}{\mathrm{t}}+1}, \frac{\mathrm{p}^{2}}{\mathrm{qp}^{2}}$ are called algebraic fractions.
4.4.2 Multiplication of Algebraic Fractions

We multiply two or more algebraic fractions in the same way as common fractions in arithmetic.

If $\frac{R}{T}$ and $\frac{S}{U}$ are two algebraic fractions, where $\mathrm{T} \neq 0, \mathrm{U} \neq 0$.
Then,

$$
\frac{R}{T} \times \frac{S}{U}=\frac{R S}{T U}
$$

In general, before finding the product of two or more algebraic fractions, we factorize the numerator and denominator of each fraction, if possible, and divide out all the common factors, to get the most reduced form of the resulting fraction.

Key Fact
In the process of multiplication, product of all the common factors being cancelled is in fact HCF of the expressions present in numerator and denominator.

Example 21: Find the indicated product.

$$
\frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}+4 x+4} \times \frac{x+2}{x^{2}+2 x-3}
$$

Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}+4 x+4} \times \frac{x+2}{x^{2}+2 x-3} \\
= & \frac{(x+1)(x-1)}{(x+2)(x+2)} \times \frac{x+2}{(x-1)(x+3)} \\
= & \frac{x+1}{x+2} \times \frac{1}{x+3} \\
= & \frac{x+1}{(x+2)(x+3)}=\frac{x+1}{x^{2}+5 x+6}
\end{aligned}
$$

The key to success in simplifying an algebraic fraction lies in your ability to factor the polynomials.
4.4.3 Division of Algebraic Fractions

If $\frac{S}{U}$ and $\frac{T}{Q}$ are two algebraic fractions, then

$$
\frac{S}{U} \div \frac{T}{Q}=\frac{S}{U} \times \frac{Q}{T}=\frac{S Q}{U T}, \text { where } \mathrm{U} \neq 0, \mathrm{Q} \neq 0 \text { and } \mathrm{T} \neq 0
$$

To divide one fraction by another, invert the divisor and proceed as in multiplication because 'to divide' by a fraction means 'to multiply' by its reciprocal.

Example 22: Find the indicated operation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{r}^{2}-\mathrm{s}^{2}}{\mathrm{r}} \div \frac{\mathrm{r}-\mathrm{s}}{\mathrm{~s}}
$$

Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{r^{2}-s^{2}}{r} \div \frac{r-s}{s} \\
& =\frac{(r+s)(r-s)}{r} \times \frac{s}{r-s}=\frac{r+s}{r} \times \frac{s}{1} \\
& =\frac{s(r+s)}{r}=\frac{s r+s^{2}}{r}
\end{aligned}
$$

Example 23: Simplify: $\frac{3 x^{3}+6 x^{2}}{2 x^{2}+x-6} \div\left(6 x^{2}-15 x\right)$
Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{3 x^{3}+6 x^{2}}{2 x^{2}+x-6} \div\left(6 x^{2}-15 x\right) \\
= & \frac{3 x^{3}+6 x^{2}}{2 x^{2}+x-6} \times \frac{1}{6 x^{2}-15 x} \\
= & \frac{3 x^{2}(x+2)}{(x+2)(2 x-3)} \times \frac{1}{3 x(2 x-5)} \\
= & \frac{x}{(2 x-3)(2 x-5)}=\frac{x}{4 x^{2}-16 x+15}
\end{aligned}
$$

4.4.4 Addition and Subtraction of Algebraic Fractions

Algebraic fractions are added or subtracted just like arithmetic fractions i.e., by manipulating LCM of their denominators.

Example 24: Simplify the following.

$$
\frac{x^{2}+2 x+2}{2 x}+\frac{(-2 x-2)}{2 x}
$$

Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{x^{2}+2 x+2}{2 x}+\frac{(-2 x-2)}{2 x} \\
& =\frac{x^{2}+2 x+2+(-2 x-2)}{2 x} \\
& =\frac{x^{2}+2 x+2-2 x-2}{2 x} \\
& =\frac{x^{2}}{2 x}=\frac{x}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Algebraic fractions with same denominators are called like fractions c.g., $\frac{a-2}{a+b}, \frac{b^{2}-2}{a+b}$

Fractions with different denominators are called unlike fractions e.g.,

$$
\frac{x^{2}-y}{a x+b} ; \frac{y^{2}-x}{c x+d}
$$

Example 25: Perform the indicated operations.

$$
\frac{-2 x}{x+3}+\frac{3}{3-x}-\frac{8 x-12}{x^{2}-9}
$$

Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{-2 x}{x+3}+\frac{3}{3-x}-\frac{8 x-12}{x^{2}-9} \\
& =\frac{-2 x}{x+3}+\frac{-3}{x-3}-\frac{8 x-12}{(x+3)(x-3)} \\
& =\frac{-2 x(x-3)+(-3)(x+3)-(8 x-12)}{(x+3)(x-3)} \leftarrow \text { LCM is }(x+3)(x-3) \\
& =\frac{-2 x^{2}+6 x-3 x-9-8 x+12}{(x+3)(x-3)} \leftarrow \text { simplify the parentheses } \\
& =\frac{-2 x^{3}-5 x+3}{(x+3)(x-3)} \longleftarrow \text { combine like terms } \\
& =\frac{-1\left(2 x^{2}+5 x-3\right)}{(x+3)(x-3)} \\
& =\frac{-1(2 x-1)(x+3)}{(x+3)(x-3)} \\
& =\frac{-(2 x-1)}{(x-3)} \\
& =-\frac{2 x-1}{x-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

4.4.5 Algebraic Fractions with Combined Operations

When two or more operations occur in any algebraic expression then the rule for order of operations (DMAS) must be followed.
Example 26: Simplify.

$$
\frac{3 u^{2}+5 u v+2 v^{2}}{u^{2}+5 u v+6 v^{2}}+\frac{2 u+6 v}{u^{2}-4 v^{2}} \div \frac{u^{2}+6 u v+9 v^{2}}{u^{2} v-2 u v^{2}}
$$

Solution: Division is performed before addition while simplifying an expression.
Therefore, first we will simplify fractions having ' $\div$ ' sign.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{3 u^{2}+5 u v+2 v^{2}}{u^{2}+5 u v+6 v^{2}}+\frac{2 u+6 v}{u^{2}-4 v^{2}} \div \frac{u^{2}+6 u v+9 v^{2}}{u^{2} v-2 u v^{2}} \\
= & \frac{3 u^{2}+5 u v+2 v^{2}}{u^{2}+5 u v+6 v^{2}}+\frac{2 u+6 v}{u^{2}-4 v^{2}} \times \frac{u^{2} v-2 u v^{2}}{u^{2}+6 u v+9 v^{2}} \\
= & \frac{3 u^{2}+5 u v+2 v^{2}}{u^{2}+5 u v+6 v^{2}}+\frac{2(u+3 v)}{(u+2 v)(u-2 v)} \times \frac{u v(u-2 v)}{(u+3 v)^{2}} \\
= & \frac{3 u^{2}+5 u v+2 v^{2}}{u^{2}+5 u v+6 v^{2}}+\frac{2 u v}{(u+2 v)(u+3 v)}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{3 u^{2}+5 u v+2 v^{2}}{(u+2 v)(u+3 v)}+\frac{2 u v}{(u+2 v)(u+3 v)} \\
& =\frac{3 u^{2}+5 u v+2 v^{2}+2 u v}{(u+2 v)(u+3 v)} \\
& =\frac{3 u^{2}+7 u v+2 v^{2}}{(u+2 v)(u+3 v)} \\
& =\frac{(3 u+v)(u+2 v)}{(u+2 v)(u+3 v)}=\frac{3 u+v}{u+3 v}
\end{aligned}
$$

6. $\frac{8 a^{3}-1}{4 a^{3}+2 a^{2}} \div \frac{6 a^{2}-13 a+5}{15 a-25} \times \frac{2 a^{4}+a^{3}}{15 a^{2}}$
7. $\frac{x^{2}-8 x-9}{x^{2}-17 x+72} \times \frac{x^{2}-25}{x^{2}-1} \div \frac{x^{2}+4 x-5}{x^{2}-9 x+8}$

10. $\frac{5 x+5}{3(2 x-1)}+\frac{6-2 x}{2(1-2 x)}$
11. $\frac{2 a}{2 a-3}-\frac{5}{6 a+9}-\frac{4(3 a+2)}{3\left(4 a^{2}-9\right)}$
12. $\frac{5}{5+x-18 x^{2}}-\frac{2}{2+5 x+2 x^{2}}$

summary: This note explains least common multiples of algebraic expressions by factorization, including highest-power factor selection.

The square root of an algebraic expression is defined as one of its equal factors e.g., $x+y$ is the square root of $x^{2}+2 x y+y^{2}$ because,

$$
x^{2}+2 x y+y^{2}=(x+y)^{2}
$$

The square root of an algebraic expression P is another algebraic expression Q which, when squared, gives $P$. Thus, if $P=(-Q)^{2}$ then $Q$ and $-Q$ both are square roots of $P$.

Square root of an algebraic expression can be obtained in two ways.
i. Factorization Method
ii. Division Method
4.5.1 Square Root by Factorization Method

In this method, before applying the square root, given expression is written in the form of a complete square. For example, to find the square root of $4 a^{2}+12 a b+9 b^{2}$, first we will convert the given expression into a complete square as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4 a^{2}+12 a b+9 b^{2} & =(2 a)^{2}+2(2 a)(3 b)+(3 b)^{2} \\
& =(2 a+3 b)^{2} \\
& =[ \pm(2 a+3 b)]^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying square root on both sides, we get.

$$
\sqrt{4 a^{2}+12 a b+9 b^{2}}= \pm(2 a+3 b)
$$

Example 27: Find the square root of $\left(a+\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)$.
Solution: To find square root of such type of expressions, we can adopt two methods.
Method-I

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(a+\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right) & =a^{2}+2(a)\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)+\frac{1}{a^{2}}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right) \\
= & a^{2}+2+\frac{1}{a^{2}}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right) \\
= & a^{2}-2+\frac{1}{a^{2}}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)+2+2 \\
= & \left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)+4 \\
= & \left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}-2\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)(2)+(2)^{2} \\
= & \left(a-\frac{1}{a}-2\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

$\sqrt{\left(a+\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)}= \pm\left(a-\frac{1}{a}-2\right) \ldots$ (applying square root)

Method-II

$$
\begin{align*}
\left(a+\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right) & =a^{2}+2+\frac{1}{a^{2}}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right) \\
& =\left(a^{2}+\frac{1}{a^{2}}\right)+2-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right) \tag{i}
\end{align*}
$$

Let,

$$
\begin{equation*}
a-\frac{1}{a}=x \tag{a}
\end{equation*}
$$

Then,

$$
\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}=x^{2}
$$

or

$$
a^{2}-2+\frac{1}{a^{2}}=x^{2}
$$

or

$$
\begin{equation*}
a^{2}+\frac{1}{a^{2}}=x^{2}+2 \tag{b}
\end{equation*}
$$

Substituting values from equations (a) and (b) in equation (i)

$$
\begin{align*}
\left(a+\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right) & =\left(x^{2}+2\right)+2-4 x \\
& =x^{2}-4 x+4 \\
& =(x-2)^{2} \tag{ii}
\end{align*}
$$

Now, replace $x$ by $a-\frac{1}{a}$ in equation (ii)

$$
\left(a+\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)=\left(a-\frac{1}{a}-2\right)^{2}
$$

Applying square root on both sides, we get

$$
\sqrt{\left(a+\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}-4\left(a-\frac{1}{a}\right)}= \pm\left(a-\frac{1}{a}-2\right) .
$$

Example 28: Find the square root of $(2 a+1)(2 a+3)(2 a+5)(2 a+7)+16$.
Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2 a+1)(2 a+3)(2 a+5)(2 a+7)+16 & =[(2 a+1)(2 a+7)][(2 a+3)(2 a+5)]+16 \\
& =\left(4 a^{2}+16 a+7\right)\left(4 a^{2}+16 a+15\right)+16 \\
& =\left(4 a^{2}+16 a+7\right)\left(4 a^{2}+16 a+7+8\right)+16
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2 a+1)(2 a+3)(2 a+5)(2 a+7)+16 & =x(x+8)+16 \ldots \ldots\left(\text { put } 4 a^{2}+16 a+7=x\right) \\
& =x^{2}+8 x+16 \\
& =x^{2}+2(x)(4)+(4)^{2}=(x+4)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now replace $x$ by $4 a^{2}+16 a+7$

$$
(2 a+1)(2 a+3)(2 a+5)(2 a+7)+16=\left(4 a^{2}+16 a+7+4\right)^{2}=\left(4 a^{2}+16 a+11\right)^{2}
$$

Applying square root on both sides, we get

$$
\sqrt{(2 a+1)(2 a+3)(2 a+5)(2 a+7)+16}= \pm\left(4 a^{2}+16 a+11\right)
$$

4.5.2 Square Root by Division Method

To understand this method, consider the following example.
Example 29: Find the square root of $9 x^{2}-42 x y+49 y^{2}$ by division method.

Solution:

$$
3 x-7 y \leftarrow \text { root }
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg2176j997s4mnybbhpjnsc7yd8bv76p" alt="" caption="" />

$$
\text { ∴ Square root }= \pm(3 x-7 y)
$$

Example 30: Find the square root of $4\left(x^{2}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)+12\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)+17, x \neq 0$.
Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 4\left(x^{2}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)+12\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)+17=4 x^{2}+\frac{4}{x^{2}}+12 x+\frac{12}{x}+17 \\
& \quad=4 x^{2}+12 x+17+\frac{12}{x}+\frac{4}{x^{2}} \text { arrange in descending order }
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
2 x+3+\frac{2}{x}
$$

$$
4 x+3 \sqrt{\frac{4 x^{2}+12 x+17+\frac{12}{x}+\frac{4}{x^{2}}}{ \pm 4 x^{2}}}
$$

∴ Required square root is $\pm\left(2 x+3+\frac{2}{x}\right)$

Sometimes the given expression is not a perfect square and to make it a perfect square, we add (subtract) some value to (from) it. Consider the following example.

Example 31: To convert $x^{4}+4 x^{3}+10 x^{2}+10 x+5$ into a perfect square,

i. What should be added to it?
ii. What should be subtracted from it?
iii. What should be the value of $x$ ?

Solution: First we try to find the square root of the given expression as
<CaptionedImage src="kg2bvfm3rnew0dp2hk81wb7ysh8bvx9w" alt="" caption="" />
For a perfect square, remainder must be zero, but here remainder is $-2 x-4$.
Hence,

i. Expression will be a perfect square if we add $-(-2 x-4)=2 x+4$ in it.
ii. Expression will be a perfect square if we subtract $-2 x-4$ from it.
iii. For the value of $x$ put remainder equal to zero as
$$
\begin{aligned}
-2 x-4 & =0 \\
-2 x & =4 \text { or } x=-2
\end{aligned}
$$

∴ For $x=-2$, expression will be a perfect square.

Example 32: For what values of $m$ and $n, 9 x^{4}-24 x^{3}-14 x^{2}+m x+n$ is a complete square or perfect squre?
Solution: First we try to find the square root of $9 x^{4}-24 x^{3}-14 x^{2}+m x+n$.

$$
\begin{gathered}
3 x^{2} \sqrt{\frac{9 x^{4}-24 x^{3}-14 x^{2}+m x+n}{ \pm 9 x^{4}}} \\
6 x^{2}-4 x \sqrt{\frac{-24 x^{3}-14 x^{2}+m x+n}{x^{2}-8 x-5} \sqrt{-24 x^{3}+16 x^{2}}} \\
-30 x^{2}+m x+n \\
-30 x^{2}+40 x+25 \\
+40 x+n-25 \\
=x(m-40)+(n-25)
\end{gathered}
$$

The, given expression will be a complete square if the remainder is zero. This is only possible if,

$$
\begin{aligned}
m-40 & =0 \quad \text { and } \quad n-25 \\
\text { or } \quad \mathrm{m} & =40
\end{aligned} \quad \begin{aligned}
n & \text { and } \\
n & =25
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, for $m=40$ and $n=25$ given expression will be a complete square

## Application of Factorization in Daily Life

We use various basic principles of mathematics quite unknowingly in our daily life. Like, we are always using addition, subtraction, division and multiplication everywhere, from restaurants to public transport. When children learn about numbers and basic mathematics. This happens because, with time, we become familiar with the concepts. They can frequently apply these concepts in solving their real life problems. Factorization is a similar example of this, we have a bunch of reallife examples where we use factorization extensively, making our daily lives easier.
Example 33:
Mustafa is working on a space project to make a cuboid with the volume as the difference of 2 cubes of sides $x$ and $y$ respectively. Help him to find:

a. Expression for volume of the required cuboid.
b. Expression for any one side of required cuboid.
c. Expression for Area of any one surface of required cuboid.

Solution:
Mustafa is working with cubes of volumes:
Volume 1: $x^{3}$
Difference of 2 volumes $=x^{3}-y^{3}$

a. Volume of required cuboid $=x^{3}-y^{3}$
b. $x^{3}-y^{3}=(x-y)\left(x^{2}+x y+y^{2}\right)$ (by factorizing)

The volume of a cuboid is factorized in one linear and one quadratic factor. So the expression for length is " $x-y$ "

c. The quadratic factor in above factorization represents Area of a surface. i-e Area of one surface is $x^{2}+x y+y^{2}$.

Example 34:
Volume of a cubical container is given by expression $\left(x^{3}-6 x^{2} y+12 x y^{2}-8 y^{3}\right) m^{3}$. Find:

a. Expression for length of each side
b. Expression for area of the base
c. Expression for total surface area
d. Expression for cost of painting all outer surfaces at the rate of $\mathrm{Rs} .50 / \mathrm{m}^{2}$.

Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Volume of cube }=l^{3}= & x^{3}-6 x^{2} y+12 x y^{2}-8 y^{3} \\
& =(x-2 y)^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

a. Length of each side is $(x-2 y) \mathrm{m}$
b. Base area $=l^{2}=(x-2 y)^{2} m^{2}$
c. Surface area $=6 l^{2}=6(x-2 y)^{2} m^{2}$
d. Cost = rate × surface area = Rs. $50 \times 6 \times(x-2 y)^{2}$
$$
=\text { Rs. } 300(x-2 y)^{2}
$$

## KEY POINTS

- Factorization of expressions of the following types.
Type-I: $\quad \mathrm{ka}+\mathrm{kb}+\mathrm{kc}=\mathrm{k}(\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}+\mathrm{c})$
Type-II: $\mathrm{ac}+\mathrm{ad}+\mathrm{bc}+\mathrm{bd}=(\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b})(\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{d})$
Type-III: $\mathrm{a}^{2}+2 \mathrm{ab}+\mathrm{b}^{2}=(\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b})^{2}$ and $\mathrm{a}^{2}-2 \mathrm{ab}+\mathrm{b}^{2}=(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{b})^{2}$
Type-IV: $\mathrm{a}^{2}-\mathrm{b}^{2}=(\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b})(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{b})$
Type-V: $\mathrm{a}^{2}+2 \mathrm{ab}+\mathrm{b}^{2}-\mathrm{c}^{2}=(\mathrm{a}+b+c)(a+b-c)$ and
$$
\mathrm{a}^{2}-2 \mathrm{ab}+\mathrm{b}^{2}-\mathrm{c}^{2}=(\mathrm{a}-b+c)(a-b-c)
$$
Type-VI: $\mathrm{a}^{4}+\mathrm{a}^{2} \mathrm{~b}^{2}+\mathrm{b}^{4}=\left(\mathrm{a}^{2}+\mathrm{b}^{2}+\mathrm{ab}\right)\left(\mathrm{a}^{2}+\mathrm{b}^{2}-\mathrm{ab}\right)$
$$
a^{4}+4 b^{4}=\left(a^{2}+2 b^{2}+2 a b\right)\left(a^{2}+2 b^{2}-2 a b\right)
$$
Type-VII: $x^{2}+\mathrm{p} x+\mathrm{q}$ (factorize it write p as the sum of the factors of q )
Type-VIII: $a x^{2}+b x+c$ (factorize it write $b$ as the sum of the factors of $a c$ )
Type-IX: $\left\{\begin{array}{l}\left(\mathrm{a} x^{2}+\mathrm{b} x+\mathrm{c}\right)\left(\mathrm{a} x^{2}+\mathrm{b} x+\mathrm{d}\right)+\mathrm{k} \\ (x+\mathrm{a})(x+\mathrm{b})(x+\mathrm{c})(x+\mathrm{d})+\mathrm{k} \\ (x+a)(x+b)(x+c)(x+d)+k x^{2}\end{array}(\right.$ where $\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}=\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{d})$
Type-X: $\quad \mathrm{a}^{3}+3 \mathrm{a}^{2} \mathrm{~b}+3 \mathrm{ab}^{2}+\mathrm{b}^{3}=(\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b})^{3}$ and $\mathrm{a}^{3}-3 \mathrm{a}^{2} \mathrm{~b}+3 \mathrm{ab}^{2}-\mathrm{b}^{3}=(\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{b})^{3}$
Type-XI: $\quad a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)\left(a^{2}-a b+b^{2}\right)$ and $a^{3}-b^{3}=(a-b)\left(a^{2}+a b+b^{2}\right)$
- HCF of two or more polynomials is a highest degree polynomial which divides the given polynomials exactly.
- LCM of two or more polynomials is a least degree polynomial which is exactly divisible by the given polynomials.
- Product of two polynomials P and Q = Product of their HCF and LCM i.e.
$$
P \times Q=H C F \times L C M
$$
- An algebraic expression of the form $\frac{P}{Q}$ where P and Q are two expressions and $\mathrm{Q} \neq 0$ is called an algebraic fraction.
- A fraction having rational expression in its denominator or numerator or both, is called a complex fraction.
- In case of division, after converting the fractions into multiplication form, follow the same rules for
simplification as applied in the product of algebraic fractions.
- Use 'DMAS' rule while simplifying the algebraic fractions having more than one operation.
- Square root of an algebraic expression is defined as one of its equal factors.
- Square root of an algebraic expression ' P ' is another expression ' Q ' which, when squared, gives 'P'
i.e., if $P=( \pm Q)^{2}$ then, $+Q$ and $-Q$ both are square roots of $P$.

mdxBody:
We can use equations and formulae to model a variety of real life problems and situations. Business, industry, science, sports, travel, architecture and banking are some of the areas that really depend upon equations and inequalities to find the solutions to their problems. For example, consider the following problem taken from our daily life. Sarim and Raahim are football players in their school team.
If we want to compare their scores for the season, only one of the following statements will be true.

- Sarim scored less umber of goals than Raahim.
- Sarim scored the same number of goals as Raahim.
- Sarim scored more number of goals than Raahim.

Let $x$ and $y$ represent the number of goals scored by Sarim and Raahim respectively. We can compare their scores by using an
<CaptionedImage src="kg2ax7x213ftxackz1pa4tqprn8bv63t" alt="" caption="" />
inequality or an equation as given below.

| $x<y$ | or | $x=\mathrm{y}$ | or | $x>\mathrm{y}$. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

A linear equation in one variable is an equation that can be written in the standard form as $\mathbf{a} \boldsymbol{x}+\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}$ where $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$ are real numbers and $\mathbf{a} \neq 0$ e.g.

$$
2 x+3=0,5 x+3=5
$$

Key Fact

1. Exponent of the variable in linear equation is always 1. The equation $x^{2}=4$ is non-linear because exponent of the variable is not ' 1 '.
2. Linear equations do not involve product of the variables. The equation $x y=14$ is a non-linear equation.
3. Linear equation is also called equation of degree one.

5.1.1 To Find the Solution of Linear Equations

The solution of a linear equation in one variable is a replacement for the variable that makes the equation true.

A linear equation in one variable (in standard form) has exactly one solution. For the solution of such equations, we have to isolate the variable on either side of equal sign by a sequence of equivalent equations.

Key Fact
Two or more equations, which have the same solutions, are called equivalent equations. e.g.

$$
2 x+3=4 \text { and } 2 x=1 \text { are two equivalent equations. }
$$

We follow properties of equality i.e. addition, subtraction, multiplication and division properties while solving first degree linear equations.
Example 1: Solve the following equation for $x$.

$$
-7 x+24=3
$$

Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-7 x+24 & =3 \\
-7 x+24-24 & =3-24 \leftarrow \text { original equation } \\
-7 x & =-21 \\
x & =3
\end{aligned}
$$

Check: To check this root, we replace the variable $x$ by its value in the original equation and simplify both sides.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \begin{aligned}
-7 x+24 & =3 \leftarrow \\
-7(3)+24 & =3 \leftarrow \\
-21+24 & =3 \leftarrow \\
3 & =3 \leftarrow \\
\text { Thus, } \quad x & =3 \text { is requal equate ' } x \text { ' by } 3
\end{aligned} \\
& \text { solution is checked root. }
\end{aligned}
$$

While checking any solution, it is better to write a question mark over the equal sign just to indicate that we are not sure of the validity of the equation.
5.1.2 Solving Linear Equations Involving Fractions
The following examples illustrate this method.
Example 2: Solve $\frac{3 x}{5}-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{x}{4}+1$
Solution: $\quad \frac{3 x}{5}-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{x}{4}+1$
LCM of 5, 2 and $4=20$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
20 \times \frac{3 x}{5}-20 \times \frac{1}{2} & =20 \times \frac{x}{4}+20 \\
12 x-10 & =5 x+20 \\
12 x-5 x & =20+10 \\
7 x & =30 \\
x & =\frac{30}{7}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $x=\frac{30}{7}$ is the required root of the given equation.
Example 3: Solve $\frac{2 x+3}{5}=\frac{3-4 x}{8}$
Solution: $\frac{2 x+3}{5}=\frac{3-4 x}{8}$
By cross multiplication we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
8(2 x+3) & =5(3-4 x) \\
16 x+24 & =15-20 x \\
16 x+20 x & =15-24 \\
36 x & =-9 \\
x & =-\frac{9}{36}=-\frac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ is the root of given equation.
Example 4: Solve $0.7(x-1)-0.5 x=1.1$
Solution: $0.7(x-1)-0.5 x=1.1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.7 x-0.7-0.5 x & =1.1 \\
0.2 x-0.7 & =1.1 \\
0.2 x & =1.8 \\
2 x & =18 \\
x & =9
\end{aligned}
$$

Check: Replace $x$ by its value in the original equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.7(9-1)-0.5(9) & =1.1 \\
5.6-4.5 & =1.1 \\
1.1 & =1.1
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $x=9$ is the required solution of the given equation.

Solve the following linear equations in one variable.

5. $\frac{x-2}{2}+\frac{x+10}{9}=5$
6. $\frac{4(x+2)}{3}-\frac{6(x-7)}{7}=12$
7. $\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x}{3}-\frac{x}{4}+\frac{x}{5}=7 \frac{5}{6}$
8. $\frac{y+1}{3}+\frac{y+1}{2}=2-\frac{y+3}{2}$
9. $\frac{1}{5}(x-8)+\frac{4+x}{7}=7-\frac{23-x}{5}$
10. $\frac{1}{2 y}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{4 y}-1-\frac{1}{y} ; y \neq 0$
11. $4-0.3(1-x)=7$
12. $0.5 x=6.3-0.2 x$
13. $1.3 x-0.2=0.3 x-1.5$
summary: Defines a linear equation in one variable in standard form and establishes the nonzero coefficient condition needed for a unique linear model.

## Radical Equations

An equation in which the unknown letter (variable) appears under a radical sign is called a radical equation.

Examples: $\sqrt{x+1}=7, \sqrt{x}=9, \sqrt{x+2}=5, \sqrt{2 x-3}=\sqrt{x+5}$

## Key Fact

- If two numbers are equal, then their squares are also equal i.e. if $x=y$ then $x^{2}=y^{2}$
- If the squares of two numbers are equal, the numbers may or may not be equal. e.g. $(-5)^{2}=(5)^{2}$ but $-5 \neq 5$

## To Solve a Radical Equation

L. Arrange the terms such that a term with a radical sign is by itself on one side of the equation.
II. Square both sides of the equation.
III. Solve the resulting linear equation for corresponding variable.
IV. Check the solution in the original equation.

Example 5: Solve $\sqrt{x}+3=7$
Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{x}+3 & =7 \\
\sqrt{x} & =4 \\
(\sqrt{x})^{2} & =(4)^{2} \\
x & =16
\end{aligned}
$$

Check: Replace $x$ by 16 in the original equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{16}+3 & =7 \\
4+3 & =7 \\
7 & =7
\end{aligned} \text { □ solution is checked }
$$

Hence, $x=16$ is required solution.
While squaring both sides of a radical equation it is possible to get an extra root called extraneous root that does not satisfy the original equation. Therefore, it is necessary to check every root by substituting it into the original equation. Consider the following example for such case:
Example 6: Solve 4+2 $\sqrt{3 y+1}=3$
Solution: $4+2 \sqrt{3 y+1}=3$

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 \sqrt{3 y+1} & =-1 \ldots \ldots(\mathrm{i}) \\
(2 \sqrt{3 y+1})^{2} & =(-1)^{2} \\
4(3 y+1) & =1 \\
12 y+4 & =1 \\
12 y & =-3 \\
y & =-\frac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $y=-\frac{1}{4}$ is an extraneous root and solution set is $\phi$.
Note: In example 6 , there is no need to solve the equation after step (i). We can directly say that equation has no solution.

EXERCISE 5.2

Reduce the following radical equations into simple linear equations then find their solution. In case of extraneous solution, write $\phi$ for the solution set.

1. $\sqrt{2 x}=4$
2. $\sqrt{x-3}=2$
3. $\sqrt{x-5}=3$
4. $\sqrt{2 x+1}=9$
5. $\sqrt{5 x-4}=14$
6. $\sqrt{3 x-5}=-10$
7. $\sqrt{y+4}-3=2$
8. $5-\sqrt{2 x-1}=0$,
9. $\sqrt{y+1}-12=-10$
10. $\sqrt{5 t-2}=\sqrt{3 t+4}$
11. $\sqrt{9-2 x}=\sqrt{5 x-12}$
12. $12-\sqrt{y+1}=14$
13. $4 \sqrt{z}+8=40$
14. $\sqrt{\frac{a+6}{a+2}}=\sqrt{\frac{a+2}{a-1}}$
15. $\sqrt{\frac{z}{z+3}}=\sqrt{\frac{z+2}{z+6}}$
16. $\sqrt{5 x-4}=\sqrt{7 x+2}$
summary: Explains the radical-equation workflow: isolate the radical, square both sides, solve the resulting linear equation, and check the original equation for extraneous roots.
title: 5.2 Linear Equations Involving Radicals
