## Defining an Absolute Value

The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0 on the number line. If $x$ is any point on the number line then its distance from 0 is denoted by $|x|$. The two vertical bars are called absolute value bars. Since distance between any two points is always a positive number or zero, thus the absolute value of a number is always a positive number or zero e.g. distance from 0 to 5 or from 0 to - 5 is 5 units on the number line.
Thus, $|5|=5$ and $|-5|=5$
The absolute value of a real number $x$, written as $|x|$, is defined as

- $|x|=x$, if $x \geq 0$
- $|x|=-x$ if $x<0$ e.g. $|9|=9$ or $|-3|=-(-3)=3$

5.3.2 Solution of Absolute Value Equations

An equation that contains a variable inside the absolute value bars is called an absolute value equation.

e.g. $|x|+1=5,|x-3|=4$

To solve the equations involving absolute value, we apply the basic definition of absolute value.
Example 7: Solve the equation $|x|=8$.
Solution: To solve such equation we have to consider both the possible values of the number with absolute value.
Thus, if $|x|=8$ then $x=8$ or $x=-8$.
The solution set is $\{-8,8\}$.
Example 8: Solve the equation $|x|=-6$.
Solution There is no real number $x$ such that $|x|=-6$. So, this equation has no solution. Hence the solution set is $\phi$.

Conclusions
An absolute value equation of the form $|a x+b|=c$, where $a, b$ and $c$ are real numbers, $a \neq 0$ and $c>0$ is equivalent to two equations:

$$
a x+b=c \quad \text { or } \quad a x+b=-c .
$$

For the required solution set of the given absolute value equation, we solve both the equations separately.
Example 9: Solve the equation:

$$
|2 x+5|=11 \text {, where } x \in \mathrm{R} \text {. }
$$

Solution:
Step-I: Remove the absolute value bars and write two equations as

$$
2 x+5=11 \quad \text { or } \quad 2 x+5=-11
$$

Step-II: Now solve both the equations for $x$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 x+5 & =11 \\
2 x & =11-5 \\
2 x & =6 \\
x & =3
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 x+5 & =-11 \\
2 x & =-11-5 \\
2 x & =-16 \\
x & =-8
\end{aligned}
$$

Step-III: Hence 3 and -8 are roots of the absolute value equations. Thus, the solution set is $\{3,-8\}$

- The equation $|x|=k$ and $k>0$ has two solutions $k$ and $-k$.
- The equation $|x|=0$ has one solution, namely $x=0$.
- The equation $|x|=k$ and $k<0$ has no solution and the solution set in this case is $\phi$.

Example 10: Solve the absolute value equation.

$$
\frac{|10-x|}{5}=\frac{|2 x-5|}{2} \quad, \quad \text { where } x \in R
$$

Solution: Before we remove the absolute value bars, try to isolate the absolute value expressions on either side as

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\frac{|10-x|}{5}=\frac{|2 x-5|}{2} \\
\frac{|10-x|}{|2 x-5|}=\frac{5}{2} \\
\frac{|10-x|}{2 x-5}=\frac{5}{2} \longleftrightarrow \frac{|a|}{|b|}=\left|\frac{a}{b}\right| \\
\frac{10-x}{2 x-5}=\frac{5}{2} & \text { or } \\
\frac{10-x}{2 x-5}=\frac{-10 x}{2} & \frac{10-x}{2 x-5}=-\frac{5}{2} \\
2(10-x)=5(2 x-5) & 2(10-x)=-5(2 x-5)
\end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{rlrl}
20-2 x & =10 x-25 & 20-2 x & =-10 x+25 \\
-12 x & =-45 & 8 x & =5 \\
x & =\frac{45}{12}=\frac{15}{4} & x & =\frac{5}{8}
\end{array}
$$

Thus, the solution set is $\left\{\frac{15}{4}, \frac{5}{8}\right\}$.
Example 11: Solve the following absolute value equaiton.

$$
|\mathrm{a}-1|=|2 \mathrm{a}-3|, \mathrm{a} \in \mathrm{R}
$$

Solution:
By removing the absolute value bars we get two equations as:

a $$
\begin{aligned}
-1 & =2 a \\
-a & =-2 \\
a & =2
\end{aligned}
$$

The solution set is $\left\{2, \frac{4}{3}\right\}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a-1 & =-(2 a-3) \\
a-1 & =-2 a+3 \\
3 a & =4 \\
a & =\frac{4}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

EXERCISE 5.3

Solve the following absolute value equations, where $x, y, \mathrm{z} \in \mathrm{R}$.

1. $|x|=\frac{5}{3}$
2. $|x+2|=6$
3. $|5 y-1|=9$
4. $|x+1|=2$
5. $|6-3 y|=0$
6. $3|z-2|-4=-2$
7. $|2 x-1|=5$
8. $|3 x+2|=7$
9. $\frac{|4 x|}{3}=12$
10. $|5 x|+10=5$
11. $\frac{|1-2 y|}{4}=3$
12. $\frac{|x+1|}{2}=\frac{|2 x-1|}{3}$
13. $|5 x-3|=|x+7|$
14. $|z+3|-3=5-|z+3|$
5.4 Linear Inequalities (or Inequations) in one Variable
5.4.1 Defining an Inequality

There are many ways in which two expressions may be unequal. The following symbols express some inequalities. Inequality Symbols

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
< & \text { is less than e.g. }-5<7 \\
> & \text { is greater than e.g. } 10>-3 \\
\leq \quad & \text { is less than or equal to e.g. } 7 \leq 7 \\
\geq & \text { is greater than or equal to e.g. } 5 \geq 1 \\
\neq & \text { is not equal to e.g. } 3, \neq 5
\end{array}
$$

A statement that "two algebraic expressions are not equal" is called an "inequality" or "inequation."

A linear inequality in one variable is an inequality (inequation) that can be written in the standard form of $a x+b<0$ (or $a x+b>0$ ) where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers and $a \neq 0$.

Examples: $\quad x \leq 3, \quad x \geq-2, x-5<-10,5 y-7<3 y+9,-5>-7,-3 \neq x+1$
Remark: Above mentioned definition is also valid for the symbols $\leq$ and $\geq$.
Some examples of linear inequations are $4 x+3 \geq 0, y>-7,8(x-2) \leq 3-5 x$ and $x+3<-5$

An inequality written with the symbols < or > is called a strict inequality.

## Solution of Linear Inequalities (in one variable)

The definitions of solution and solution set for inequalities are same as for equations.
A solution of an inequality is a replacement for the variable that makes the inequality true.
Solution set of an inequality is the set of all real numbers that satisfy the inequality.

Procedure:
The procedure for solving a linear inequality in one variable is almost identical to that for solving a linear equation. Here, also to isolate the variable, we use "properties of inequalities". These properties are similar to the properties of equality but there is one important difference that when both sides of an inequality are multiplied or divided by a negative number then direction of the inequality symbol is reversed. e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{cl}
\text { original inequality } & \longleftarrow \\
(-3)(-2)>(-3)(5) & \longleftarrow \\
6>-15 & \longleftarrow \\
6> & \text { multiplying both sides by }-3 \text { and reversing } \\
\text { inequality symbol } & \text { simplest form }
\end{array}
$$

Two or more inequalities that have the same solution set are called equivalent inequalities e.g. $x+5<8$ and $x<3$ are two equivalent inequalities.

Example 12: Solve the following inequality.

$$
8 x+9<6 x-7, \text { where } x \in \mathrm{R} .
$$

Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
8 x+9 & <6 x-7 \\
8 x-6 x & <-7-9 \\
2 x & <-16 \\
x & <-8
\end{aligned}
$$

The solution contais all real numbers less than -8.
Check the solution by replacing $x$ with any number less than -8 , for example -9 , as

$$
\begin{aligned}
8(-9)+9 & <6(-9)-7 \\
-72+9 & <-54-7 \\
-63 & <-61 \longleftarrow \text { true statement }
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the solution set is $\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{R} \wedge x<-8\}$.

Example 13: Solve the inequality.

$$
3(-4+5 y) \leq-8(1-2 y)+6, x \in \mathrm{R}
$$

Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3(-4+5 y) & \leq-8(1-2 y)+6 \\
-12+15 y & \leq-8+16 y+6 \\
-12+15 y & \leq 16 y-2 \\
-y & \leq 10 \\
y & \geq-10
\end{aligned}
$$

∴ Solution Set $=\left\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{R}_{A y} \geq-10\right\}$
Example 14: Solve. $\frac{1}{2} x+3 \geq \frac{1}{4} x+2, x \in \mathrm{R}$
Solution:

$$
\frac{1}{2} x+3 \geq \frac{1}{4} x+2
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
4\left(\frac{1}{2} x+3\right) & \geq 4\left(\frac{1}{4} x+2\right) \leftarrow \text { multiply both sides by LCM of denominators } \\
2 x+12 & \geq x+8 \\
x+12 & \geq 8 \\
x & \geq-4
\end{aligned}
$$

The solution set is $\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{R} \wedge x \geq-4\}$.
Compound Inequalities
Two inequalities that are joined by the word "and" or the word "or" are called compound inequalities e.g. $2 x<6$ and $3 x+2>-4,3 x+5>7$ or $4 x-1<3$
5.4.3 Solution of Compound Inequalities Joined with 'or'

When two inequalities are joined with connective word 'or', it is necessary to solve each inequality separately. The solution set of the compound inequality will be the union of both the solution sets i.e., the solution set will satisfy either one or both the inequalities.
Example 15: Solve the following.

$$
2 x+3>7 \text { or } 4 x-1<3 ; x \in \mathrm{R}
$$

Solution: We will solve both the inequalities for $x$ separately.

$$
\begin{array}{rlc}
2 x+3>7 & \text { or } & 4 x-1<3 \\
2 x>4 & \text { or } & 4 x<4 \\
x>2 & \text { or } & x<1
\end{array}
$$

$$
\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{R} \wedge x>2\} \text { or }\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{R} \wedge x<1\}
$$

Now the union of both the solution sets is

$$
\{x \mid x \in \text { R } \wedge x>2 \text { or } x<1\}
$$

Hence, the solution set of the given compound inequality contains all real numbers greater than 2 or less than 1 .
5.4.4 Solution of Compound Inequalities Joined with 'and'
When two inequalities are joined with the connective word 'and' then the solution set of the compound inequality will be the intersection of both the solution sets i.e. the solution set contains all the solutions that satisfy both of the inequalities.

Example 16: Solve the compound inequality.

$$
x-5 \geq-1 \text { and } x+3 \leq 10, x \in \mathrm{R}
$$

Solution: Solve both the inequalities for ' $x$ '.

$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
x-5 \geq-1 & \text { and } & x+3 \leq 10 \\
x \geq 4 & \text { and } & x \leq 7 \\
\{x \mid x \in R \wedge x \geq 4\} & \text { and } & \{x \mid x \in R \wedge x \leq 7\}
\end{array}
$$

Intersection of two solution sets is $\{x \mid x \in \mathrm{R} \wedge 4 \leq x \leq 7\}$
i.e. Solution set consists of all real numbers that are greater than or equal to 4 and less than or equal to 7 .

Key Fact

- Two inequalities $-6<5 x+3$ and $5 x+3<5$ can be written in combined form as $-6<5 x+3<5$.
- There is no short way to write a compound inequality containing 'or'.
- Compound inequality containing and is true if its both inequalities are true.

Example 17: The sum of two times a number $x$ and 3 is between 5 and 17 . Between what two numbers is the given number $x$ ?

Solution: Expression 'sum of 2 times a number $x$ and 3' can be written as $2 x+3$. Then given compound inequality is ' $5<2 x+3<17$ '.
Now we solve this compound inequality.

$$
\begin{aligned}
5 & <2 x+3<17 \\
5-3 & <2 x<17-3 \\
2 & <2 x<14 \\
1 & <x<7
\end{aligned} \text { - subtracting } 3 \text { from each part }
$$

Thus, $x$ lies in between 1 and 7.

Vath Play Ground

a. Take students to the play ground.
b. Give each student a paper strip with some equation or inequality written on.
c. Spread solutions of all students in the play ground.
d. Ask them to find the respective answers as a game of treasure hunt.
summary: Uses the definition of absolute value to solve equations by considering both signed cases and recognizing when a negative absolute-value target has no real solution.
title: 5.3 Equations Involving Absolute Value

mdxBody:
Trigonometry is the branch of Mathematics that deals with the relationship of sides with angles in a triangle. With trigonometry, finding out the heights of big mountains or towers is possible. It is also used to find the distance between stars or planets in astronomy and is widely used in physics, architecture, engineering and GPS navigation systems. Trigonometry is based on the principle that if two triangles have the same set of angles, their corresponding sides are in the same ratio.

The measurement along with direction of angles plays an important role in satellite navigation. By using trigonometric and bearing principles, navigation has become easier for the military and hikers . Direction compass supports in getting clear picture of the angle between cardinal and intercardinal directions.
<CaptionedImage src="kg22n4jjvpdvbxvnjjdttk67c18bv8zd" alt="" caption="" />
<CaptionedImage src="kg22zjsq74nqx809djwbtx7e6x8bvryb" alt="" caption="" />
<CaptionedImage src="kg2622tmv53pf3v3ybxvrttjs58bt5ac" alt="" caption="" />

Union of two rays having common end point forms an angle. An angle is positive or negative if measured in anti-clockwise or clockwise direction respectively.
<CaptionedImage src="kg22x5pjqynvjcbfpcfap9rjnh8btsxn" alt="" caption="" />
<CaptionedImage src="kg2bg45543cm7xkyz16b1bqngd8bvs3x" alt="" caption="" />
Angle in standard position
An angle when drawn in the cartesian plane(rectangular coordinate system) is in standard position if its vertex is at the origin and its initial arm. is directed along positive x-axis. Its terminal arm may lie either on any of the axis or in any of the quadrants.
There are three systems of measurement of an angle.

i. Sexagesimal System or English System
ii. Radian measure or Circular System
iii. Centesimal or French System

Centesimal or French system is beyond the scope of this book.

## Sexagesimal System

Draw a circle and divide its boundary into 360 equal arcs. The central angle of each arc is of measure 1 degree $\left(1^{\circ}\right)$. To draw an angle of $30^{\circ}$, we need 30 consecutive arcs of $1^{\circ}$ As $90^{\circ}$ is one fourth of $360^{\circ}$, so 90 consecutive arcs of $1^{\circ}$ form a quadrant of the circle. i.e., central angle of quadrant of a circle is $90^{\circ}$. There are 180 arcs of $1^{\circ}$ in a half circle and all 360 arcs form a complete circle. i.e., central angle of half circle is $180^{\circ}$ and that of full circle it is $360^{\circ}$. To measure the central angle of an arc whose length is smaller than the length of $\operatorname{arc}$ of $1^{\circ}$, we divide the arc of $1^{\circ}$ into further 60 equal arcs. The central angle of each of these small arcs is of measure 1 minute denoted as $1^{\prime}$. So, there are $60^{\prime}$ in a degree. Similarly, there are 60 seconds $\left(60^{\prime \prime}\right)$ in a minute.
<CaptionedImage src="kg28nqrk22bspav3d5x565qp218btjrg" alt="" caption="" />
Thus, $1^{\circ}=60^{\prime}, 1^{\prime}=60^{\prime \prime}, 1^{\circ}=3600^{\prime \prime}$.

$$
1^{\prime}=\left(\frac{1}{60}\right)^{\circ}, 1^{\prime \prime}=\left(\frac{1}{60}\right)^{\prime}, 1^{\prime \prime}=\left(\frac{1}{3600}\right)^{\circ} .
$$

In sexagesimal system, an angle is measured in Degrees, Minutes and Seconds.
Example 1: Convert the following measures of angles into seconds.
i. $30^{\prime}$
ii. 60°
iii. $45^{\circ} 45^{\prime} 45^{\prime \prime}$

Solution:

i. $30^{\prime}=30 \times 60^{\prime \prime}=1800^{\prime \prime}$

ii. $60^{\circ}=60 \times 60^{\prime}=3600^{\prime}=3600 \times 60^{\prime \prime}=216000^{\prime \prime}$

iii. $$
\begin{aligned}
45^{\circ} 45^{\prime} 45^{\prime \prime} & =45^{\circ}+45^{\prime}+45^{\prime \prime} \\
& =45 \times 3600^{\prime \prime}+45 \times 60^{\prime \prime}+45^{\prime \prime} \\
& =162000^{\prime \prime}+2700^{\prime \prime}+45^{\prime \prime}=164745^{\prime \prime}
\end{aligned}
$$

Example 2: Convert the following measures of angles into minutes
i. $36^{\circ}$
ii. 45''
iii. $36^{\circ} 45^{\prime} 30^{\prime \prime}$

Solution:

i. $\quad 36^{\circ}=36 \times 60^{\prime}=2160^{\prime}$.
ii. $\quad 45^{\prime \prime}=\left(45 \times \frac{1}{60}\right)^{\prime}=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{\prime}=0.75^{\prime}$
iii. $36^{\circ} 45^{\prime} 30^{\prime \prime}=36^{\circ}+45^{\prime}+30^{\prime \prime}$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& =36 \times 60^{\prime}+45^{\prime}+\left(\frac{30}{60}\right)^{\prime} \\
& =2160^{\prime}+45^{\prime}+0.5^{\prime}=2205.5^{\prime}
\end{aligned}
$$

Example 3: Write the following measures of angles into $\mathrm{D}^{\circ} \mathrm{M}^{\prime} \mathrm{S}^{\prime \prime}$.
i. $60.5^{\circ}$
ii. 45.125°
iii. $3600^{\prime \prime}$
iv. 216000"
v. $20.555^{\prime}$

Solution:

i. $$
\begin{aligned}
60.5^{\circ} & =60^{\circ}+0.5^{\circ} \\
& =60^{\circ}+0.5 \times 60^{\prime} \\
& =60^{\circ}+30^{\prime}=60^{\circ} 30^{\prime}
\end{aligned}
$$
ii. $$
\begin{aligned}
45.125^{\circ} & =45^{\circ}+0.125^{\circ} \\
& =45^{\circ}+0.125 \times 60^{\prime} \\
& =45^{\circ}+7.5^{\prime} \\
& =45^{\circ}+7^{\prime}+0.5 \times 60^{\prime \prime}=45^{\circ} 7^{\prime} 30^{\prime \prime}
\end{aligned}
$$
iii. $3600^{\prime \prime}=\left(\frac{3600}{60}\right)^{\prime}=60^{\prime}=1^{\circ}=1^{\circ} 0^{\prime} 0^{\prime \prime}$
iv. $216000^{\prime \prime}=\left(\frac{216000}{60}\right)^{\prime}=3600^{\prime}=\left(\frac{3600}{60}\right)^{\circ}=60^{\circ} 0^{\prime} 0^{\prime \prime}$
v. $$
\begin{aligned}
20.555^{\prime} & =20^{\prime}+0.555^{\prime} \\
& =20^{\prime}+0.555 \times 60^{\prime \prime} \\
& =20^{\prime}+33.3^{\prime \prime}=0^{\circ} 20^{\prime} 33^{\prime \prime}
\end{aligned}
$$

Example 4: Write the following measures of angles in degrees correct to 4 decimal places.
i. $60^{\circ} 30^{\prime} 30^{\prime \prime}$
ii. 75°25'35''

Solution:

i. $$
\begin{aligned}
60^{\circ} 30^{\prime} 30^{\prime \prime} & =60^{0}+\left(\frac{30}{60}\right)^{0}+\left(\frac{30}{3600}\right)^{0} \\
& =60^{\circ}+0.5^{0}+0.0083^{0}=60.5083^{0}
\end{aligned}
$$
ii. $$
\begin{aligned}
75^{\circ} 25^{\prime} 35^{\prime \prime} & =75^{0}+\left(\frac{25}{60}\right)^{0}+\left(\frac{35}{3600}\right)^{0} \\
& =75^{0}+0.4167^{0}+0.0097^{0}=75.4264^{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Circular System or Radian Measure

The ratio between length of circular arc and radius is called radian. If length of an arc is equal to radius of circle, then their ratio is 1 radian. i.e., one radian is measure of central angle of an arc whose length is equal to radius of the circle.
The ratio between circumference and radius of a circle is $2 \pi$, therefore measure of a complete angle in circular system is $2 \pi$ radians.
<CaptionedImage src="kg20zd9zaxvqrptyh7aqyr51vh8btvej" alt="" caption="" />

In circular system, an angle is measured in radians.
In sexagesimal system measure of a complete angle is $360^{\circ}$,
so

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 \pi \text { radians } & =360^{\circ} \\
\pi \text { radians } & =180^{\circ} \\
1 \text { radian } & =\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^{\circ} \\
& \approx 57^{\circ} 17^{\prime} 45^{\prime \prime}
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
1^{0}=\frac{\pi}{180} \text { radians } \approx 0.0175 \text { radians }
$$

To convert measure of an angle given in radians to degrees, multiply its value by $\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^{0}$ and to convert measure of an angle given in degrees to radians, multiply its value by $\frac{\pi}{180}$ radians.
<CaptionedImage src="kg23m4xkrec90dp0shf8fqd3fs8btfd6" alt="" caption="" />

Example 5:
Convert the following measures of angles in sexagesimal system ( $\mathrm{D}^{\circ} \mathrm{M}^{\prime} \mathrm{S}^{\prime}$ ).
i. 2.125 radians
ii. 0.5 radians
iii. $\frac{\pi}{3}$ radians
iv. $\frac{3 \pi}{4}$ radians

Solution:

i. $$
\begin{aligned}
2.125 \text { radians } & =2.125 \times\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^{0} \\
& \approx 2.125 \times 57.2958^{0} \\
& \approx 121.7535^{0} \\
& =121^{0}+0.7535 \times 60^{\prime} \\
& =121^{0}+45.21^{\prime} \\
& =121^{0}+45^{\prime}+0.21 \times 60^{\prime \prime}=121^{0} 45^{\prime} 13^{\prime \prime}
\end{aligned}
$$

ii. $\quad 0.5$ radians $=0.5 \times\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^{0}$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \approx 0.5 \times 57.2958^{0} \\
& \approx 28.6479^{0} \\
& =28^{0}+0.6479 \times 60^{\prime} \\
& =28^{0}+38.874^{\prime} \\
& =28^{0}+38^{\prime}+0.874 \times 60^{\prime \prime}=28^{0} 38^{\prime} 52^{\prime \prime}
\end{aligned}
$$
iii. $\quad \frac{\pi}{3}$ radians $=\frac{\pi}{3} \times\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^{0}$
$$
=\left(\frac{180}{3}\right)^{0}=60^{0}
$$
iv. $\quad \frac{3 \pi}{4}$ radians $=\frac{3 \pi}{4} \times\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^{0}$
$$
=\left(\frac{540}{4}\right)^{0}=135^{0}
$$

Example 6:
Convert the following measures of angles in radians.
i. $45^{0}$
ii. $150^{0}$
iii. $300^{0}$
iv. $30^{\circ} 30^{\prime} 30^{\prime \prime}$

Solution:

i. $\quad 45^{0} \quad=45 \times \frac{\pi}{180}$ radians $=\frac{\pi}{4}$ radians $\approx 0.7854$ radians
ii. $150^{0}=150 \times \frac{\pi}{180}$ radians
$$
=\frac{5 \pi}{6} \text { radians } \approx 2.618 \text { radians }
$$
iii. $300^{0}=300 \times \frac{\pi}{180}$ radians
$$
=\frac{5 \pi}{3} \text { radians } \approx 5.236 \text { radians }
$$
iv. $\quad 30^{\circ} 30^{\prime} 30^{\prime \prime}=30.5083^{\circ}$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& =30.5083 \times \frac{\pi}{180} \text { radians } \\
& \approx 30.5083 \times 0.0175 \text { radians } \\
& \approx 0.5325 \text { radians }
\end{aligned}
$$

EXERCISE 6.1

ii. 30'

$$
\pi=3.1416 .
$$

6.2.1 Length of an Are

Length of a circular arc and radian measure of its central angle are directly proportional. i.e., ratio between length of an arc and radian measure of its central angle remains constant.
Consider a circle of radius r with centre O . Choose an arc of length $l$ on circumference. Let $\theta$ be the radian measure of central angle of that arc. Now choose another are whose central angle is of 1 radian. The length $\left(l_{1}\right)$ of such arc is equal to the radius. i.e. $l_{1}=\mathrm{r}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& l: \theta:: l_{1}: 1 \\
& l: \theta:: \mathrm{r}: 1 \\
& l: 1=\mathrm{r} \times \theta \\
& l=\mathrm{r} \theta
\end{aligned}
$$

So, length of a circular arc is product of radius and radian measure of central angle.

<CaptionedImage src="kg22dc4e057rz6gh7mrgq7zg558bvk37" alt="" caption="(i)" />

6.2.2 Area of Sector of a Circle

The union of a circle and its interior region is the circular region. The circular region bounded by an arc and its two corresponding radial segments is called sector of the circle. In figure (i) shaded region is a sector of the circle with radius r and $\theta$ the radian measure of central angle. Like arc length, area(A) of sector is directly proportional to the radian measure of central angle.
area of sector : $\theta$ : : area of circle : complete angle

$$
\begin{aligned}
A: \theta:: & \pi \mathrm{r}^{2}: 2 \pi \\
2 \pi A & =\pi \mathrm{r}^{2} \theta \\
A & =\frac{\pi \mathrm{r}^{2} \theta}{2 \pi} \\
& =\frac{\mathrm{r}^{2} \theta}{2},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\theta$ is in radians.
Example 7:
Find length of an arc of a circle whose central angle and radius are given below.
i. $\quad \theta=\frac{\pi}{4} \mathrm{rad}, \mathrm{r}=2 \mathrm{~cm}$
ii. $\theta=60^{\circ}, \mathrm{r}=30 \mathrm{~cm}$

Solution:
i.

$$
\begin{aligned}
l & =\mathrm{r} \theta \\
& =2 \times \frac{\pi}{4} \\
& =\frac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{~cm} \\
& =\frac{3.14}{4} \\
& =1.57 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

ii.

$$
\theta=60^{\circ}=\frac{\pi}{3} \mathrm{rad}, \mathrm{r}=30 \mathrm{~cm}
$$

Example 8:
Find area of the sector of a circle whose central angle is $120^{\circ}$ and radius 5 cm .
Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{r} & =5 \mathrm{~cm}, \\
\theta & =120^{\circ}=\frac{2 \pi}{3} \mathrm{rad} \\
\mathrm{~A} & =\frac{\mathrm{r}^{2} \theta}{2}=\frac{1}{2}(5)^{2}\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right) \\
& =\frac{25 \pi}{3} \mathrm{~cm}^{2}=26.18 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Example 9:
The length of an arc and area of sector of a circle are 4 cm and $16 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ respectively. Find radius and central angle of sector.
Solution:

$$
l=4 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~A}=16 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}, \mathrm{r}=?, \theta=?
$$

As, $l=\mathrm{r} \theta$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & r \theta=4 \\
\therefore & \theta=\frac{l}{r}=\frac{4}{r}
\end{array}
$$

Now

$$
\mathrm{A}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{r}^{2} \theta
$$

$16=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{r}^{2} \times \frac{4}{r}$ (substituting the value of $\theta$ )

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 16=2 r \\
& r=8 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \theta & =\frac{4}{r} \\
& =\frac{4}{8} \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{rad} .
\end{aligned}
$$

5. A 30 inch pendulum swings through an angle of 30°. Find the length of the arc in inches through which the tip of the pendulum swings.
6. A motorcycle is traveling on a curve along a highway. The curve is an arc of a circle with radius of 10 km . If the motorcycle's speed is $42 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$, what is the angle in degrees through which the motorcycle will turn in 21 minutes?
7. Find perimeter and area of a half circle in the following figure by using the formulae $l=r \theta, A=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{r}^{2} \theta$.

## General Angle

In coordinate plane, the two axes divide the plane in four equivalent parts called quadrants. If we place an angle in the coordinate plane such that its vertex coincides with origin and one of its rays lies along $\overrightarrow{O X}$ (+ve x-axis), then this angle is said to be in standard position. The ray along $\overrightarrow{O X}$ is called initial ray and second ray in the plane is called terminal ray. Such an angle is called general angle. Measure of an angle is positive in anticlockwise direction and is negative in clockwise direction.
<CaptionedImage src="kg22zxy03q2dj3cn8k5c5nrq8x8bvx6k" alt="" caption="" />
In the adjoining figure two angles in standard position are drawn. Both have same terminal ray. One of them is $150^{\circ}$ (in anticlock wise direction) and the other is $-210^{0}$ (in clock wise direction). Two angles having same terminal ray in standard position are called co-terminal angles. The measure of a general angle can be greater than $360^{\circ}$.
<CaptionedImage src="kg2dn0wnn3wm9w1fwdgmj4fv2h8btm15" alt="" caption="" />

To draw a general angle whose measure is greater than $360^{\circ}$, we subtract any multiple of $360^{\circ}$ from its value and try to find a value less than $360^{\circ}$. Terminal ray of $360^{\circ}$ or that of any of its multiple coincides with $0^{0}$, i.e., $\overrightarrow{O X}$. In general, two angles are co-terminal if their measures differ by some multiple of $360^{\circ}$. e.g., to draw an angle of $390^{\circ}$, first find $390^{\circ}-360^{\circ}=30^{\circ}$, then draw $30^{\circ}$ in anticlockwise direction. $390^{\circ}$ and $30^{\circ}$ have same terminal ray so they are co-terminal angles. Similarly, $150^{\circ}$ and $-210^{0}$ are co-terminal angles.
<CaptionedImage src="kg24bhpag6yv8xs8jjaxem36p18btydq" alt="" caption="" />
6.3.2 Quadrantal Angles

If terminal ray of an angle in standard position coincides with any of the axes, then it is called quadrantal angle. The measure of a quadrantal angle is a multiple of $90^{\circ}$.
e.g., $0^{0}, 90^{0}, 180^{0}, 270^{0}, 360^{0}, 450^{0}, \ldots$ are the quadrantal angles.
In radian measure, quadrantal angle is a multiple of $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
e.g., $0, \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \frac{3 \pi}{2}, 2 \pi, \frac{5 \pi}{2}, 3 \pi \ldots$ are quadrantal angles.
Terminal rays of $0^{0}, 360^{0}, 720^{0}, \ldots$ are along $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OX}}$.
Terminal rays of $180^{\circ}, 540^{\circ}, 900^{\circ}, \ldots$ are along $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OX}}$.
Terminal rays of $90^{\circ}, 450^{\circ}, 810^{\circ}, \ldots$ are along $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OY}}$.
Terminal rays of $270^{\circ}, 630^{\circ}, 990^{\circ}, \ldots$ are along $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OY}^{\prime}}$.
Unit Circle
A circle whose radius is of 1 unit is called a unit circle.
In standard position centre of a unit circle is O (Origin).
The equation of a unit circle centered at O is $\mathrm{x}^{2}+y^{2}=1$.
Trigonometric Ratios
The ratio between any two sides of a right-angled triangle
<CaptionedImage src="kg21w0dys253zw2ww3jc9h18a18btarn" alt="" caption="" /> is called a trigonometric ratio. There are six possible trigonometric ratios corresponding to an angle.In triangle $\mathrm{ABC}, \angle \mathrm{C}=90^{\circ}, \angle \mathrm{A}=\theta, \mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{BC}=\mathrm{a}$ and $\mathrm{CA}=\mathrm{b}$.With respect to an acute angle $\theta, a$ is the length of perpendicular, $b$ is the length of base and $c$ is the length of hypotenuse.
Various trigonometric ratios are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\text { Perpendicular }}{\text { Hypotenuse }}=\frac{a}{c}, \frac{\text { Base }}{\text { Hypotenuse }}=\frac{b}{c}, \frac{\text { Perpendicular }}{\text { Base }}=\frac{a}{b}, \\
& \frac{\text { Hypotenuse }}{\text { Perpendicular }}=\frac{c}{a}, \frac{\text { Hypotenuse }}{\text { Base }}=\frac{c}{b}, \frac{\text { Base }}{\text { Perpendicular }}=\frac{b}{a}
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg2dzmkrc6qq607re4f8xmy7rn8bvkb9" alt="" caption="" />

- The ratio of perpendicular and hypotenuse is $\sin e$ of $\theta$ denoted by $\sin \theta$.
$$
\therefore \sin \theta=\frac{\text { Perpendicular }}{\text { Hypotenuse }}=\frac{a}{c}
$$
- The ratio of base and hypotenuse is cosine of $\theta$ denoted by $\cos \theta$.
$$
\therefore \cos \theta=\frac{\text { Base }}{\text { Hypotenuse }}=\frac{b}{c}
$$
- The ratio of perpendicular and base is tangent of $\theta$ denoted by $\tan \theta$.
$$
\therefore \tan \theta=\frac{\text { Perpendicular }}{\text { Base }}=\frac{a}{b}
$$
- The ratio of hypotenuse and perpendicular is cosecant $\theta$ denoted by $\operatorname{cosec} \theta$.
$$
\therefore \operatorname{cosec} \theta=\frac{\text { Hypotenuse }}{\text { Perpendicular }}=\frac{c}{a}=\frac{1}{\sin \theta}
$$
- The ratio of hypotenuse and base is secant of $\theta$ denoted by $\sec \theta$.
$$
\therefore \sec \theta=\frac{\text { Hypotenuse }}{\text { Base }}=\frac{c}{b}=\frac{1}{\cos \theta}
$$
- The ratio of base and perpendicular is cotangent of $\theta$ denoted by $\cot \theta$.
$$
\therefore \cot \theta=\frac{\text { Base }}{\text { Perpendicular }}=\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1}{\tan \theta}
$$
- $\operatorname{cosec} \theta, \sec \theta$ and $\cot \theta$ are respectively reciprocals of $\sin \theta, \cos \theta$ and $\tan \theta$.

6.3.3 Trigonometric Ratios with the Help of Unit Circle
Consider a unit circle centered at O .
Mark a point $\mathrm{P}(x, \mathrm{y})$ on the circle. Join P with O .
Draw PA perpendicular to x -axis.
$\mathrm{OA}=x, \mathrm{PA}=y$ and $\mathrm{OP}=1$ (radius of circle).
If $\angle \mathrm{AOP}=\theta$, then $\sin \theta=\frac{y}{1}=\mathrm{y}$ and $\cos \theta=\frac{x}{1}=x$.
So, coordinates of P are $(\cos \theta, \sin \theta)$.
i.e., $x=\cos \theta$ and $y=\sin \theta$. Also, $\tan \theta=\frac{y}{x}$.
<CaptionedImage src="kg2bakv6svbf538wx2z59mzkhd8bv8bp" alt="" caption="" />
Reciprocal of $y$ is $\operatorname{cosec} \theta$, reciprocal of $x$ is $\sec \theta$ and reciprocal of $\frac{y}{x}$ is $\cot \theta$.
If P is a point on a unit circle centered at O and $\angle \mathrm{AOP}=\theta$, then coordinates of P are $(\cos \theta, \sin \theta)$.
6.3.4 Trigonometric Ratios of $30^{\circ}, 45^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$
Trigonometric Ratios of $30^{\circ}$
To find trigonometric ratios of $30^{\circ}$, choose a point $\mathrm{P}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ on unit circle in standard position such that $\angle \mathrm{O}=\theta=30^{\circ}$. Draw PA perpendicular to x-axis. As in a right-angled triangle length of side opposite to $30^{\circ}$ is half of hypotenuse, so in right angled triangle $\mathrm{OAP}, \mathrm{y}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$.
Equation of unit circle is $\mathrm{x}^{2}+y^{2}=1$.
Put $x=x_{1}$ and $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{y}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ in above equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{1}^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=1 \\
& x_{1}^{2}=1-\frac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

Coordinates of P are $\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$.
<CaptionedImage src="kg27tpw87zxj044pfpzvt915t58bt85n" alt="" caption="" />
So, $\cos 30^{\circ}=x_{1}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \sin 30^{\circ}=y_{1}=\frac{1}{2}, \tan 30^{\circ}=\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$
$\sec 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{x_{1}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \operatorname{cosec} 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{y_{1}}=2$, and $\cot 30^{\circ}=\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}=\sqrt{3}$.
Trigonometric Ratios of $\mathbf{4 5}^{\mathbf{0}}$
To find trigonometric ratios of $45^{\circ}$, choose a point $\mathrm{P}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ on a unit circle in standard position such that $\angle \mathrm{O}=\theta=45^{\circ}$. Draw PA perpendicular to x-axis. Triangle OAP is right isosceles.
Therefore, $\mathrm{AP}=\mathrm{OA}$ or $x_{1}=y_{1}$.
Equation of unit circle is $\mathrm{x}^{2}+y^{2}=1$.
Put $x=x_{1}$ and $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{y}_{1}=x_{1}$ in above equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{1}^{2}+x_{1}^{2}=1 \\
& 2 x_{1}^{2}=1 \\
& x_{1}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \text { also } y_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg22562tsjg48zd0yemavgfjrd8btk7b" alt="" caption="" />

Coordinates of P are $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$.
So, $\cos 45^{\circ}=x_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \quad \sin 45^{\circ}=y_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \quad \tan 45^{\circ}=\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}}=1$,

$$
\sec 45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{x_{1}}=\sqrt{2}, \operatorname{cosec} 45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{y_{1}}=\sqrt{2}, \text { and } \cot 45^{\circ}=\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}=1 .
$$

Trigonometric Ratios of $\mathbf{6 0}^{\mathbf{0}}$
To find trigonometric ratios of $60^{\circ}$, choose a point $\mathrm{P}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ on unit circle in standard position such that $\angle \mathrm{O}=\theta=60^{\circ}$. Draw PA perpendicular to x-axis. As in a right-angled triangle two acute angles are complementary so $\angle \mathrm{OPA}=30^{\circ}$. As in a right-angled triangle length of side opposite to $30^{\circ}$ is half of hypotenuse, so $x_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$.
Equation of unit circle is $\mathrm{x}^{2}+y^{2}=1$.
Put $x=x_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=y_{1}$ in above equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+y_{1}^{2}=1 \\
& y_{1}^{2}=1-\frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow y_{1}^{2}=\frac{3}{4} \Rightarrow y_{1}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \text { also } x_{1}=\frac{1}{2},
\end{aligned}
$$

Coordinates of P are $\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.
So, $\cos 60^{\circ}=x_{1}=\frac{1}{2}, \quad \sin 60^{\circ}=y_{1}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$,
<CaptionedImage src="kg25pptr4bwhgadk4d1rsnrybd8bt35j" alt="" caption="" />

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tan 60^{\circ}=\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}}=\sqrt{3}, \quad \sec 60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{x_{1}}=2 \\
& \operatorname{cosec} 60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{y_{1}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \text { and } \cot 60^{\circ}=\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

6.3.5 Signs of Trigonometric Ratios in the Four Quadrants
If $\mathrm{P}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ is a point on a unit circle such that $\angle \mathrm{XOP}=\theta$, then $\mathrm{x}_{1}=\cos \theta$ and $\mathrm{y}_{1}=\sin \theta$.
First Quadrant
If P lies in first quadrant, then $\theta$ lies between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{0}$. Both coordinates of P are positive i.e., $x_{1}>0$ and $y_{1}>0$. So, in first quadrant $\cos \theta>0$ and $\sin \theta>0$. As the quotient and reciprocals of positive numbers are also positive so in first quadrant all trigonometric ratios are positive.
Second Quadrant
<CaptionedImage src="kg24q1hnj5e73q5rkd9raqf11x8btsay" alt="" caption="" />
If P lies in second quadrant, then $\theta$ lies between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$. In second quadrant abscissa of a point is negative and ordinate is positive i.e. $x_{1}<0$ and $y_{1}>0$.
So, in second quadrant $\cos \theta<0$ and $\sin \theta>0$.
As the quotient of a negative and a positive number is negative so $\tan \theta<0$ and $\cot \theta<0$.
As reciprocal of a negative number is negative and that of positive number is positive so $\sec \theta<0$ and $\operatorname{cosec} \theta>0$.
<CaptionedImage src="kg2cxtsm2h91dhjf28h3x674418btea1" alt="" caption="" />

Third Quadrant
If P lies in third quadrant, then $\theta$ lies between $180^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$. In third quadrant both abscissa and ordinate of a point are negative i.e., $x_{1}<0$ and $y_{1}<0$. So, in third quadrant $\cos \theta<0$ and $\sin \theta<0$. As the quotient of two negative numbers is positive so $\tan \theta>0$ and $\cot \theta>0$. As reciprocals of negative numbers are negative, so $\sec \theta<0$ and $\operatorname{cosec} \theta<0$.
<CaptionedImage src="kg2748e7w5k1mbyf40d79s2y898bv60t" alt="" caption="" />

Fourth Quadrant
If P lies in fourth quadrant, then $\theta$ lies between $270^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$. In fourth quadrant abscissa of a point is positive and ordinate is negative i.e. $x_{1}>0$ and $y_{1}<0$.
So in fourth quadrant $\cos \theta>0$ and $\sin \theta<0$. As the quotient of a negative and a positive number is negative so $\tan \theta<0$ and $\cot \theta<0$. As reciprocal of a negative number is negative and that of positive number is positive, so $\sec \theta>0$ and $\operatorname{cosec} \theta<0$.
<CaptionedImage src="kg2406w1qw527kb94qda6j1m2h8bvqfz" alt="" caption="" />

The figure at right would be helpful to understand the signs of trigonometric ratios in different quadrants.

<CaptionedImage src="kg257v0dmwknpztc9sm2e3nhgs8bt3zv" alt="" caption="" />
To Be Observed!
When point P lies in any of the quadrants or on any of the axis, by joining it to origin, we get the angle $\theta$ formed by terminal arm OP in standard position, then:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sin \theta=\frac{\text { algebraic distance of } P \text { from } x \text {-axis }}{\text { distance of } P \text { from origin }}=\frac{y}{r} \\
& \cos \theta=\frac{\text { algebraic distance of } P \text { from } y \text {-axis }}{\text { distance of } P \text { from origin }}=\frac{x}{r} \\
& \tan \theta=\frac{\text { algebraic distance of } P \text { from } x \text {-axis }}{\text { algebraic distance of } P \text { from } y \text {-axis }}=\frac{y}{x}
\end{aligned}
$$
(due to the word 'algebraic', $x$ and $y$ will get +/-sign according to the quadrant of P ) We consider $r=1$ in a unit circle.

6.3.6 Evaluation of Trigonometric Ratios of an Angle if One of Them is Given
We can find all the trigonometric ratios of a particular angle if one of them is given i.e. if value of ' $\sin \theta$ ' is given, then we can find the remaining ratios, for the same value of $\theta$.
Example 10:
If $\sin \theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and terminal ray of $\theta$ is in first quadrant, then find remaining trigonometric ratios for same value of $\theta$.
Solution: Method I
Consider a right-angled triangle ABC, in which $\mathrm{m} \angle \mathrm{C}=90^{\circ}, \mathrm{m} \angle \mathrm{A}=\theta$.
By definition $\sin \theta=\frac{\text { perpendicular }}{\text { hypotenuse }}=\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AB}}$
But $\sin \theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (given)
So, $\mathrm{BC}=\sqrt{3}$ and $\mathrm{AB}=2$
By Pythagoras theorem $\mathrm{AB}^{2}=\mathrm{AC}^{2}+\mathrm{BC}^{2}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 2^{2}=A \mathrm{C}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2} \\
& 4=A \mathrm{C}^{2}+3 \\
& 4-3=A \mathrm{C}^{2} \\
& A \mathrm{C}^{2}=1 \Rightarrow A C=1
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg204849eg5bes16rv17y6mm3n8bvt9f" alt="" caption="" />

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \cos \theta=\frac{\text { base }}{\text { hypotenuse }}=\frac{A C}{A B}=\frac{1}{2}, \quad \sec \theta=\frac{1}{\cos \theta}=2 \\
& \tan \theta=\frac{\text { perpendicular }}{\text { base }}=\frac{B C}{A C}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1}=\sqrt{3}, \quad \cot \theta=\frac{1}{\tan \theta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \quad \operatorname{cosec} \theta=\frac{1}{\sin \theta}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Method II
Consider a unit circle at $O$. Mark a point $P$ on the circle in first quadrant whose y coordinate is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. The equation of unit circle is $\mathrm{x}^{2}+y^{2}=1$.
Put $\mathrm{y}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{x}^{2}+\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{2}=1 \\
& \mathrm{x}^{2}=1-\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow x= \pm \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since, P is in first quadrant so $x>0$. i.e., $x=\frac{1}{2}$
So, $\cos \theta=x=\frac{1}{2}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tan \theta=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\sqrt{3}, \quad \operatorname{cosec} \theta=\frac{1}{\sin \theta}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\
& \sec \theta=\frac{1}{\cos \theta}=2, \quad \cot \theta=\frac{1}{\tan \theta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

6.3.7 Trigonometric Ratios of Quadrantal Angles
Trigonometric Ratios of $0^{\mathbf{0}}$
To find trigonometric ratios of $0^{0}$, choose a point $\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{x}_{1}, \mathrm{y}_{1}\right)$ on unit circle in standard position such that $\angle \mathrm{XOP}=\theta=0^{0}$.
As P lies on x -axis so its coordinates are $x_{1}=1$ and $\mathrm{y}_{1}=0$.
So, $\cos 0^{0}=x_{1}=1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sin 0^{\circ}=y_{1}=0 \\
& \tan 0^{\circ}=\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}}=\frac{0}{1}=0 \\
& \sec 0^{\circ}=\frac{1}{x_{1}}=\frac{1}{1}=1 \\
& \operatorname{cosec} 0^{\circ}=\frac{1}{y_{1}}=\frac{1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) } \\
& \cot 0^{\circ}=\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}=\frac{1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) }
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg21stwhmhddct9a6p78fegtn58btwrq" alt="" caption="" />
Trigonometric Ratios of $90^{0}$
To find trigonometric ratios of $90^{\circ}$, choose a point $\mathrm{P}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ on unit circle in standard position such that $\angle \mathrm{XOP}=\theta=90^{\circ}$.
As P lies on y -axis so its coordinates are $x_{1}=0$ and $\mathrm{y}_{1}=1$.
So, $\cos 90^{\circ}=x_{1}=0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sin 90^{\circ}=y_{1}=1 \\
& \tan 90^{\circ}=\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}}=\frac{1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) } \\
& \sec 90^{\circ}=\frac{1}{x_{1}}=\frac{1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) } \\
& \operatorname{cosec} 90^{\circ}=\frac{1}{y_{1}}=\frac{1}{1}=1 \\
& \cot 90^{\circ}=\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}=\frac{0}{1}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg2025w1ka82bbnb5rmxeeabqn8btq91" alt="" caption="" />
Trigonometric Ratios of $\mathbf{1 8 0}^{\mathbf{0}}$
To find trigonometric ratios of $180^{\circ}$, choose a point $\mathrm{P}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ on unit circle in standard position such that $\angle \mathrm{XOP}=\theta=180^{\circ}$.
As P lies on x -axis at left side of O so its coordinates are $x_{1}=-1$ and $y_{1}=0$.
So, $\cos 180^{\circ}=x_{1}=-1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sin 180^{\circ}=y_{1}=0 \\
& \tan 180^{\circ}=\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}}=\frac{0}{-1}=0 \\
& \sec 180^{\circ}=\frac{1}{x_{1}}=\frac{1}{-1}=-1 \\
& \operatorname{cosec} 180^{\circ}=\frac{1}{y_{1}}=\frac{1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) } \\
& \cot 180^{\circ}=\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}=\frac{-1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) }
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg29hmd0pkzk11zrrn3a5vh60x8bvr3f" alt="" caption="" />

Trigonometric Ratios of $\mathbf{2 7 0}^{\mathbf{0}}$
To find trigonometric ratios of $270^{\circ}$, choose a point $\mathrm{P}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ on unit circle in standard position such that $\angle \mathrm{XOP}=\theta=270^{\circ}$.
As P lies on y -axis below origin, therefore its coordinates are $x_{1}=0$ and $\mathrm{y}_{1}=-1$.
So, $\cos 270^{\circ}=\mathrm{x}_{1}=0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sin 270^{\circ}=y_{1}=-1 \\
& \tan 270^{\circ}=\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}}=\frac{-1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) } \\
& \sec 270^{\circ}=\frac{1}{x_{1}}=\frac{1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) } \\
& \operatorname{cosec} 270^{\circ}=\frac{1}{y_{1}}=\frac{1}{-1}=-1 \\
& \cot 270^{\circ}=\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}=\frac{0}{-1}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg2dm0srnc6w2ffrq0nzsn19cd8bvbzc" alt="" caption="" />

Trigonometric Ratios of $360^{0}$
To find trigonometric ratios of $360^{\circ}$, choose a point $\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{x}_{1}, \mathrm{y}_{1}\right)$ on unit circle in standard position such that $\angle \mathrm{XOP}=\theta=360^{\circ}$. It coincides with $0^{\circ}$.
As P lies on x -axis so its coordinates are $\mathrm{x}_{1}=1$ and $\mathrm{y}_{1}=0$.
So, $\cos 360^{\circ}=\mathrm{x}_{1}=1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sin 360^{\circ}=y_{1}=0 \\
& \tan 360^{\circ}=\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}}=\frac{0}{1}=0 \\
& \sec 360^{\circ}=\frac{1}{x_{1}}=\frac{1}{1}=1 \\
& \operatorname{cosec} 360^{\circ}=\frac{1}{y_{1}}=\frac{1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) } \\
& \cot 360^{\circ}=\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}=\frac{1}{0}=\infty \text { (undefined) }
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg2fc6axxsvzezmgy24f68mq0x8bvbpe" alt="" caption="" />

EXERCISE 6.3

1. Complete the following table.

| 0 | $0^{0}$ | $30^{0}$ | $45^{0}$ | $60^{0}$ | $90^{0}$ | $180^{\circ}$ | $270^{\circ}$ | $360^{0}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sin \theta$ | 0 |  |  | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ |  |  | -1 |  |
| $\cos \theta$ |  |  |  |  |  | -1 |  |  |
| $\tan \theta$ |  |  | 1 |  |  |  |  |  |
| $\operatorname{cosec} \theta$ | $\infty$ |  |  |  |  | $\infty$ |  |  |
| $\sec \theta$ |  |  |  | 2 |  |  |  | 1 |
| $\cot \theta$ |  | $\sqrt{3}$ |  |  | 0 |  |  |  |

2. Evaluate the following.
i. $\quad \sin 60^{\circ}-\cos 30^{\circ}$
ii. $\sec 45^{\circ} \operatorname{cosec} 45^{\circ}-\sin 30^{\circ} \cos 60^{\circ}$
iii. $\quad \frac{\tan \frac{\pi}{3}-\tan \frac{\pi}{6}}{1+\tan \frac{\pi}{3} \tan \frac{\pi}{6}}$
iv. $\cos ^{2} \frac{\pi}{3}-\sin ^{2} \frac{\pi}{3}$
v. $\sin \frac{\pi}{2} \cos \frac{\pi}{3}-\cos \frac{\pi}{2} \sin \frac{\pi}{3}$
3. For $\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}$, verify the following statements.
i. $\tan 2 \theta=\frac{2 \tan \theta}{1-\tan ^{2} \theta}$
ii. $\sin 3 \theta=3 \sin \theta-4 \sin ^{3} \theta$
iii. $\cos 2 \theta=1-2 \sin ^{2} \theta$
iv. $\sec ^{2} \theta-\tan ^{2} \theta=1$
v. $\operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta=1+\cot ^{2} \theta$
4. Write value of $\theta$ for the following ratios $(0<\theta<2 \pi)$.
i. $\sin \theta=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$
ii. $\operatorname{cosec} \theta=-1$
iii. $\tan \theta=1$
iv. $\sec \theta=\frac{\sqrt{12}}{3}$
v. $\cos \theta=0$
5. If terminal ray of $\theta$ is in first quadrant and $\cos \theta=\frac{1}{2}$, then find remaining trigonometric ratios of $\theta$.
6. If terminal ray of $\theta$ is in second quadrant and $\operatorname{cosec} \theta=2$, then find the value of $\cos \theta\left(\frac{\sin ^{2} \theta-\cos ^{2} \theta}{\sin ^{2} \theta+\cos ^{2} \theta}\right)$.
7. If $\tan \theta=-1$, and terminal ray of $\theta$ is not in second quadrant, then find remaining trigonometric ratios of $\theta$.

mdxBody:
Identity is an equation which remains true for all possible replacements of variable involved in it. e.g. $(x+1)(x-1)=x^{2}-1$ is an identity.
Trigonometric identity is an identity involving different trigonometric ratios in it. Trigonometric identities are of many types. Some of them are given below.

i. Reciprocal identities
ii. Quotient identities
iii. Pythagorean identities

6.4.1 Reciprocal Identities
$\operatorname{Cosec} \theta, \sec \theta$ and $\cot \theta$ are reciprocals of $\sin \theta, \cos \theta$ and $\tan \theta$ respectively.

i.e. $\operatorname{cosec} \theta=\frac{1}{\sin \theta}, \quad \sec \theta=\frac{1}{\cos \theta}$ and $\cot \theta=\frac{1}{\tan \theta}$

Proves of these identities are left for students.
6.4.2 Quotient Identities
i. $\tan \theta=\frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}$
ii. $\cot \theta=\frac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}$

Proof:
Consider a right-angled triangle ABC, in which $\angle C=90^{\circ}$, $\angle A=\theta, A B=c, B C=a$ and $A C=b$.
By definition, $\sin \theta=\frac{a}{c}, \cos \theta=\frac{b}{c}$ and $\tan \theta=\frac{a}{b}$.
<CaptionedImage src="kg28gpbbrrb5yehe7ezn3986bs8bvw4s" alt="" caption="" />
$\tan \theta=\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\frac{a}{c}}{\frac{b}{c}}$ (dividing numerator and denominator by c)

$$
=\frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}
$$

Similarly, we can prove the second quotient identity.
6.4.3 Pythagorean Identities

i. $\sin ^{2} \theta+\cos ^{2} \theta=1$
ii. $\sec ^{2} \theta-\tan ^{2} \theta=1$
iii. $\operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta-\cot ^{2} \theta=1$

Proof:
Consider a right-angled triangle ABC, in which $\angle C=90^{\circ}, \angle A=\theta, A B=c, B C=a$ and $A C=b$.

i. $\sin ^{2} \theta+\cos ^{2} \theta=1$

By definition, $\sin \theta=\frac{a}{c}$ and $\cos \theta=\frac{b}{c}$
By Pythagoras theorem, $\mathrm{a}^{2}+\mathrm{b}^{2}=\mathrm{c}^{2}$
Dividing this Pythagorean equation by $\mathrm{c}^{2}$ we get
<CaptionedImage src="kg28f3qftpcbvedvv563ncan5s8bvrpn" alt="" caption="" />

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{a^{2}}{c^{2}}+\frac{b^{2}}{c^{2}}=\frac{c^{2}}{c^{2}} \\
& \left(\frac{a}{c}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{b}{c}\right)^{2}=1
\end{aligned}
$$

$(\sin \theta)^{2}+(\cos \theta)^{2}=1$ or $\sin ^{2} \theta+\cos ^{2} \theta=1 \quad\left(\because(\sin \theta)^{2}=\sin ^{2} \theta\right)$
ii. $\sec ^{2} \theta-\tan ^{2} \theta=1$
By definition, $\sec \theta=\frac{c}{b}$ and $\tan \theta=\frac{a}{b}$
By Pythagoras theorem, $\mathrm{a}^{2}+\mathrm{b}^{2}=\mathrm{c}^{2}$
Dividing this Pythagorean equation by $b^{2}$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}+\frac{b^{2}}{b^{2}}=\frac{c^{2}}{b^{2}} \\
& \left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{2}+1=\left(\frac{c}{b}\right)^{2} \\
& (\tan \theta)^{2}+1=(\sec \theta)^{2} \\
& \tan ^{2} \theta+1=\sec ^{2} \theta \text { or } \sec ^{2} \theta-\tan ^{2} \theta=1
\end{aligned}
$$

iii. $\operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta-\cot ^{2} \theta=1$
By definition, $\operatorname{cosec} \theta=\frac{c}{a}$ and $\cot \theta=\frac{b}{a}$
<CaptionedImage src="kg29gz6hqt6jr468kk8pj9kwa58bvaj7" alt="" caption="" />
<CaptionedImage src="kg2eyx3m46m43njfxx3jtwm5618btfbx" alt="" caption="" />

By Pythagoras theorem, $\mathrm{a}^{2}+\mathrm{b}^{2}=\mathrm{c}^{2}$
Dividing this Pythagorean equation by $\mathrm{a}^{2}$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \quad \frac{a^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}=\frac{c^{2}}{a^{2}} \\
& 1+\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{c}{a}\right)^{2} \\
& 1+(\cot \theta)^{2}=(\operatorname{cosec} \theta)^{2} \\
& 1+\cot ^{2} \theta=\operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta \\
& \text { or } \operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta-\cot ^{2} \theta=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Example 11:
Use basic trigonometric identities to prove the following relations.

i. $\quad \cos \alpha+\sin \alpha \tan \alpha=\sec \alpha$
ii. $\frac{\tan \alpha}{\sec \alpha-1}=\frac{\sec \alpha+1}{\tan \alpha}$
iii. $\frac{\sin ^{2} \alpha+2 \cos \alpha-1}{\sin ^{2} \alpha+3 \cos \alpha-3}=\frac{1}{1-\sec \alpha}$

Solution:

i. $$
\begin{aligned}
\text { L.H.S. } & =\cos \alpha+\sin \alpha \tan \alpha \\
& =\cos \alpha+\sin \alpha \frac{\sin \alpha}{\cos \alpha} \\
& =\cos \alpha+\frac{\sin ^{2} \alpha}{\cos \alpha} \\
& =\frac{\cos ^{2} \alpha+\sin ^{2} \alpha}{\cos \alpha} \\
& =\frac{1}{\cos \alpha}=\sec \alpha=\text { R.H.S. }
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence, $\cos \alpha+\sin \alpha \tan \alpha=\sec \alpha$
ii. $$
\begin{aligned}
\text { L.H.S. } & =\frac{\tan \alpha}{\sec \alpha-1} \\
& =\frac{\tan \alpha}{\sec \alpha-1} \times \frac{\sec \alpha+1}{\sec \alpha+1} \\
& =\frac{\tan \alpha(\sec \alpha+1)}{\sec ^{2} \alpha-1} \\
& =\frac{\tan \alpha(\sec \alpha+1)}{\tan ^{2} \alpha} \\
& =\frac{\sec \alpha+1}{\tan \alpha}=\text { R.H.S. }
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence, $\frac{\tan \alpha}{\sec \alpha-1}=\frac{\sec \alpha+1}{\tan \alpha}$
iii. $$
\begin{aligned}
\text { L.H.S. } & =\frac{\sin ^{2} \alpha+2 \cos \alpha-1}{\sin ^{2} \alpha+3 \cos \alpha-3} \\
& =\frac{1-\cos ^{2} \alpha+2 \cos \alpha-1}{1-\cos ^{2} \alpha+3 \cos \alpha-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{-\cos ^{2} \alpha+2 \cos \alpha}{-\cos ^{2} \alpha+3 \cos \alpha-2} \\
& =\frac{-\cos \alpha(\cos \alpha-2)}{-\left(\cos ^{2} \alpha-3 \cos \alpha+2\right)} \\
& =\frac{\cos \alpha(\cos \alpha-2)}{\cos ^{2} \alpha-2 \cos \alpha-\cos \alpha+2} \\
& =\frac{\cos \alpha(\cos \alpha-2)}{\cos \alpha(\cos \alpha-2)-1(\cos \alpha-2)} \\
& =\frac{\cos \alpha(\cos \alpha-2)}{(\cos \alpha-1)(\cos \alpha-2)}=\frac{\cos \alpha}{\cos \alpha-1}=\frac{\frac{\cos \alpha}{\cos \alpha-1}}{\frac{\cos \alpha}{\cos \alpha}} \\
& =\frac{1}{\frac{\cos \alpha}{\cos \alpha}-\frac{1}{\cos \alpha}}=\frac{1}{1-\sec \alpha}=\text { R.H.S. }
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $\frac{\operatorname{Sin}^{2} \alpha+2 \operatorname{Cos} \alpha-1}{\operatorname{Sin}^{2} \alpha+3 \operatorname{Cos} \alpha-3}=\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{Sec} \alpha}$
Example 12:
Solve the following triangles. (Find unknown elements of the following triangles)

i. $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}, \angle \mathrm{C}=90^{\circ}, \angle \mathrm{A}=30^{\circ}, \mathrm{a}=6 \mathrm{~cm}$
ii. $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}, \angle \mathrm{C}=90^{\circ}, \mathrm{c}=12 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~b}=6 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~cm}$
i. Given Elements:
$$
\triangle \mathrm{ABC}, \angle \mathrm{C}=90^{\circ}, \angle \mathrm{A}=30^{\circ}, \mathrm{a}=6 \mathrm{~cm}
$$
Required Elements:
$\angle \mathrm{B}, \quad \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}$.

Solution:

$$
\text { In } \triangle A B C, \begin{aligned}
& \angle A+\angle B+\angle C=180^{\circ} \\
& 30^{\circ}+\angle B+90^{\circ}=180^{\circ} \\
& \angle B=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-30^{\circ} \\
& \angle B=60^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\sin \theta=\frac{\text { Perpendicular }}{\text { Hypotenuse }}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg28m2erhx201zt4hs62gssmxn8efrmn" alt="A right triangle with a 30 degree angle, side a = 6 cm, and hypotenuse c, used to derive a trigonometric identity." caption="A right triangle with a 30 degree angle, side a = 6 cm, and hypotenuse c, used to derive a trigonometric identity." />

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin 30^{\circ} & =\frac{a}{c} \\
\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{6}{c} \\
c & =12 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

Math Play Ground
In $\triangle A B C$, by Pythagoras theorem,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2} \\
& 12^{2}=6^{2}+b^{2} \\
& 144=36+b^{2} \\
& b^{2}=144-36
\end{aligned}
$$

1. Make a hopscotch as given in the phayground.
2. Ask a student to start hopping and finding answers.

<CaptionedImage src="kg29575ktfv27ctv9jxwvf28s58eemsm" alt="A board-game-style diagram ("Wheel") posing trigonometric identity problems, such as 1+cot squared theta and 1-csc squared theta, around a central start point." caption="A board-game-style diagram ("Wheel") posing trigonometric identity problems, such as 1+cot squared theta and 1-csc squared theta, around a central start point." />

$$
\begin{aligned}
& b^{2}=108 \\
& b=\sqrt{108}=6 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, required elements are $\angle \mathrm{B}=60^{\circ}, \mathrm{b}=6 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{c}=12 \mathrm{~cm}$.

ii. Given Elements:
$$
\triangle \mathrm{ABC}, \angle \mathrm{C}=90^{\circ}, \mathrm{c}=12 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~b}=6 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~cm}
$$
Required Elements:
    $\angle \mathrm{A}, \angle \mathrm{B}$, a

Solution: In $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$, by Pythagoras theorem,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2} \\
& 12^{2}=a^{2}+(6 \sqrt{2})^{2} \\
& 144=a^{2}+72 \\
& a^{2}=144-72 \\
& a^{2}=72 \\
& a=\sqrt{72}=6 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~cm} \\
& \cos \theta=\frac{\text { Base }}{\text { Hypotenuse }} \\
& \cos \angle A=\frac{b}{c} \\
& \cos \angle A=\frac{6 \sqrt{2}}{12}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
& \angle A=45^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg23kghh9ncbv8y3sjaabjeqyx8btf8e" alt="" caption="" />

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { In } \triangle A B C, \angle A+\angle B+\angle C=180^{\circ} \\
& 45^{\circ}+\angle B+90^{\circ}=180^{\circ} \\
& \angle B=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-45^{\circ} \Rightarrow \angle B=45^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, required elements are $\angle A=45^{\circ}, \angle B=45^{\circ}, a=6 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~cm}$.

EXERCISE 6.4

1. Prove the following relations by using basic trigonometric identities.
    i. $\quad\left(1-\sin ^{2} \theta\right) \sec ^{2} \theta=1$
    ii. $\frac{1-\sin \theta}{1+\sin \theta}=(\sec \theta-\tan \theta)^{2}$
    iii. $\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos \theta}{1+\cos \theta}}=\frac{\sin \theta}{1+\cos \theta}$
    iv. $\frac{\sin \theta-2 \sin ^{3} \theta}{2 \cos ^{3} \theta-\cos \theta}=\tan \theta$
    v. $\sqrt{\sec ^{2} \theta+\operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta}=\tan \theta+\cot \theta$
    vi. $\frac{1}{\sec \theta-\tan \theta}=\sec \theta+\tan \theta$

vii. $\sin ^{2} \theta+\cos ^{4} \theta=\sin ^{4} \theta+\cos ^{2} \theta$
viii. $\frac{\tan \theta+\sin \theta}{\tan \theta-\sin \theta}=\frac{\sec \theta+1}{\sec \theta-1}$
ix. $\sec ^{2} \theta+\operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta=\sec ^{2} \theta \operatorname{cosec}^{2} \theta$
x. $\sin ^{6} \theta+\cos ^{6} \theta=1-3 \sin ^{2} \theta \cos ^{2} \theta$
2. If $x \cos \theta+y \sin \theta=m$ and $x \sin \theta-y \cos \theta=n$, prove that $x^{2}+y^{2}=m^{2}+n^{2}$.
3. Find values of $\theta$ for the following equations in the interval $0 \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}$.
i $2 \sin ^{2} \theta=\frac{1}{2}$
ii. $\sin \theta=\cos \theta$
iii. $\sec ^{2} \theta-2 \tan ^{2} \theta=0$
4. Solve the following right-angled triangles
    i. $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}, \angle \mathrm{C}=90^{\circ}, a=4 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{c}=4 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~cm}$.
    ii. $\triangle \mathrm{PQR}, \angle \mathrm{Q}=90^{\circ}, \angle \mathrm{P}=60^{\circ}, \mathrm{PQ}=4 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~cm}$.
    iii. $\triangle \mathrm{PQR}, \angle \mathrm{R}=90^{0}, \mathrm{PR}=8 \mathrm{~m}, \mathrm{RQ}=8 \mathrm{~m}$.
    iv. $\triangle X Y Z, \angle X=90^{\circ}, Y Z=16 \mathrm{~m}, X Z=8 \mathrm{~m}$.
    v. $\triangle \mathrm{LMN}, \mathrm{LM}=10 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{MN}=8 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{NL}=6 \mathrm{~cm}$.
5. If $x=\mathrm{r} \cos \alpha \sin \beta, y=\mathrm{r} \cos \alpha \cos \beta$ and $z=\mathrm{r} \sin \alpha$, then find value of $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}$.

mdxBody:
Line of Sight
If an object P is observed from a point of observation O , then the line OP is called line of sight. Angle of Elevation
If O is point of observation, OX is a horizontal line (ray)and an object P lies above the line OX, then the angle between the horizontal line and the line of sight to an object above the horizontal line
<CaptionedImage src="kg2cybqdz8cdf2wfepxp48v9tx8bv3wy" alt="" caption="" />
is called angle of elevation. In the adjoining figure $\angle \mathrm{XOP}$ is angle of elevation.

Angle of Depression
If O is point of observation, OX is a horizontal line (ray) and an object P lies below the line OX, then angle between the horizontal line and the line of sight to an object below the horizontal line is called
<CaptionedImage src="kg2cpxe17k961hz782m1xje4ys8btmy6" alt="" caption="" />
angle of depression. In the adjoining figure $\angle \mathrm{XOP}$ is angle of depression.

## Applications

Example 13:
A ladder 10 m long leaning against a vertical wall makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with wall. Find height of ladder along the wall.

Solution:
Let AB is a ladder. BC is height of ladder along wall.
$A C$ is along horizontal ground. In triangle $A B C, \angle C=90^{\circ}$,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\angle B=60^{\circ} \text { and } A B=10 \mathrm{~m} . \\
\cos 60^{\circ}=\frac{B C}{A B} \\
\frac{1}{2}=\frac{B C}{10} \\
B C=5 \mathrm{~m}
\end{gathered}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg23vmrjpwa7pa9vezdb4x85d58btqv5" alt="" caption="" />
So, height of ladder along wall $=10 \mathrm{~m}$.
Example 14:
An aeroplane at an altitude of 900 m finds that two ships are sailing towards it in the same direction. The angles of depression of ships as observed from plane are $30^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$. Find distance between ships.

Solution:
In the figure O is position of plane. A and B are two ships. $\angle \mathrm{XOA}$ and $\angle \mathrm{XOB}$ are angles of depression. As alternate angles of parallel lines are equal.
So, $\angle \mathrm{A}=30^{\circ}$ and $\angle \mathrm{B}=60^{\circ}$
Let $\mathrm{AC}=x$ and $\mathrm{BC}=y$.
In right angled triangle ACO ,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tan 30^{\circ}=\frac{900}{x} \\
& \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{900}{x} \\
& x=900 \sqrt{3}=1558.85 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

In right angled triangle BCO ,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tan 60^{\circ}=\frac{900}{y} \\
& \sqrt{3}=\frac{900}{y} \Rightarrow y=\frac{900}{\sqrt{3}}=519.62 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

Distance between ships $=x-y$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =1558.85-519.62 \\
& =1039.23 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

1. From a point at a distance of 20 m from a tree, angle of elevation of top of a tree is $30^{\circ}$. Find height of the tree.
2. The length of shadow of 10 m high pole is $10 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~m}$. Find angle of elevation of thesun.
3. The window of a room is in the shape of an equilateral triangle. The length of each side is 1.6 m . Find height of the window.
4. The height of a slide in a children park is 5 m . A girl standing at the top of the slide observes that angle of depression of its bottom is $30^{\circ}$. Find length of the slide.
5. Two pillars of equal height stand on either side of a roadway which is 120 m wide. At a point on the road between pillars, the angles of elevation of the pillars are $60^{\circ}$ and $30^{\circ}$. Find height of each pillar and position of the point.
6. From the top of a tower of height 120 m , angles of depression of two boats on same side of tower at water level are $60^{\circ}$ and $45^{\circ}$. Find distance between the boats.
7. Two men on opposite sides of a tree are in line with it. They observe that angles of elevation of top of tree are 30° and 60°. The height of tree is 15 m. Find distance between the men.
8. From the top of a tree, the angles of elevation and depression of the top and bottom of a building are $30^{\circ}$ and $45^{\circ}$ respectively. If height of tree is 12 m , find height of building and distance between tree and building.
9. From a point A on ground at a distance of 200 m . angle of elevation of top of a tower is $\alpha$. There is another point B 80m nearer to the tower. The angle of elevation of top of tower from B is $\beta$. If $\tan \alpha=\frac{2}{5}$, find height of tower and value of $\beta$.
10. A boat moving away from a light house 206.6 m high, takes 120 seconds to change the angle of elevation of top of light house from $60^{\circ}$ to $45^{\circ}$. Find the speed of boat.
summary: Defines angle of elevation as the angle between a horizontal line and the line of sight to an object above it.
title: 6.5 Angles of Elevation and Depression

A ship sails from port A to port B at a bearing of 040° for 35 km. Then, it sails at a bearing of $130^{\circ}$ for 50 km from port B to port C . Find:

(a) the distance between port A and port C
(b) the bearing of C from A

Solution:

(a) By drawing the path according to given information, we observe that $\theta=130^{\circ}-40^{\circ}=90^{\circ}$ (since two norths at A and B are parallel).
Therefore, $\beta=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}=90^{\prime \prime}$.
Thus, triangle ABC is right with right angle at B.
In right $\triangle A B C$ by using Pythagoras theorem,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{m} \overline{A C} & =\sqrt{(m \overline{A B})^{2}+(m \overline{B C})^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{(35)^{2}+(50)^{2}}=\sqrt{3725} \approx 61.03 \mathrm{~km}
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg255d491dmwjkmt7ggpnf94ch8btv87" alt="" caption="" />

(b) Bearing of C from $\mathrm{A}=040^{\circ}+\alpha$
First we find $\alpha$ in right $\triangle A B C$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\tan \alpha & =\frac{m \overline{B C}}{m \overline{A B}} \\
& =\frac{50}{35} \approx 1.4286 \\
\Rightarrow \alpha & =\tan ^{-1}(1.4286)=55^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus, bearing of C from $\mathrm{A}=040^{\circ}+055^{\circ}=095^{\circ}$

## Applying the Distance Formula

Given the two points $P_{1}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $P_{2}\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$, the distance between these points is given by the formula:

$$
\mathrm{d}\left(\mathrm{P}_{1}, \mathrm{P}_{2}\right)=\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2}=\sqrt{\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)^{2}}
$$

Proof: If $x_{1} \neq x_{2}$ and $y_{1} \neq y_{2}$, then plot two points $\mathrm{P}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{P}_{2}$ with coordinates $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ respectively as

Key Fact illustrated in figure (ii).
<CaptionedImage src="kg20n966gdbar10nj1t7as0jts8efbqk" alt="A coordinate-plane diagram showing two points P1(x1,y1) and P2(x2,y2) with their projections onto the axes, used to derive the distance formula." caption="A coordinate-plane diagram showing two points P1(x1,y1) and P2(x2,y2) with their projections onto the axes, used to derive the distance formula." />

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2}=\mathrm{d}\left(\mathrm{P}_{1}, \mathrm{P}_{2}\right) \\
& \mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2}^{2}=\left(\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

In the above figure $\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{~A}$ and $\mathrm{P}_{2} \mathrm{~B}$ are perpendiculars drawn from two points $\mathrm{P}_{1}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $\mathrm{P}_{2}\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ on $x$-axis, and $\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{P}_{2} \mathrm{D}$ are perpendiculars on $y$-axis.
The coordinates of the points $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}$ and D are also shown in figure accordingly.
Let the point where $\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{C}$ meets $\mathrm{P}_{2} \mathrm{~B}$ be $\mathrm{P}_{3}$, with coordinate $\left(x_{2}, y_{1}\right)$ so that $\Delta \mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2} \mathrm{P}_{3}$ is a right triangle with right angle at $\mathrm{P}_{3}$.
From figure, we have

$$
\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{~A}, \mathrm{~B})=\mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{3}=\left|x_{2}-x_{1}\right|
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D})=\mathrm{CD}=\mathrm{d}\left(\mathrm{P}_{2}, \mathrm{P}_{3}\right)=\mathrm{P}_{2} \mathrm{P}_{3}=\left|y_{2}-y_{1}\right|
$$

We next use the Pythagoras Theorem in right triangle $\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2} \mathrm{P}_{3}$

$$
\left[d\left(P_{1}, P_{2}\right)\right]^{2}=\left[d\left(P_{1}, P_{3}\right)\right]^{2}+\left[d\left(P_{2}, P_{3}\right)\right]^{2}
$$

or

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2}^{2}=\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{3}^{2}+\mathrm{P}_{2} \mathrm{P}_{3}^{2} \\
& \mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2}^{2}=\left|x_{2}-x_{1}\right|^{2}+\left|y_{2}-y_{1}\right|^{2} \\
& \mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2}=\sqrt{\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

So $\mathrm{d}\left(\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2}\right)=\mathrm{P}_{1} \mathrm{P}_{2}=\sqrt{\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right)^{2}}$

Example 2:
Find the distance between the two points $\mathrm{A}(-1,3)$ and $\mathrm{B}(4,15)$.
Solution:
By distance formula distance between two points with coordinates $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ is

$$
d=\sqrt{\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)^{2}}
$$

Let ( $-1,3$ ) be denoted by ( $x_{1}, y_{1}$ ) i.e. $x_{1}=-1, y_{1}=3$ and (4,15) be denoted by ( $x_{2}, y_{2}$ )
i.e. $x_{2}=4, y_{2}=15$
Now put them into the distance formula

$$
\begin{aligned}
A B=d & =\sqrt{(4-(-1))^{2}+(15-3)^{2}} \\
d & =\sqrt{(4+1)^{2}+(12)^{2}} \\
d & =\sqrt{5^{2}+12^{2}} \\
d & =\sqrt{25+144} \\
d & =\sqrt{169} \\
d & =13
\end{aligned}
$$

Check Point
Find the distance between $\mathrm{A}\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{3}{2}\right)$ and $\left(\frac{9}{2},-\frac{8}{2}\right)$

Collinear and Non-Collinear Point
A set of points that lie on a same straight line are said to be ccollinear.
If three points $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and C are collinear then, by distance formula, we have:

$$
d(A, C)=d(A, B)+d(B, C)
$$

or

$$
A C=A B+B C
$$

When three or more points do not lie on the same straight line, they are said to be non-collinear points.
In the figure, points $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}$ and R are non-collinear
<CaptionedImage src="kg2acf1eaw3ga0ee5zf7aw3zr58eejs0" alt="A triangle diagram with points P, Q, R, illustrating three points used in a distance-formula example." caption="A triangle diagram with points P, Q, R, illustrating three points used in a distance-formula example." />

Application of Distance Formula

Example 3:
Prove that A (3, 2), B (4, 4) and C (5, 6) are collinear points.
Solution:
In first step we find the distance between them.

By Distance Formula, distance between two points $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ is

$$
d=\sqrt{\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)^{2}}
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
d(A, B)= & A B=\sqrt{(4-3)^{2}+(4-2)^{2}} \\
& A B=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{1+4} \\
& A B=\sqrt{5} \ldots \ldots \ldots . \tag{i}
\end{align*}
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{~B}, \mathrm{C})=\mathrm{BC} & =\sqrt{(5-4)^{2}+(6-4)^{2}} \\
\mathrm{BC} & =\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{1+4} \\
\mathrm{BC} & =\sqrt{5} \ldots \ldots \ldots(\text { ii }) \\
\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{~A}, \mathrm{C})=\mathrm{AC} & =\sqrt{(5-3)^{2}+(6-2)^{2}} \\
\mathrm{AC} & =\sqrt{2^{2}+4^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{4+16}=\sqrt{20} \\
& =2 \sqrt{5} \ldots \ldots .(\text { iii }) \tag{iii}
\end{align*}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg2f1e11esxv74csac3cqa2mvd8eetc4" alt="A coordinate-plane diagram showing three points A(3,2), B(4,4), and C(5,6) plotted and connected, used in a distance-formula example." caption="A coordinate-plane diagram showing three points A(3,2), B(4,4), and C(5,6) plotted and connected, used in a distance-formula example." />
From (i), (ii) and (iii), we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& A C=A B+B C \\
& 2 \sqrt{5}=\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5} \\
& 2 \sqrt{5}=2 \sqrt{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the given points are collinear.
Example 4:
Prove that the points $(3,4),(3,1)$ and $(8,4)$ are the vertices of a right triangle.
Solution:
Suppose $\mathrm{A}(3,4), \mathrm{B}(3,1)$ and $\mathrm{C}(8,4)$ are the vertices of a triangle.
In first step we find the distance between them.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{~A}, \mathrm{~B})=\mathrm{AB} & =\sqrt{(1-4)^{2}+(3-3)^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+0^{2}} \\
\mathrm{AB} & =\sqrt{9+0} \\
\mathrm{AB} & =3
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{~B}, \mathrm{C})=\mathrm{BC} & =\sqrt{(4-1)^{2}+(8-3)^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{3^{2}+5^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{9+25} \\
\mathrm{BC} & =\sqrt{34} \\
\mathrm{~d}(\mathrm{~A}, \mathrm{C})=\mathrm{AC} & =\sqrt{(8-3)^{2}+(4-4)^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

<CaptionedImage src="kg2d2zq9xe7rbzfg6ntxtkxvn18bt2qd" alt="" caption="" />

$$
\mathrm{AC}=\sqrt{25+0}=5
$$

In right triangle we know that the greatest length is always the hypotenuse. So, BC is the hypotenuse. By Pythagoras Theorem,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{BC}^{2}=\mathrm{AB}^{2}+\mathrm{AC}^{2} \\
&(\sqrt{34})^{2}=5^{2}+3^{2} \\
& 34=25+9 \\
& 34=34
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence; $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and C form a right triangle.

Mid-Point of Two given Points in a Coordinate Plane
Suppose, we have two points $(2,4)$ and $(6,10)$ and we want to find the distance between them. First, we plot the points on the graph and join them. Then we can draw the lines that form a right triangle by using these points as two of the corners.
<CaptionedImage src="kg28ct4h207g56gpzqs3zmc74x8bvag9" alt="" caption="" />
In the diagram, $\Delta \mathrm{ABC}$ is drawn by drawing AC parallel to the $x$-axis and BC parallel to the $y$-axis. The coordinates of C are $(6,4)$, where two lines AC and BC intersect.
Let $\mathrm{P}(x, y)$ be the mid point of AB . Draw PD parallel to the $y$-axis and PE parallel to the $x$-axis. Then the coordinate of D and E are $(x, 4)$ and $(6, y)$ and, $\triangle \mathrm{APD}$ and $\triangle \mathrm{PBE}$ are congruent by (ASA).

We have $\mathrm{AD}=\mathrm{PE} \quad, \quad \mathrm{PD}=\mathrm{BE}$

$$
\begin{array}{rlrl}
x-2 & =6-x, & & y-4 \\
2 x & =8, & & 10-y \\
x & =4, & & 2 y=14 \\
& =7
\end{array}
$$

The mid point of $A B$ is $P(4,7)$.
We can also find the mid point of $A(2,4)$ and $B(6,10)$ in this way

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P\left(\frac{2+6}{2}, \frac{4+10}{2}\right) \\
& =P(4,7)
\end{aligned}
$$
summary: This section derives and applies the distance formula between two points in the coordinate plane.

## Finding Midpoints in a Coordinate Plane

In the above figure (iii) if we take $\mathrm{A}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ instead of $\mathrm{A}(2,4)$ and $\mathrm{B}\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ instead of $B(6,10)$, then we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x-2=x-x_{1} \text { and } \quad 6-x=x_{2}-x \\
& y-4=y-y_{1} \text { and } \quad 10-y=y_{2}-y
\end{aligned}
$$

We have already proved that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AD} & =\mathrm{PE} & , & \mathrm{PD}
\end{aligned}=\mathrm{BE} ~ g-x=y_{1}=y_{2}-y ~ 2 y=y_{1}+y_{2} . \quad y=\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2}
$$

To apply the mid point formula remember that: the $x$-coordinate of the midpoint = the average of the $x$-coordinates and the $y$-coordinate of the midpoint = the average of the $y$-coordinates.

The mid-point $P$ of the line segment from $P_{1}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ to $P_{2}\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ is

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2}, \frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2}\right) .
$$

Example 5:
By using mid point formula, prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram with vertices (1 , 1), (2 , 4), $(6,1)$ and $(7,4)$ bisect each other.
Solution:
First we plot these vertices on a Cartesian plane as shown in the fig.(iv). In parallelogram ABCD, AC and BD are its diagonals.

Let both the diagonals intersect each other at point $\mathrm{E}(x, y)$. By mid point formula, mid point of AC has the coordinates as
<CaptionedImage src="kg209pyer9txf4kf7yfs7m5w858bv9x6" alt="" caption="" />

$$
\begin{align*}
& \left(\frac{7+1}{2}, \frac{4+1}{2}\right) \\
& =(4,2.5) \ldots \tag{i}
\end{align*}
$$

and the coordinates of the mid point of diagonal BD is $\left(\frac{2+6}{2}, \frac{4+1}{2}\right)$

$$
\begin{equation*}
=(4,2.5) \tag{ii}
\end{equation*}
$$

From (i) and (ii) both the diagonals have the same mid point, so they bisect each other at point E(4 , 2.5).

Example 6:
If $(1,4)$ is the midpoint of the line segment joining $(6, b)$ and $(a, 2)$. Find $a$ and $b$.
Solution:
By mid point formula, mid point of the line segment with end points $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ is

$$
\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2}, \frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2}\right),
$$

So, mid point of the line segment joining the end points $(6, b)$ and $(a, 2)$ is

$$
\left(\frac{6+a}{2}, \frac{b+2}{2}\right)
$$

By using the given condition, we have

$$
\left(\frac{6+a}{2}, \frac{b+2}{2}\right)=(1,4)
$$

By the definition of equal ordered pairs,

$$
\begin{array}{llrl}
\frac{6+a}{2} & =1 & \text { and } & \\
6+a=2 & \text { and } & b+2 & b+2=8 \\
a=2-6 & \text { and } & b=8-2 \\
a=-4 & \text { and } & b=6 \\
a=-4 & \text { and } & b=6
\end{array}
$$

Example 7:
Use $\Delta \mathrm{XYZ}$ in the adjoining figure to find the following.

(i) Midpoint L and M of XY and YZ respectively
(ii) $\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{M})$ and $\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Z})$
(iii) The relationship between LM and XZ.

Solution:

(i) By mid point formula the coordinates of L are $\left(\frac{2+5}{2}, \frac{12+3}{2}\right)=\left(\frac{7}{2}, \frac{15}{2}\right)$

<CaptionedImage src="kg23j24h8tjvwfq5enyqhahxtd8ef6a8" alt="A triangle with vertices X(5,12), Y(2,3) and Z(7,4), and a point L on side XY, used in a midpoint-formula example." caption="A triangle with vertices X(5,12), Y(2,3) and Z(7,4), and a point L on side XY, used in a midpoint-formula example." />

Coordinates of M are $\left(\frac{2+7}{2}, \frac{3+4}{2}\right)=\left(\frac{9}{2}, \frac{7}{2}\right)$

(ii) $$
\begin{aligned}
d(L, M)=\sqrt{\left(\frac{7}{2}-\frac{9}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{15}{2}-\frac{7}{2}\right)^{2}} & \\
& =\sqrt{\left(\frac{-2}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{8}{2}\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{1+16}=\sqrt{17}
\end{aligned}
$$
Now,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Z}) & =\sqrt{(12-4)^{2}+(5-7)^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{8^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{64+4}=\sqrt{68}=2 \sqrt{17}
\end{aligned}
$$
(iii) From part (ii), we observe that
$$
\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Z})=2 \text { times } \mathrm{d}(\mathrm{~L}, \mathrm{M})
$$
Or
$$
\mathrm{XZ}=2 \mathrm{LM}
$$
Or
$$
\mathrm{LM}=\frac{X Z}{2}
$$
Hence,
Length of the line which is obtained by joining the mid points of any two sides of a triangle is half of the length of third side.
