He walks exactly $50 m$ from the base of the tree and looks up that the angle from the ground to the top of the tree is $33^{\circ}$. How tall is the tree? 11. From a 100 m observation tower on the beach, a man sights a whale in difficulty. The angle of depression of the whale is $7^{\circ}$. How far is the whale from the shoreline? 12. Urooba is sitting on the ground midway between two trees, 100 m apart. The angles of elevation of the tops of the trees are $13^{\circ}$ and $18^{\circ}$. How much taller is one tree than the other? 13. The angle of elevation of the top of a tree, T is $27^{\circ}$. From the same point on the ground, the angle of elevation of a hawk H , flying directly above the tree is $43^{\circ}$. The tree is 12.7 m tall. How high is the hawk above the ground? 14. This diagram shows a falcon F , on a tree, with a squirrel S , and a chipmunk $\mathbf{C}$, on the ground. From the falcon, the angles of depression of the animals are $36^{\circ}$ and $47^{\circ}$. How far apart are the animals on the ground? 15. Two guy wires support a flagpole FH. The first wire is 11.2 m long and has an angle of elevation of $39^{\circ}$. The second wire has an angle of elevation of $47^{\circ}$. How tall is the flagpole? ## Oblique Triangles An oblique triangle is any triangle that is not a right triangle. It could be an acute triangle or it could be an obtuse triangle. Acute Triangle Obtuse Triangle The Pythagoras Theorem along with trigonometric ratios allow us to easily handle any given right triangle problem, but what if the triangle is not a right triangle i.e. the triangle is oblique? To solve oblique triangles, we use certain laws known as "law of cosines", "law of sines" and "law of tangents". ## Law of Cosines When we know the measures of two sides and the included angle of a triangle (SAS), the size and shape of the triangle are determined. Therefore, we should be able to find the measure of the third side of the triangle. Sometimes three sides of oblique triangles are given (SSS) and we have to find the three angles of triangle. Such cases are easily handled by using law of cosines. ## Statement: If $a, b, c$ are three sides and $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are three angles of an oblique triangle with usual notation, then law of cosines is stated as follows: $$ \begin{align*} & a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c \cos \alpha \tag{1}\\ & b^{2}=a^{2}+c^{2}-2 a c \cos \beta \tag{2}\\ & c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}-2 a b \cos \gamma \tag{3} \end{align*} $$ Proof: Consider an acute angled triangle ABC with usual notations as shown in the figure. Draw $\overline{\mathrm{AD}} \perp \overline{\mathrm{BC}}$. In right $\triangle \mathrm{ABD}$, $$ \begin{align*} & \frac{\mathrm{BD}}{\mathrm{AB}}=\cos \beta \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{BD}=\mathrm{AB} \cos \beta=c \cos \beta \tag{i} \end{align*} $$ Again, $\frac{\mathrm{AD}}{\mathrm{AB}}=\sin \beta$ $$ \begin{equation*} \Rightarrow \mathrm{AD}=\mathrm{AB} \sin \beta=c \sin \beta . \tag{ii} \end{equation*} $$ Now, $\mathrm{CD}=\mathrm{BC}-\mathrm{BD}=a-c \cos \beta$ In right $\triangle A C D$, $$ \begin{aligned} (\mathrm{AC})^{2} & =(\mathrm{AD})^{2}+(\mathrm{CD})^{2} \quad \ldots \ldots(\text { Pythagoras Theorem }) \\ b^{2} & =(c \sin \beta)^{2}+(a-c \cos \beta)^{2} \\ b^{2} & =c^{2} \sin ^{2} \beta+a^{2}+c^{2} \cos ^{2} \beta-2 a c \cos \beta \\ b^{2} & =a^{2}+c^{2}\left(\sin ^{2} \beta+\cos ^{2} \beta\right)-2 a c \cos \beta \\ b^{2} & =a^{2}+c^{2}-2 a c \cos \beta \end{aligned} $$ Law of cosines is applicable when: - Two sides and included angle are given. * Three sides are given. Similarly, we can prove that: $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c \cos \alpha \quad$ and $\quad c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}-2 a b \cos \gamma$ From laws of cosines, $$ \cos \alpha=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2 b c}, \cos \beta=\frac{a^{2}+c^{2}-b^{2}}{2 a c}, \cos \gamma=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}}{2 a b} $$ These laws are useful when three sides of oblique triangles are given and we have to find their angles. ## Check Point: Prove law of cosines by taking an obtuse triangle. Example: Use the law of cosines to solve the triangle ABC when: $a=12 c m, b=7 c m, \gamma=59^{\circ} 30^{\prime}$ Solution: Using law of cosines, we have: $$ \begin{aligned} & c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}-2 a b \cos \gamma \\ & c^{2}=12^{2}+7^{2}-2 \times 12 \times 7 \times \cos 59^{\circ} 30^{\prime} \\ & c^{2}=144+49-168 \times 0.506=108 \\ & c=\sqrt{108}=10.4 \mathrm{~cm} \end{aligned} $$ Now to find angle $\alpha$, we use following formula. $$ \begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} \cos \alpha=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2 b c} & =\frac{7^{2}+10.4^{2}-12^{2}}{2 \times 7 \times 10.4} \\ & =\frac{13.16}{145.6}=0.0904 \end{aligned} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \alpha=\cos ^{-1}(0.0904)=84^{\circ} 49^{\prime} \\ & \text { Finally, } \alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^{\circ} \\ & \beta=180^{\circ}-\alpha-\gamma=180^{\circ}-84^{\circ} 49^{\prime}-59^{\circ} 30^{\prime} \\ & \beta=35^{\circ} 41^{\prime} \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$ ## Kevinact: If in the law of cosines, $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c \cos \alpha$ angle $\alpha$ is $90^{\circ}$, then $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c \cos 90^{\circ}$ $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c \times 0 \Rightarrow a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}$ which becomes Pythagoras Theorem. Thus Pythagoras Theorem is a special case of "law of cosines". ## Check Point: Two forces of magnitude 20 N and 30 N are inclined at angle of $105^{\circ}$ with each other. Find the magnitude of resultant force. Can you find the angle between force of magnitude 20 N and resultant force? ## Law of Sines Law of cosines is not applicable when two angles and one side (AAS or ASA) or one angle and two sides (angle not included (SSA)) of an oblique triangle are given. In order to handle such situation, we use another law known as "law of sines". ## Statement: If $a, b, c$ are three sides and $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are three angles of an oblique triangle with usual notation, then law of sines is stated as follows: $$ \frac{a}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{b}{\sin \beta}=\frac{c}{\sin \gamma} $$ Proof: Consider an obtuse triangle ABC as shown in the figure below. Let $h$ be the height of triangle ABC with respect to base $\overline{\mathrm{AC}}$. In right $\triangle \mathrm{ABD}$, $$ \begin{align*} & \frac{\mathrm{BD}}{\mathrm{AB}}=\sin \alpha \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{BD}=\mathrm{AB} \sin \alpha=c \sin \alpha \\ & \Rightarrow h=c \sin \alpha \ldots \ldots(i) \tag{i} \end{align*} $$ In right $\triangle \mathrm{CBD}$, $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{\mathrm{BD}}{\mathrm{CB}}=\sin (\pi-\gamma) \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{BD}=\mathrm{CB} \sin (\pi-\gamma) \\ & \Rightarrow h=a \sin \gamma \ldots \ldots(i i) \end{aligned} $$ [as $\sin (\pi-\gamma)=\sin \gamma$ ] From (i) and (ii), we get: $$ a \sin \gamma=c \sin c^{c} $$ Or $$ \frac{a}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{c}{\sin \gamma} $$ Similarly, by drawing perpendiculars on other two sides of $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$, we get: $$ \frac{a}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{b}{\sin \beta} \text { and } \frac{c}{\sin \gamma}=\frac{b}{\sin \beta} $$ Combining above results, we obtain the following law known as "law of sines". $$ \frac{a}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{b}{\sin \beta}=\frac{c}{\sin \gamma} \quad \text { or } \quad \frac{\sin \alpha}{a}=\frac{\sin \beta}{b}=\frac{\sin \gamma}{c} $$ ## To Determine the Number of Solutions in $\mathbf{\triangle} \mathbf{A B C}$ Task: Given measure of sides $a, b$ and angle $\alpha$. Use the law of sines to solve the $\Delta \mathrm{ABC}$ for $\sin \beta$. ## Case-1: (i) When $\sin \beta>1$, there is no triangle, so no solution. (ii) When $\sin \beta=1$, there is one right triangle (one solution) if $\alpha$ is acute and no triangle (no solution) if $\alpha$ is obtuse. Case-2: When $\alpha$ is acute and $\sin \beta<1$, there are two possible values of $\beta$, acute or obtuse. $$ 0<\beta<90^{\circ} \text { and } \beta^{\prime}=180^{\circ}-\beta $$ (i) If $\alpha+\beta^{\prime}<180^{\circ}$, there are two possible triangles $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$ and $\triangle \mathrm{AB}^{\prime} C$. (ii) If $\alpha+\beta^{\prime} \geq 180^{\circ}$, there is only one $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$. Case-3: When $\alpha$ is obtuse and $\sin \beta<1$, then $\beta$ must be acute. (i) If $\alpha+\beta<180^{\circ}$, there is only one $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$. (ii) If $\alpha+\beta^{\prime} \geq 180^{\circ}$, there is no triangle, so no solution. Alternatively, if we let $h=b \sin \alpha$, the height of triangle, we can summarize the number of possible triangles given $a, b$ and $\alpha$ in $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$. | Angle is | Acute | Acute | Acute | Acute | Obtuse | Obtuse | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | $\alpha$ | $ab$ | $ab$ | | Possible
Triangles | none | one right
triangle | two
triangles | one
triangle | none | one
triangle | ## Example: Use the law of sines to solve the triangle ABC when: $a=25 c m, \alpha=66^{\circ} 51^{\prime}, \gamma=44^{\circ} 12^{\prime}$ ## Solution: Given: $a=25 \mathrm{~cm}, \alpha=66^{\circ} 51^{\prime}, \gamma=44^{\circ} 12^{\prime}$ To Find: $b, c$ and $\beta$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^{\circ} \\ & 66^{\circ} 51^{\prime}+\beta+44^{\circ} 12^{\prime}=180^{\circ} \\ & \beta=180^{\circ}-66^{\circ} 51^{\prime}-44^{\circ} 12^{\prime}=68^{\circ} 57^{\prime} \end{aligned} $$ Using law of sines, we have: $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{a}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{c}{\sin \gamma} \Rightarrow \frac{25}{\sin 66^{\circ} 51^{\prime}}=\frac{c}{\sin 44^{\circ} 12^{\prime}} \\ & c=\frac{25 \times \sin 44^{\circ} 12^{\prime}}{\sin 66^{\circ} 51^{\prime}}=18.96 \mathrm{~cm} \end{aligned} $$ Again, by law of sines, $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{b}{\sin \beta}=\frac{a}{\sin \alpha} & \Rightarrow \frac{b}{\sin 68^{\circ} 57^{\prime}}=\frac{25}{\sin 66^{\circ} 51^{\prime}} \\ & \Rightarrow b=\frac{25}{\sin 66^{\circ} 51^{\prime}} \times \sin 68^{\circ} 57^{\prime}=25.37 \mathrm{~cm} \end{aligned} $$ ## Example: Find the values of unknowns in the adjoining figure. Figure is not drawn according to scale. ## Solution: In $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$, $$ \angle A C B=180^{\circ}-70^{\circ}=110^{\circ} $$ and $\angle \mathrm{ABC}=180^{\circ}-32^{\circ}-110^{\circ}=38^{\circ}$ Using law of sines for triangle ABC , $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{a}{\sin 32^{\circ}}=\frac{900}{\sin 38^{\circ}} \\ & \Rightarrow a=\frac{900}{\sin 38^{\circ}} \times \sin 32^{\circ}=774.66 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} $$ Again for the $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$, $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{c}{\sin 110^{\circ}}=\frac{774.66}{\sin 32^{\circ}} \\ & c=\frac{774.66}{\sin 32^{\circ}} \times \sin 110^{\circ}=1375.69 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} $$ Now in $\triangle \mathrm{BCD}$, $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{a}{\sin \angle \mathrm{D}}=\frac{12 c^{\circ} v}{\sin 70^{\circ}} \Rightarrow \frac{774.66}{\sin \angle \mathrm{D}}=\frac{1200}{\sin 70^{\circ}} \\ & \sin \angle \mathrm{D}=\frac{774.66 \times \sin 70^{\circ}}{1200}=0.607 \\ & \angle \mathrm{D}=\sin ^{-1}(0.607)=37^{\circ} 21^{\prime} \end{aligned} $$ ## Law of Tangents Law of tangents is also used to solve oblique triangles. This law handles the same situations for which the law of cosines is used. ## Statement: If $a, b, c$ are three sides and $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are three angles of an oblique triangle with usual notation, then law of tangents is stated as follows: $$ \frac{a+b}{a-b} \cdot \frac{\tan \left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right)}, \frac{b+c}{b-c}=\frac{\tan \left(\frac{\beta+\gamma}{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\frac{\beta-\gamma}{2}\right)}, \frac{c+a}{c-a}=\frac{\tan \left(\frac{\gamma+\alpha}{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\frac{\gamma-\alpha}{2}\right)} $$ ## Proof: For any oblique triangle ABC , the law of sines is given as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{a b}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{}{\sin \beta} \\ & \frac{a}{b}=\frac{\sin \alpha}{\sin \beta} \end{aligned} $$ Using componendo and dividendo property, we get: $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{a+b}{a-b}=\frac{\sin \alpha+\sin \beta}{\sin \alpha-\sin \beta} \\ & \frac{a+b}{a-b}=\frac{2 \sin \frac{\alpha+\beta}{2} \cos \frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}}{2 \cos \frac{\alpha+\beta}{2} \sin \frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}} \\ & \frac{a+b}{a-b}=\frac{\tan \frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}}{\tan \frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}} \end{aligned} $$ ## Check Point: Prove that $$ \frac{a+c}{a-c}=\frac{\tan \left(\frac{\alpha+\gamma}{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\frac{\alpha-\gamma}{2}\right)} $$ Similarly, we can prove that: $$ \frac{b+c}{b-c}=\frac{\tan \left(\frac{\beta+\gamma}{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\frac{\beta-\gamma}{2}\right)}, \quad \frac{c+a}{c-a}=\frac{\tan \left(\frac{\gamma+\alpha}{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\frac{\gamma-\alpha}{2}\right)} $$ ## Example: Use the law of tangents to solve the triangle ABC when $a=500 \mathrm{~mm}, b=600 \mathrm{~mm}, \gamma=50^{\circ} 20^{\prime}$ ## Solution: Given: $a=500 c m, b=600 c m, \gamma=50^{\circ} 20^{\prime}$ To Find: $c, \alpha$ and $\beta$ ## Keyplact: It is better to use formula As in any triangle, $$ \begin{aligned} & \alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^{\circ} \Rightarrow \beta+\alpha=180^{\circ}-\gamma \\ \Rightarrow & \beta+\alpha=180^{\circ}-50^{\circ} 20^{\prime}=129^{\circ} 40^{\prime} \ldots . . .(i) \end{aligned} $$ Now using law of tangents for $b>a$, $$ \frac{a+c}{a-c}=\frac{\tan \left(\frac{\alpha+\gamma}{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\frac{\alpha-\gamma}{2}\right)} $$ $\frac{b+a}{b-a}=\frac{\tan \frac{\beta+\alpha}{2}}{\tan \frac{\beta-\alpha}{2}}$ Substituting the values of $b, c$ and $\beta+\alpha$, we get: rather than the formula $$ \frac{c+a}{c-a}=\frac{\tan \left(\frac{\gamma+\alpha}{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\frac{\gamma-\alpha}{2}\right)} $$ when $a>c$ in the given situation. $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{600+500}{600-500} & =\frac{\tan \frac{129^{\circ} 40^{\prime}}{2}}{\tan \frac{\beta-\alpha}{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{1100}{100}=\frac{\tan 64^{\circ} 50^{\prime}}{\tan \frac{\beta-\alpha}{2}} \\ \tan \frac{\beta-\alpha}{2} & =\frac{\tan 64^{\circ} 50^{\prime}}{11} \Rightarrow \tan \frac{\beta-\alpha}{2}=0.193 \\ \frac{\beta-\alpha}{2} & =\tan ^{-1}(0.193)=10^{\circ} 57^{\prime} \\ \beta-\alpha & =21^{\circ} 54^{\prime} \ldots \ldots . .(i i) \end{aligned} $$ Solving (i) and (ii), we get: $$ \beta=75^{\circ} 47^{\prime}, \alpha=53^{\circ} 53^{\prime} $$ To find $c$, we use law of sines (we can also use law of cosines). $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{c}{\sin \gamma}=\frac{b}{\sin \beta} \Rightarrow c=\frac{b \times \sin \gamma}{\sin \beta} \\ & c=\frac{600 \times \sin 50^{\circ} 20^{\prime}}{\sin 75^{\circ} 47^{\prime}}=476.45 \mathrm{~mm} \end{aligned} $$ ## When Law of Sines and Law of Cosines are Used The Law of Cosines and the Law of Sines can be used to find the remaining three measures of any triangle when we know the measure of a side and the measures of any two other components (two sides, two angles, one side one angle) of the triangle. 1. Given: Two sides and the included angle. - Use the Law of Cosines to find the measure of the third side. - Use the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to find the measure of another angle. - Use the sum of the angles of a triangle to find the measure of the third angle. 2. Given: Three sides. - Use the Law of Cosines to find the measure of an angle. - Use the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to find the measure of another angle. - Use the sum of the angles of a triangle to find the measure of the third angle. 3. Given: Two angles and a side. - Use the sum of the angles of a triangle to find the measure of the third angle. - Use the Law of Sines to find the remaining sides. 4. Given: Two sides and an angle opposite to one of them - Use the Law of Sines to find the possible measure(s) of another angle. - Determine if there are two, one, or no possible triangles. - If there is a triangle, use the sum of the angles of a triangle to find the measure(s) of the third angle. - Use the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to find the measure(s) of the third side. ## Half Angle Formulae Sometimes it is convenient to use half angle formulae for the solution of oblique triangles when measures of three sides of a triangle are given. In this section, we will study half angles formulae for sines, cosines and tangents. Let us derive them one by one. (a) Cosines of Half Angle Statement: In any triangle ABC with usual notations, $\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{S(S-a)}{b c}}, \quad \cos \frac{\beta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{S(S-b)}{a c}}, \quad \cos \frac{\gamma}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{S(S-c)}{a b}}$ where $S=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$. Proof: We know that: $$ \begin{aligned} & \cos \alpha=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2 b c} \\ & 2 \cos ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}-1=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2 b c} \Rightarrow 2 \cos ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2 b c}+1 \\ \Rightarrow & 2 \cos ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}+2 b c-a^{2}}{2 b c}=\frac{(b+c)^{2}-(a)^{2}}{2 b c} \\ \Rightarrow & 2 \cos ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{(b+c+a)(b+c-a)}{2 b c} \end{aligned} $$ As $a+b+c=2 S \Rightarrow b+c-a=2 S-2 a=2(S-a)$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \therefore 2 \cos ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{2 S \times 2(S-a)}{2 b c} \\ & \cos ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{S(S-a)}{b c} \\ & \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{S(S-a)}{b c}} \end{aligned} $$ Similarly, it can be proved that: Similarly, it can be proved that: $$ \cos \frac{\beta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{S(S-b)}{a c}} \text { and } \cos \frac{\gamma}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{S(S-c)}{a b}} $$ ## (b) Sines of Half Angle Statement: In any triangle ABC with usual notations, $$ \sin \frac{\alpha}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{b c}}, \quad \sin \frac{\beta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-c)}{a c}}, \quad \sin \frac{\gamma}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-b)}{a b}} $$ where $S=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$. Proof: We know that $$ \begin{aligned} & \cos \alpha=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2 b c} \\ & 1-2 \sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2 b c} \Rightarrow 2 \sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=1-\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2 b c} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{(a)^{2}-(b-c)^{2}}{2 b c}=\frac{(a-b+c)(a+b-c)}{2 b c} \end{aligned} $$ As $a+b+c=2 S \Rightarrow a+c-b=2 S-2 b=2(S-b)$ and $a+b-c=2 S-2 c=2(S-c)$ $$ \begin{array}{ll} \therefore 2 \sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{2(S-b) \times 2(S-c)}{2 b c}=\frac{2(S-b)(S-c)}{b c} \\ \sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{b c} & \text { Prove that } \\ \sin \frac{\alpha}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{b c}} & \cos \frac{\gamma}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{S(S-c)}{a b}} \text { and } \sin \frac{\gamma}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-b)}{a b}} \end{array} $$ Similarly, it can be proved that: $$ \sin \frac{\beta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-c)}{a c}} \text { and } \sin \frac{\gamma}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-b)}{a b}} $$ (c) Tangents of Half Angle Statement: In any triangle ABC with usual notations, $$ \tan \frac{\alpha}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{S(S-a)}}, \quad \tan \frac{\beta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-c)}{S(S-b)}}, \quad \tan \frac{\gamma}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-b)}{S(S-c)}} $$ where $S=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$. Proof: $\tan \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{\sin \frac{\alpha}{2}}{\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{b c}}}{\sqrt{\frac{S(S-a)}{b c}}}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{S(S-a)}}$ $$ \therefore \tan \frac{\alpha}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{S(S-a)}} $$ Similarly, it can be proved that: ## Check Point: Solve the triangle ABC when $a=5 \mathrm{~cm}, b=6 \mathrm{~cm}$, $c=7 \mathrm{~cm}$ using half angle formulae for sines and tangents. Which one method do you think easy? $$ \tan \frac{\beta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-c)}{S(S-b)}}, \quad \tan \frac{\gamma}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-b)}{S(S-c)}} $$ ## Example: Use half angle formulae to solve the triangle ABC when $a=5 \mathrm{~cm}, b=6 \mathrm{~cm}, c=7 \mathrm{~cm}$. ## Solution: Given: $a=5 \mathrm{~cm}, b=6 \mathrm{~cm}, c=7 \mathrm{~cm}$. To Find: $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ We use half angle formula for cosines here. Now $S=\frac{a+b+c}{2}=\frac{5+6+7}{2}=9$ $\therefore \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{S(S-a)}{b c}}=\sqrt{\frac{9(9-5)}{6 \times 7}}=\sqrt{\frac{36}{42}}=0.926$ $\frac{\alpha}{2}=\cos ^{-1}(0.926)=22.18^{\circ} \Rightarrow \alpha=44.36^{\circ}$ Now $\cos \frac{\beta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{S(S-b)}{a c}}=\sqrt{\frac{9(9-6)}{5 \times 7}}$ $$ =\sqrt{\frac{27}{35}}=0.878 $$ $\frac{\beta}{2}=\cos ^{-1}(0.878)=28.58^{\circ} \Rightarrow \beta=57.20^{\circ}$ To find third angle, we have: $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^{\circ} \Rightarrow \gamma=180^{\circ}-\alpha-\beta$ $\Rightarrow \gamma=180^{\circ}-44.36^{\circ}-57.20^{\circ}=78.44^{\circ}$ ## Check Point: The base of an isosceles triangle measures 14.5 cm and the vertex angle measures $110^{\circ}$. a. Find the measure of one of the congruent sides of the triangle to the nearest hundredth. b. Find the perimeter of the triangle. 1. Use the Law of Cosines to find the remaining side(s) and angle(s) in triangle ABC . (i) $a=7, b=12, \gamma=58.5^{\circ}$ (ii) $b=20, c=15, \alpha=36^{\circ}$ (iii) $a=150, c=150, \beta=15^{\circ}$ (iv) $\beta=45^{\circ}, a=30, c=42$ (v) $a=7, b=10, c=12$ (vi) $a=3, b=3, c=5$ (vii) $a=30, b=45, c=50$ (viii) $a=6, b=6, c=6$ (ix) $a=5, b=12, c=13$ 2. Use the half angles formulae to solve parts (v) to (ix) in Q. 1 where possible. 3. Use the Law of Sines to solve triangle ABC in the following (where possible). (i) $a=10, \alpha=40^{\circ}, \beta=60^{\circ}$ (ii) $b=20, \alpha=50^{\circ}, \beta=70^{\circ}$ (iii) $c=12, \alpha=45^{\circ}, \beta=75^{\circ}$ (iv) $b=18, \beta=40^{\circ} 35^{\prime}, \gamma=120^{\circ}$ (v) $a=14.6, \alpha=25^{\circ} 10^{\prime}, \beta=85.5^{\circ}$ (vi) $c=52, \alpha=42.3^{\circ}, \gamma=85^{\circ} 14^{\prime}$ 4. Solve parts (i) to (iv) of Q. 1 by using the Law of Tangents. 5. Solve by using appropriate law. (i) $a=10, b=8, \beta=80^{\circ}$ (ii) $b=20, c=14, \beta=70^{\circ}$ (iii) $c=12, b=10, \gamma=64^{\circ}$ (iv) $b=18, \alpha=55^{\circ} 5^{\prime}, a=37$ (v) $a=14.6, b=10.6, c=17.2$ (vi) $c=88, \beta=23.2^{\circ}, \gamma=73^{\circ} 14^{\prime}$ 6. A pilot is flying from city A to city C, 500 km apart. He starts his flight $20^{\circ}$ off course and flies on this course for 150 km and is above city B . How far is he from city C ? 7. Two sides of a triangular plot have lengths 400 m and 600 m . The measurement of angle between the sides is $45^{\circ}$. Find the perimeter and area of the plot. 8. The sides of a triangle are $6.5 \mathrm{~cm}, 8.2 \mathrm{~cm}$ and 5.8 cm . Find the measurement of smallest and largest angles. 9. The sides of a parallelogram are 50 cm and 70 cm . Find the length of each diagonal if the larger angle measures $110^{\circ}$. 10. For parallelogram ABCD , find : 11. For the figure below find: 12. Rangers at fire tower A spots a fire at $42^{\circ}$, and rangers at fire tower $B$ spot the same fire at $64^{\circ}$. How far from tower $A$ is the fire to the nearest tenth of a mile? 14. Circle O has a radius of 15 cm . The angle between radii $\overline{\mathrm{OA}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{OB}}$ is $120^{\circ}$. Find the length of chord $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$. 15. Two lighthouses are 12 miles apart along a straight shore. A ship is 15 miles from one lighthouse and 20 miles from the other. Find, to the nearest degree, the measure of the angle between the lines of sight from the ship to each lighthouse. ## Area of Triangular Region (a) Area of Triangular Region when Two Sides and Included Angle are Given When the measures of two sides and the included angle of a triangle are known, the size and shape of the triangle is determined. Therefore, it is possible to use these known values to find the area of the triangle. Let us find the area of an acute angled triangle ABC given below. We know that: Area ( $\Delta$ ) of triangle $\mathrm{ABC}=\frac{1}{2} \times$ base × height Area ( $\Delta$ ) of triangle $\mathrm{ABC}=\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{AB} \times \mathrm{CD}=\frac{1}{2} \times c \times h$ Now in right angled triangle $\mathrm{ACD}, \mathrm{AB}=c$ and $\frac{h}{b}=\sin \alpha \Rightarrow h=b \sin \alpha$ Therefore from (i), $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} \times c \times b \sin \alpha=\frac{1}{2} b c \sin \alpha$ Again, in right angled triangle BCD $\frac{h}{a}=\sin \beta \Rightarrow h=a \sin \beta$ Therefore from (i), $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} \times c \times a \sin \beta=\frac{1}{2} a c \sin \beta$ ## Check Points 1. Rashid found the area of parallelogram $A B C D$ by using $(A B)(B C)(\sin \angle B)$. Shehzad found the area of parallelogram $A B C D$ by using $(A B)(B C)(\sin \angle A)$. Explain why Rashid and Shehzad both got the correct answer. Similarly, we can prove that: $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} a b \sin \gamma$ Hence $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} b c \sin \alpha=\frac{1}{2} a c \sin \beta=\frac{1}{2} a b \sin \gamma$ ## Example: Find the area of triangle DEF if $\mathrm{DE}=10, \mathrm{EF}=8$ and $\angle \mathrm{E}=30^{\circ}$. ## Solution: $$ \begin{aligned} \text { Area of triangle } \mathrm{DEF} & =\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{DE} \times \mathrm{EF} \times \sin (\angle \mathrm{E}) \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 8 \times \sin 30^{\circ} \\ & =40 \times 0.5=20 \text { sq. units } \end{aligned} $$ ## Challenge: Take an obtuse angled triangle and prove that $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} a b \sin \gamma$ (b) Area of Triangular Region when Two Angles and One Side are Given If $a$ is measure of side of a triangle ABC and any two angles let's say $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are given then: Area of triangle $\mathrm{ABC}=\Delta=\frac{1}{2} a^{2} \frac{\sin \beta \sin \gamma}{\sin \alpha}$ Let us prove this formula. We have proved in the previous section that: ## Check Pooint: Urwa said that the area of rhombus $P Q R S$ is $(P Q)^{2}(\sin P)$. Do you agree with Urwa? Explain why or why not. Area of triangle $\mathrm{ABC}=\Delta=\frac{1}{2} a b \sin \gamma$ But in the current situation, $b$ is not given. We can replace $b$ by using law of sines as follows. $\frac{b}{\sin \beta}=\frac{a}{\sin \alpha} \Rightarrow b=\frac{a \sin \beta}{\sin \alpha}$ Substituting the value of $b$ in (i), we get: Chicesipointsing Prove that (i) $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} b^{2} \frac{\sin \alpha \sin \gamma}{\sin \beta}$ (ii) $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} c^{2} \frac{\sin \alpha \sin \beta}{\sin \gamma}$ $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} a\left(\frac{a \sin \beta}{\sin \alpha}\right) \sin \gamma=\frac{1}{2} a^{2} \frac{\sin \beta \sin \gamma}{\sin \alpha}$ In the same way, we can prove that: $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} b^{2} \frac{\sin \alpha \sin \gamma}{\sin \beta} \quad$ and $\quad \Delta=\frac{1}{2} c^{2} \frac{\sin \alpha \sin \beta}{\sin \gamma}$ Hence, $\quad \Delta=\frac{1}{2} a^{2} \frac{\sin \beta \sin \gamma}{\sin \alpha}, \quad \Delta=\frac{1}{2} b^{2} \frac{\sin \alpha \sin \gamma}{\sin \beta}, \quad \Delta=\frac{1}{2} c^{2} \frac{\sin \alpha \sin \beta}{\sin \gamma}$ ## Example: Calculate the cost of grass cutting @ Rs. 10 per sq. unit of a triangular plot ABC if $a=16.5, \alpha=40.5^{\circ}, \beta=65^{\circ}$. Solution: To find the cost of grass cutting, we need area of plot and to find area, we need the third angle $\gamma$. $$ \begin{aligned} \gamma & =180^{\circ}-\alpha-\beta \\ \Rightarrow \gamma & =180^{\circ}-40.5^{\circ}-65^{\circ}=74.5^{\circ} \end{aligned} $$ Now, area of triangle $\mathrm{ABC}=\frac{1}{2} a^{2} \frac{\sin \beta \sin \gamma}{\sin \alpha}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2} \times(16.5)^{2} \times \frac{\sin 65^{\circ} \times \sin 74.5^{\circ}}{\sin 40.5^{\circ}} \\ & =183.05 \text { sq. units } \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the cost of grass cutting @ Rs. 10 per sq. unit $=$ Rs. $10 \times 183.05=$ Rs. 1830.50 ## (c) Area of Triangular Region when Three Sides are Given If $a, b, c$ are measure of sides of a triangle ABC then: Area of triangle $\mathrm{ABC}=\Delta=\sqrt{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}$ where $S=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$ Let us prove this formula. We have proved in the previous section that: Area of triangle $\mathrm{ABC}=\Delta=\frac{1}{2} b c \sin \alpha$ Using half angle formula, we have: $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} b c \times 2 \sin \frac{\alpha}{2} \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}=b c \times \sqrt{\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{b c}} \times \sqrt{\frac{S(S-a)}{b c}}$ ## EX W. Checkent GLERTES Two sides of a triangle are 20 cm long each. Find the angle between both sides if area of triangle is 200 sq. unit. $\Delta=b c \times \sqrt{\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{b c}} \times \sqrt{\frac{S(S-a)}{b c}}=\sqrt{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}$ This formula is known as hero's formula or Heron's formula. Example: Find area of a triangle with dimensions $16,18,20$. Solution: Let $a=16, b=18, c=20$. Area of triangle $=\sqrt{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}$ Where $S=\frac{16+18+20}{2}=\frac{54}{2}=27$ Now, area of triangle $=\sqrt{27(27-16)(27-18)(27-20)}=\sqrt{18711}$ $$ =136.79 \text { sq.unit } $$

## Circhles Connected with Triangles

## (a) Circumcircle

A circle passing through the vertices of any triangle (polygon) is called circumcircle.
The centre of this circle is called the circumcentre and its radius is called the circumradius.
The radius of circumcircle is denoted by $R$.

## (b) Incircle

A circle drawn inside and touching the sides of a triangle (polygon) is called incircle or inscribed circle. It is the largest circle contained in the triangle. The centre of this circle is called the incentre usually denoted by I and its radius is called the inradius denoted by $r$.

## (c) Escribed Circle

A circle touching one of the sides of a triangle externally and the extensions of its two other sides internally, is called an escribed circle (e-circle or ex-circle). The centre of this circle is called the e-centre and its radius is called the e-radius.
If a circle touches extended arms of angle $A$ (circle is drawn opposite to vertex $A$ ) of a triangle ABC , then its centre and radius are respectively denoted by $\mathrm{I}_{1}$ and $r_{1}$. Similarly,
(i) Centre and radius of e-circle opposite to vertex B are denoted by $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ and $r_{2}$.
(ii) Centre and radius of e-circle opposite to vertex C are denoted by $\mathrm{I}_{3}$ and $r_{3}$.

\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}=\frac{a}{2 \sin \alpha}=\frac{a}{2 \times 2 \sin \frac{\alpha}{2} \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}}=\frac{a}{4 \times \frac{\sqrt{(S-b)(S-c)}}{b c} \frac{\sqrt{S(S-a)}}{b c}} \\
& \mathrm{R}=\frac{a b c}{4 \times \sqrt{\frac{(S-b)(S-c)}{b c}} \sqrt{\frac{S(S-a)}{b c}}}=\frac{a}{4 \sqrt{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}} \\
& \mathrm{R}=\frac{a b c}{4 \Delta}
\end{aligned}
$$

Where $\Delta=\sqrt{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}$ and $\sin \alpha=2 \sin \frac{\alpha}{2} \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}$.

## In-Radius of a Circle in a Triangle

Consider a triangle ABC . Draw the three angle bisectors of triangle which intersect at point I which is in-centre of circle.
By drawing angle bisectors, the given triangle ABC has been Livided into three triangles IAB, IBC and IAC.
Draw altitude ID of triangle IBC, altitude IE of triangle IAC and altitude IF of triangle IAB. Note that
$\mathrm{ID}=\mathrm{IE}=\mathrm{IF}=$ radius of in-circle $=r$
Now if $\mathrm{AB}=c, \mathrm{BC}=a, \mathrm{AC}=b$ and $\Delta$ is the area of
triangle ABC , then from the figure:
area of triangle $\mathrm{ABC}=$ area of triangle $\mathrm{IBC}+$ area of triangle $\mathrm{IAC}+$ area of triangle IAB

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta & =\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{BC} \times \mathrm{ID}+\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{AC} \times \mathrm{IE}+\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{AB} \times \mathrm{IF} \\
\Delta & =\frac{1}{2} \times a \times r+\frac{1}{2} \times b \times r+\frac{1}{2} \times c \times r=\frac{1}{2} \times r \times(a+b+c) \\
\Delta & =r \times \frac{a+b+c}{2}=r S \\
r & =\frac{\Delta}{S}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Ken Face

The two geometrical figures, circle and triangle are made up of distinct conception. The triangle is made with straight lines, whereas circle is made by curve lines (arcs). The beauty of circum-circle and in-circle of a triangle is a combination of a triangle and a circle. Engineers use this combination in making parts of machines.

## E-Radius of a Circle of a Triangle

Consider a triangle ABC . Draw internal bisector of $\angle \mathrm{A}$ and external bisectors of $\angle \mathrm{B}$ and $\angle \mathrm{C}$ of triangle intersecting at $\mathrm{I}_{1}$ which is the centre of ex-circle.
By drawing angle bisectors, the given triangle ABC has been divided into three triangles $\mathrm{I}_{1} \mathrm{AB}, \mathrm{I}_{1} B C$ and $I_{1} A C$.

Draw altitude $I_{1} D$ of triangle $I_{1} A B$, altitude $I_{1} E$ of triangle $I_{1} B C$ and altitude $\mathrm{I}_{1} \mathrm{~F}$ of triangle $\mathrm{I}_{1} \mathrm{AC}$. Note that $\mathrm{I}_{1} \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{I}_{1} \mathrm{E}=\mathrm{I}_{1} \mathrm{~F}=$ radius of e-circle $=r_{1}$
Now if $\mathrm{AB}=c, \mathrm{BC}=a, \mathrm{AC}=b$ and $\Delta$ is the area of triangle ABC , then from the figure: area of triangle $A B C=$ area of triangle $I_{1} A B+$ area of triangle $I_{1} A C+$ area of triangle $I_{1} B C$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta & =\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{AB} \times \mathrm{I}_{1} \mathrm{D}+\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{AC} \times \mathrm{I}_{1} \mathrm{~F}-\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{BC} \times \mathrm{I}_{1} \mathrm{E} \\
\Delta & =\frac{1}{2} \times c \times r_{1}+\frac{1}{2} \times b \times r_{1}-\frac{1}{2} \times a \times r_{1}=\frac{1}{2} \times r_{1} \times(c+b-a) \\
\Delta & =r_{1} \times \frac{2 S-a-a}{2}=r_{1} \times \frac{2 S-2 a}{2}=r_{1} \times \frac{2(S-a)}{2} \\
& r_{1}=\frac{\Delta}{S-a}
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we can prove that:

$$
r_{2}=\frac{\Delta}{S-b} \quad \text { and } \quad r_{3}=\frac{\Delta}{S-c}
$$

## Example:

Find $r, \mathrm{R}$ and $r_{2}$ when $a=8, b=9, c=11$.
Solution: Given: $a=8, b=9, c=11$
To find: $r, \mathrm{R}$ and $r_{2}$
First of all, we find $S$ and $\Delta$.
and

$$
\begin{aligned}
S & =\frac{8+9+11}{2}=\frac{28}{2}=14 \\
\Delta & =\sqrt{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)} \\
& =\sqrt{14(14-8)(14-9)(14-11)}=\sqrt{1260}=35.5
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $r=\frac{\Delta}{S}=\frac{35.5}{14}=2.54$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}=\frac{a b c}{4 \Delta}=\frac{792}{142}=5.58 \\
& r_{2}=\frac{\Delta}{S-b}=\frac{35.5}{14-9}=\frac{35.5}{5}=7.1
\end{aligned}
$$

## Example:

Prove that $r_{2}=4 R \cos \frac{\alpha}{2} \cos \frac{\gamma}{2} \sin \frac{\beta}{2}$

## Kevisact:

We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{R}=\frac{a}{2 \sin \alpha}=\frac{b}{2 \sin \beta}=\frac{c}{2 \sin \gamma} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{a}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{b}{\sin \beta}=\frac{c}{\sin \gamma}=2 \mathrm{R} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{a}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{b}{\sin \beta}=\frac{c}{\sin \gamma}
\end{aligned}
$$

Which is law of sines.

## Check Rounts:

Find $r_{1}, r_{2}$ and $r_{3}$ when $a=5.4, b=7.6$ and $c=10.2$.

## Check Points

Show that

$$
4 R \cos \frac{\alpha}{2} \cos \frac{\beta}{2} \sin \frac{\gamma}{2}=r_{3}
$$

## Solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { R.H.S } & =4 R \cos \frac{\alpha}{2} \cos \frac{\gamma}{2} \sin \frac{\beta}{2} \\
& =4 \times \frac{a b c}{4 \Delta} \times \sqrt{\frac{S(S-a)}{b c}} \times \sqrt{\frac{S(S-c)}{a b}} \times \sqrt{\frac{(S-a)(S-c)}{a c}} \\
& =\frac{a b c}{\Delta} \times \sqrt{\frac{S^{2}(S-a)^{2}(S-c)^{2}}{a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}}}=\frac{a b c}{\Delta} \times \frac{S(S-a)(S-c)}{a b c} \\
& =\frac{1}{\Delta} \times \frac{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}{S-b}=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{\Delta(S-b)} \\
& =\frac{\Delta}{S-b}=r_{2}=\text { L.H.S }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Chord and Arcs of a Circle

## After studying this unit students will be able to:

- One and only one circle can pass through three non collinear points.
- A straight line drawn from the centre of a circle to bisect the chord is perpendicular to the chord.
- Perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle on a chord, bisects it.
- Two congruent chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre.
- Two chords of a circle equidistant from the centre are congruent.
- If two arcs of a circle (or of congruent circles) are congruent, then the corresponding chords are equal.
- If two chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) are equal, then their corresponding arcs (minor, major or semicircle) are congruent.
- Equal chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) subtend equal angles at the centre (at the corresponding centres).
- If the angles subtended by two chords of a circle (or congruent circles) at the centre (corresponding circles) are equal, the chords are equal.
- Apply concepts of chords and ares to real life word problems such as decorative features, rainbow, bridges and roller coaster track.

Circle theorems are statements in geometry that state important results related to circles that are used to solve various questions in geometry. They have very useful applications within design and engineering.
These theorems show relationships between angles within the geometry of a circle. We can use these theorems along with prior knowledge of other angle properties to calculate missing angles, without the use of a protractor.
Can you find the value of angle in the figure below.

## Chords of a Circle

## Definition

A line segment joining two points of a circle is called chord of that circle.

## Theorem 9.1

Statements One and only one circle can pass through three non collinear points.

## Class Activity:

(i) Take three non-collinear points A, B and C on the paper and join them to obtain the triangle.
(ii) Draw right bisectors of the sides. They will meet at only one point P (say).
(iii) With centre P , draw a circle of radius PA .

What do you notice? Does the circle pass through B and C also?

Corollaries: (i) One and only one circle can pass through two points lying on the same line.
(ii) Two circles cannot intersect each other at more than two points.

## Example:

Construct a square with sides 6 cm long. Show that one and only one circle can be drawn through vertices of the square. Measure the radius of the circle.

## Solution:

(i) Construct a square ABCD having side equal to 6 cm long.
(ii) Draw diagonals $\overline{\mathrm{AC}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{BD}}$.
(iii) The two diagonals bisect each other at point O .
(iv) With centre O , construct a circle with radius OA .
(v) You will see that the circle will also pass through vertices B, C and D.
As diagonals $\overline{\mathrm{AC}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{BD}}$ bisect each other. Therefore:

$$
\mathrm{OA}=\mathrm{OB}=\mathrm{OC}=\mathrm{OD}
$$


Furthermore, there is only one centre O of the circle, therefore we can say that only one circle can be drawn through vertices of the square.
Now in right triangle $A B C$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (A C)^{2}=(A B)^{2}+(B C)^{2} \\
& (A C)^{2}=(6)^{2}+(6)^{2}=36+36=72
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking square root on both sides, we have:
$\mathrm{AC}=\sqrt{72}=6 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~cm}$

## Kev Fact:

If two chords of a circle do not pass through the centre, they cannot bisect each other.

Radius $=\mathrm{OA}=$ half of $\mathrm{AC}=3 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~cm}$

## Theorem 9.2

Statement: A straight line drawn from the centre of a circle to bisect the chord is perpendicular to the chord.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a chord AB of a circle with centre O .
(ii) Take a point C on the chord such that $\mathrm{AC}=\mathrm{BC}$.
(iii) Join O to C and measure $\angle \mathrm{OCA}$ and $\angle \mathrm{OCB}$.

Are the angles equal? Yes! they are.

$$
\therefore \quad \angle \mathrm{OCA}=\angle \mathrm{OCB} \quad \text { i.e., } \quad \overline{\mathrm{OC}} \perp \overline{\mathrm{AB}}
$$

## Corollaries:

(i) If a diameter or radial segment of a circle bisects the chord, it is perpendicular to the chord.
(ii) The diameter or radial segment of a circle passes through the mid points of two parrallel chords of a circle.

## Theorem 9.3

Statement: Perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle on a chord, bisects it.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a chord AB of a circle with centre O .
(ii) Take a point C on the chord such that $\angle \mathrm{OCA}=90^{\circ}$.
(iii) Measure AC and BC .

Are they equal?

Yes! they are. i.e., $\mathrm{AC}=\mathrm{BC}$

## Corollaries:

(i) If a diameter of a circle is perpendicular to the chord, it bisects the chord.
(ii) Perpendicular (right) bisector of a chord of a circle passes through the centre of a circle.

## Example:

Diameter and chord of a circle are 20 cm and 16 cm long respectively and are perpendicular to each other. Calculate the distance of chord form the centre.

## Solution:

Diameter = CD = 20 cm
Radius $=\mathrm{OA}=10 \mathrm{~cm}$
Chord $=\mathrm{AB}=16 \mathrm{~cm}$
As the diameter and chord are perpendicular to each other.
Therefore, diameter bisects the chord.
Hence, $\mathrm{AE}=\mathrm{BE}=8 \mathrm{~cm}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Iow in right triangle } \mathrm{AEO} \text { : } \\
& \quad(\mathrm{AE})^{2}+(\mathrm{OE})^{2}=(\mathrm{OA})^{2} \Rightarrow(8)^{2}+(\mathrm{OE})^{2}=(10)^{2} \\
& \Rightarrow(\mathrm{OE})^{2}=(10)^{2}-(8)^{2}=100-64=36 \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{OE}=\sqrt{36}=6 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$


Diameters of a circle bisect each other.
∴ The distance of chord from the centre $=6 \mathrm{~cm}$

## Theorem 9.4

Statement: Two congruent chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw two equal chords AB and CD of a circle as shown in the adjoining figure.
(ii) Draw perpendiculars OE and OF on the chords AB and CD respectively.
(iii) Measure OE and OF.

Are they equal? Yes! they are equal.

## Theorem 9.5

## Statement:

Two chords of a circle equidistant from the centre, are congruent.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw two chords AB and CD of a circle such that they are equidistant from the centre as shown in the adjoining figure.
(ii) Measure chords AB and CD .

You will see that they are equal in length.

## Corollary:

(i) If two chords of a circle are unequal, then longer chord is nearer to the centre and vice versa.
(ii) If two chords of two congruent circles are congruent, then they are equidistant from their respective centres and vice versa.

## Example:

In the adjoining figure, $\overline{\mathrm{AB}} \| \overline{\mathrm{CD}}$ such that $\mathrm{AB}=24 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $\mathrm{CD}=10 \mathrm{~cm}$. Find the radius of the circle if distance between chords is 17 cm .

## Solution:

Let the radius of circle be r cm with centre P .

Draw $\overline{\mathrm{PE}} \perp \overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{PF}} \perp \overline{\mathrm{CD}}$
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{BE}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{AB}$ and $\mathrm{CF}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{CD}$
As the chords AB and CD are parallel, therefore points $\mathrm{E}, \mathrm{P}$ and F are collinear and $\mathrm{EF}=17 \mathrm{~cm}$
Let $\mathrm{PE}=x$, then $\mathrm{PF}=17-x$
Join P to B and C , then $\mathrm{PB}=\mathrm{PC}=\mathrm{r}$
Now, PBE and PCF are right angled triangled. Therefore:

$$
\begin{array}{llll} 
& (\mathrm{PB})^{2}=(\mathrm{PE})^{2}+(\mathrm{EB})^{2} & \text { and } & (\mathrm{PC})^{2}=(\mathrm{PF})^{2}+(\mathrm{FC})^{2} \\
& \mathrm{r}^{2}=x^{2}+12^{2} \ldots \ldots .(\mathrm{i}) & \text { and } \quad \mathrm{r}^{2}=(17-x)^{2}+5^{2} \quad \ldots \ldots(\mathrm{ii}) \\
\Rightarrow & x^{2}+12^{2}=(17-x)^{2}+5^{2} \quad \ldots . .[\text { comparing (i) and (ii) }] \\
\Rightarrow & x^{2}+144=289+x^{2}-34 x+25 & \ldots \quad \text { KevFact: }
\end{array}
$$

## Kevinact:

If $A B$ is chord and diameter $C D$ is right bisector of AB , then:
$\mathrm{AC}=\mathrm{BC}$ and $\mathrm{AD}=\mathrm{BD}$

Now from (i), we have:
$\mathrm{r}^{2}=5^{2}+12^{2}=25+144=169$
Taking square roots on both sides, we get $\mathrm{r}=13$.
∴ Radius of circle $=\mathrm{r}=13 \mathrm{~cm}$

## Example:

Two parallel chords AB and CD of lengths 16 cm and 12 cm respectively are drawn on the opposite sides of centre $O$ of the circle. Find the distance between the chords if the radius of the circle is 10 cm .

## Solution:

Radius of circle $=\mathrm{OA}=\mathrm{OC}=10 \mathrm{~cm}$
$\mathrm{AB}=16 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{CD}=12 \mathrm{~cm}$
Draw $\overline{\mathrm{OE}} \perp \overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{OF}} \perp \overline{\mathrm{CD}}$
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{AE}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{AB}=8 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $\mathrm{CF}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{CD}=6 \mathrm{~cm}$
As $\overline{\mathrm{AB}} \| \overline{\mathrm{CD}}$, therefore points $\mathrm{E}, \mathrm{O}$ and F are collinear.
Now, OAE and OCF are right angled triangles. Therefore:

|  | $(\mathrm{OE})^{2}+(\mathrm{AE})^{2}=(\mathrm{OA})^{2}$ | and | $(\mathrm{OF})^{2}+(\mathrm{CF})^{2}=(\mathrm{OC})^{2}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Rightarrow$ | $(\mathrm{OE})^{2}+(8)^{2}=(10)^{2}$ | and | $(\mathrm{OF})^{2}+(6)^{2}=(10)^{2}$ |
| $\Rightarrow$ | $(\mathrm{OE})^{2}+64=100$ | and | $(\mathrm{OF})^{2}+36=100$ |
| $\Rightarrow$ | $(\mathrm{OE})^{2}=100-64=36$ | and | $(\mathrm{OF})^{2}=100-36=64$ |

Taking square roots, we get:

$$
\mathrm{OE}=6 \mathrm{~cm} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{OF}=8 \mathrm{~cm}
$$

∴ Distance between chords $=\mathrm{OE}+\mathrm{OF}=6+8=14 \mathrm{~cm}$

## Arcs of Circles

## Arc of a Circle

An arc is a part of a circle. In the figure, AB is an arc of the circle P .
Arc AB is denoted by $\widehat{A B}$.

## Semicircle

A diameter divides a circle into two equal parts. Each part is called semicircle or half circle. We use three letters to name a semicircle. The first and third letter are end points of diameter. In the figure, $\overline{X A Y}$ is semicircle. Can you name the other semicircle?

## Minor and Major arcs

Minor arc is the arc included in a semicircle while the arc which includes a semicircle is called major arc.
In the Fig. $\widehat{E F}$ is minor arc while $\widehat{E C F}$ is major arc.

## Kev Fact:

(i) Major arc of a circle and semicircle arc denoted by three letters.
(ii) Minor arc is less than and major arc is greater than the semicircle.

## Central Angle

Angle subtended by an arc at the centre of a circle is called central angle of the arc. An angle whose vertex is the centre of circle and whose arms pass through end points of arc is known as central angle of arc.

## Kev Fact:

If an arc is included in a semi-circle, then its central angle is less than $180^{\circ}$. Central angle of semi-circle
is straight angle $\left(180^{\circ}\right)$. Central angle of major arc of the circle is greater than $180^{\circ}$.
In the figure $\angle \mathrm{AOB}$ is central angle.

## Congruent Arcs

Two arcs of a circle (or of two congruent circles) are congruent if their central angles are congruent.

## Theorem 9.6

## Statement:

If two arcs of a circle (or of congruent circles) are congruent, then the corresponding chords are equal.

## Class Activity:

(i) Take two congruent arcs AB and CD of a circle with centre O.
(ii) Join C to D and A to B .
(iii) Measure chords AB and CD .

You will see that $A B=C D$

## Kev Fact:


If two arcs of two congruent circles are congruent, then the corresponding chords of both circles are equal.

## Theorem 9.7

## Statement;

If two chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) are equal, then their corresponding arcs (minor, major or semicircle) are congruent.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw two equal chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O.
(ii) Measure corresponding arcs AB and CD . They will be congruent.

## Corollary:

(i) If two chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) are equal, then their corresponding minor or major arcs are congruent.
(ii) If two chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) are equal, then their corresponding semicircles are congruent.

## Theorem 9.8

## Statement:

Equal chords of a circle (or of congruent circles) subtend equal angles at the centre (at the corresponding centres).

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw two equal chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O .
(ii) Join O to $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}$ and D .
(iii) Measure corresponding angles AOB and COD .

You will observe that the corresponding angles are equal in measure.

## Theorem 9.9

## Statement:

If the angles subtended by two chords of a circle (or congruent circles) at the centre (corresponding circles) are equal, the chords are equal.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw two chords AB and CD of a circle such that

$$
\angle \mathrm{AOB}=\angle \mathrm{COD}
$$

(ii) Measure corresponding chords AB and CD .

What do you notice?
You will observe that the corresponding chords are equal in measure.

## Example:

In the figure, $\widehat{A B}=4 \widehat{B C}$ and $\angle \mathrm{AOB}=120^{\circ}$, find:
(a) $\angle \mathrm{BOC}$
(b) $\angle \mathrm{OBC}$
(c) $\angle \mathrm{OBA}$
(d) $\angle \mathrm{OAB}+\angle \mathrm{ABC}+\angle \mathrm{BCO}+\angle \mathrm{COA}$

## Solution:

(a) Let $\angle \mathrm{BOC}=x$, then $\angle \mathrm{AOB}=4 x \quad \ldots(\widehat{A B}=4 \widehat{B C})$

But $\angle \mathrm{AOB}=120^{\circ} \ldots$. (Given)
$\therefore 4 x=120^{\circ} \Rightarrow x=30^{\circ}$
Hence, $\angle \mathrm{BOC}=30^{\circ}$
(b) $\triangle \mathrm{OBC}$ is an isosceles triangle. $(\mathrm{OB}=\mathrm{OC}=$ radii)
$\Rightarrow \quad \angle \mathrm{OBC}=\angle \mathrm{OCB} \quad$ (opposite angles of congruent sides of triangle)
$\therefore \angle \mathrm{OBC}=\frac{1}{2}\left(180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}\right)=75^{\circ}$
(c) $\triangle \mathrm{OAB}$ is an isosceles triangle. $(\mathrm{OA}=\mathrm{OB}=$ radii)
$\Rightarrow \cdot \angle \mathrm{OAB}=\angle \mathrm{OBA} \quad$ (opposite angles of congruent sides of triangle)
$\therefore \angle \mathrm{OBA}=\frac{1}{2}\left(180^{\circ}-120^{\circ}\right)=30^{\circ}$
(d)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\angle \mathrm{OAB}+\angle \mathrm{ABC}+\angle \mathrm{BCO}+\angle \mathrm{COA} & =30^{\circ}+\left(30^{\circ}+75^{\circ}\right)+75^{\circ}+\left(30^{\circ}+120^{\circ}\right) \\
& =30^{\circ}+105^{\circ}+75^{\circ}+150^{\circ}=360^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Example:

Diagram shows a pentagon inscribed in a circle with centre P .
If $\widehat{A B}=\widehat{B C}=\widehat{C D}$ and $\angle \mathrm{ABC}=140^{\circ}$, then find:
(a) $\angle \mathrm{AEB}$
(b) $\angle \mathrm{AED}$
(c) $\angle \mathrm{BPD}$

## Solution:

(a) Given that, $\widehat{A B}=\widehat{B C}=\widehat{C D}$, then:

Corresr -ding chords are equal in length.
i.e., $\mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{BC}=\mathrm{CD}$
ABCE is a cyclic quadrilateral.
$\therefore \quad \angle \mathrm{ABC}+\angle \mathrm{AEC}=180^{\circ}$
$\Rightarrow \angle \mathrm{AEC}=180^{\circ}-\angle \mathrm{ABC}=180^{\circ}-140^{\circ}=40^{\circ}$
$\Rightarrow \quad \angle \mathrm{AEB}+\angle \mathrm{BEC}=40^{\circ}$ (angle sum postulate)
$\Rightarrow 2 \angle \mathrm{AEB}=40^{\circ} \quad(\angle \mathrm{AEB}=\angle \mathrm{BEC})$
$\Rightarrow \angle \mathrm{AEB}=20^{\circ}$
(b) As, $\mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{BC}=\mathrm{CD}$ (given)

Kev Fact:
If two arcs of a circle are unequal, then chord and angle corresponding to greater arc are greater.
$\angle \mathrm{AEB}=\angle \mathrm{BEC}=\angle \mathrm{CED}=20^{\circ}$
(Equal chords subtend equal angle at a point on the circumference.)
Now, $\angle \mathrm{AED}=\angle \mathrm{AEB}+\angle \mathrm{BEC}+\angle \mathrm{CED}=20^{\circ}+20^{\circ}+20^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$
(c) $\angle \mathrm{BPD}=2 \angle \mathrm{BED}$ (Angle at the centre is double the angle at a point on circumference.)

$$
=2 \times 40^{\circ}=80^{\circ}
$$

## Example:

In the figure, chords $\overline{E F} \| \overline{G H}$. Prove that:

$$
\widehat{E G}=\widehat{F H}
$$

## Solution:

Draw $\overline{\mathrm{EF}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{FG}}$ passing through centre of circle P .
$\angle \mathrm{EPG}=2 \angle \mathrm{EFG}$ (Angle at the centre is double the angle at a point on the circumference.)

$$
\begin{equation*}
\therefore \quad \angle \mathrm{EFG}=\frac{1}{2} \angle \mathrm{EPG} \tag{i}
\end{equation*}
$$

Similarly, $\angle \mathrm{FGH}=\frac{1}{2} \angle \mathrm{FPH}$

But, $\angle \mathrm{EFG}=\angle \mathrm{FGH}$ (alternate angles)

## Check Point:

Prove that non-parallel sides of a cyclic trapezium are equal.
$\therefore \quad \angle \mathrm{EPG}=\angle \mathrm{FPH} \quad$ [from (i) and (ii)]
Hence, $\widehat{E G}=\widehat{F H}$ (Arcs subtending equal angles at the centre of circle are equal.)

## Excrcise 9.3

1. In the figure, chord $\mathrm{AB}=$ chord BC .
(i) Is $\widehat{A B}=\widehat{B C}$ ?
(ii) Is $\angle \mathrm{APB}=\angle \mathrm{BPC}$ ?
(iii) If $\widehat{A B}<\widehat{A D}$, then what is relation between corresponding chords?
2. In the figure,
$\widehat{A C}=\widehat{B D}$
Prove that: $\overline{A B} \| \overline{C D}$
3. In the given figure, chords $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{CD}}$ intersect at P .

If $A B=C D$, then prove that:

$$
\widehat{A B}=\widehat{C D}
$$

4. Consider two circles of radii 2 cm and 4 cm centered at P and Q respectively. $\overparen{A B}$ and $\widehat{C D}$ are their arcs such that $\angle \mathrm{APB}=\angle \mathrm{CQD}$.
i. Are $\widehat{A B}$ and $\widehat{C D}$ congruent?
ii. What is relation between the lengths of $\overparen{A B}$ and $\overparen{C D}$ ?
iii. Show that $\triangle \mathrm{APB} \sim \triangle \mathrm{CQD}$
5. O is centre of two concentric circles of radii 3 cm and 6 cm . OA and OB are radii of larger circle and they meet smaller circle at C and D respectively.
i. Are $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{CD}}$ parallel?
ii. If $A B=8 \mathrm{~cm}$, then find $C D$.
iii. Find distance between $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{CD}}$.
6. The length of an arc of a circle is 4 cm and its central angle is of measure $60^{\circ}$. Find central angle of the arc whose length is 8 cm .
7. Given that M is a point on a circle centered at P . If M is equidistant from the two radii PE and PF , show that $\widehat{M E}=\widehat{M F}$.
8. Consider two circles centered at A and B respectively. $\overline{\mathrm{CD}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{EF}}$ are their chords such that $\mathrm{CD}=12 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{EF}=8 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $\angle \mathrm{CAD}=\angle \mathrm{EBF}$. Find radius of circle A if radius of circle B is 4 cm .

Prove that:

$$
\mathrm{AC}=\mathrm{BD}
$$

10. In the given figure, ABC is an isosceles triangle inscribed in a circle centered at O .
Prove that $\kappa \stackrel{\bar{\nu}}{\Sigma}$ bisects $\angle \mathrm{BDC}$.
11. ABCDE is a pentagon inscribed in a circle.

If $\mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{BC}=\mathrm{CD}, \angle \mathrm{BCD}=130^{\circ}$ and $\angle \mathrm{BAE}=120^{\circ}$ Find:
(a) $\angle \mathrm{ABC}$
(b) $\angle \mathrm{CDE}$
(c) $\angle \mathrm{AED}$
(d) $\angle \mathrm{EAD}$
12. Given that O is the centre of a circle. Diameters $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{CD}}$ are perpendicular to each other. Prove that the line segments joining in order the end points of diameters form a square.
13. In the figure, O is centre of the circle.
$\mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{CD}$ and $\angle \mathrm{OAB}=40^{\circ}$.
Find $\angle \mathrm{AOB}$ and $\angle \mathrm{COD}$.
Are the angles equal? If yes, then why?
14. In the figure, diameters AB and CD of circle are perpendicular.
(i) Prove that all the four chords make equal central angles.
(ii) Find $\angle \mathrm{PCB}$ and $\angle \mathrm{ACB}$.
(iii) Find other angles that are equal to $\angle A C B$.
(iv) What is the name of inscribed polygon?
(v) How many circles can be drawn through the vertices of polygon formed?
15. In the adjoining figure, $\mathrm{RS}=3 \mathrm{PQ}$ and $\angle \mathrm{PTQ}+\angle \mathrm{RTS}=180^{\circ}$.
(i) Find $\angle \mathrm{PTQ}$ and $\angle \mathrm{RTS}$.
(ii) What is the ratio between measures of $\angle \mathrm{PTQ}$ and $\angle \mathrm{RTS}$ ?

## Applications of Chords and Ares

## Arc Length

The length of an arc of a circle of radius ' $r$ ' that subtends an angle $\theta$ at the center is calculated by the following formula:
Arc length $=l=\frac{\theta}{360^{\circ}} \times$ circumference of circle

$$
=\frac{\theta}{360^{\circ}} \times 2 \pi r
$$


Where $360^{\circ}$ is the interior angle subtended by a circle.

## Chord Length

Length of a chord of a circle of radius ' $r$ '
lying at a distance ' $d$ ' from the centre is:
In the adjoining figure, length of chord AB is:
$\mathrm{AB}=2 \sqrt{r^{2}-d^{2}}$

Note that $A C$ is half of $A B$.

## Perimeter of a of Semicircle

The perimeter of a semicircle is given by the following formula.
$\mathrm{P}=2 \times$ radius + arc length $=2 r+\pi r$

## Perimeter of a Segment of a Circle

Perimeter of segment of a circle is defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{P} & =\operatorname{arc} \text { length }+ \text { chord length } \\
& =\frac{\theta}{360^{\circ}} \times 2 \pi r+2 \sqrt{r^{2}-d^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$


## Area of Sector of Circle

Area of the sector of a circle having radius $r$ and central angle $\theta$ is:
$\mathrm{A}=\frac{\theta}{360^{\circ}} \times \pi r^{2}$
Where the angle $\theta$ is measured in degrees.

## Example:

Find the length of arc and area of sector a circle with central angie of $50^{\circ}$ and radius 14 cm .
Solution: Given tinat:

$$
\theta=60^{\circ} \text { and } r=14 \mathrm{~cm}
$$

Arc length $=\frac{\theta}{360^{\circ}} \times 2 \pi r$

$$
=\frac{60^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 14=14.67 \mathrm{~cm}
$$

Area $=\frac{\theta}{360^{\circ}} \times \pi r^{2}=\frac{60^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} \times \frac{22}{7} \times(14)^{2}=102.67 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$

## Example:

A circular decoration piece consists of two equal parts as shown in the figure. Find the length of one part of the piece. What is the cost of decoration piece @ Rs. 8 per centimetre? Solution:
Given that $r=56 \mathrm{~cm}, \theta=90^{\circ}$, then:
$l=\frac{\theta}{360^{\circ}} \times 2 \pi r=\frac{90^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 56$.
$l=88 \mathrm{~cm}$

Length of one part of the decoration piece is $=2 \times 88=176 \mathrm{~cm}$
Cost of decoration piece @ Rs. 8 per cm =Rs. $2 \times 176 \times 8=$ Rs. 2,816

chapterTitle: Tangents and Angles of a Circle
mdxBody:
Tangents have several important applications across various fields, particularly in mathematics, physics, engineering, and geometry. Some applications of tangents are:

- Tangents play an important role in the study of curves. They are lines that touch a curve at a single point, perpendicular to the curve's radius at that point. Tangents are used to define geometric properties such as the radius, diameter, chord, and arc length of circles.
- Tangents are used to design curves in buildings, such as arches and domes.
- Tangents are used to design curves in roads, bridges, and other structures. By using tangents, engineers can create curves that are safe and efficient for travel.
- Tangents are used to analyse the motion of objects. For example, when a car or bike travels down a road, the road becomes tangent at each location where the wheels roll.

## Tangent to a Circle

## Tangent Line

A line which touches the circle at only one point is called tangent line. A tangent line is perpendicular to the radial segment. More over the distance of tangent line from the centre is equal to radius of the circle.

## Theorem 10.1

## Statement:

If a line is drawn perpendicular to a radial segment of a circle at its outer end point, it is tangent to the circle.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a radial segment $\mathrm{AB}(\overline{\mathrm{AB}})$ of a circle as shown in the adjoining figure.
(ii) Draw a perpendicular line $\mathrm{PQ}(\overleftrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}})$ at the outer end of AB .
(iii) Check whether $\overleftrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}}$ touches the circle at only one point or not.
Is $\overleftrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}}$ tangent line?
(iv) Take any point C on $\overleftrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}}$ and join C to A .

Why $\overline{\mathrm{AC}}$ is not the radial segment?

## Theorem 10.2

## Statement:

The tangent to a circle and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are perpendicular to each other.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a radial segment $\mathrm{AB}(\overline{\mathrm{AB}})$ of a circle as shown in the adjoining figure.
(ii) Draw a tangent $\overleftrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}}$ at point B .
(iii) Measure the angel between $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ and tangent $\overleftrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}}$. i.e. $\angle \mathrm{ABC}$
What is the measure of $\angle \mathrm{ABC}$ ?
(v) Take any point C on $\overleftrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}}$ and join

C to A . Which is shortest $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ or $\overline{\mathrm{AC}}$ ? Why $\angle \mathrm{ABQ}=90^{\circ}$ and $\angle \mathrm{ACB} \neq 90^{\circ}$ ?

## Corollaries:

(i) The line perpendicular to the tangent at point of contact passes through the centre of circle.
(ii) The lines perpendicular to the diameter of a circle at its end points are tangents to the circle.
(iii) The line perpendicular to the tangent of circle from centre passes through point of contact.
(iv) The tangents at end points of diameter of a circle are parallel.

## Theorem 10.3

## Statement:

The two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside the circle are equal in length.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a circle with centre O .
(ii) Take a point A outside the circle and join with O .
(iii) Draw two tangents $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AC}}$. where $B$ and $C$ are points on the circle.
(iv) Measure $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{AC}}$. Are they equal?

## Corollary:

The two tangents drawn to a circle from an outer point make equal angles with the line segment joining the centre and outer point.

## Theorem 10.4

## Statement:

If two circles touch externally, the distance between their centres is equal to the sum of their radii.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw two circles of radii 2 cm and 1 cm with centres $A$ and $B$ respectively such that the circles touch externally as shown in the figure.
(ii) Join the centres of both circles by drawing AB .
(iii) Measure AB . It will be 3 cm .

Is 3 cm equal to the sum of radii of both the circles? Can we write $\mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{AC}+\mathrm{BC}$ ?

## Corollary:

If two congruent circles touch externally, the distance between their centres is equal to diameter of each circle.

## Theorem 10.5

## Statement:

If two circles touch internally, the distance between their centres is equal to the difference of their radii.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw two circles of radii 3.5 cm and 1 cm with centres A and B respectively such that the circles touch internally as shown in the figure.
(ii) Draw AB .
(iii) Measure AC . It will be 2.5 cm .

Is 2.5 cm equal to the difference of radii of both the circles?
Can we write $\mathrm{AC}=\mathrm{AB}-\mathrm{BC}$ ?
where $A B$ and $B C$ are radii of both circles.

## Corollary:

If two congruent circles touch intarnally, the distance between their centres is equal to zero.

## Theorem 10.6 (Alternate Segment Theorem)

## Statement:

An angle between a tangent and chord of a circle through the point of contact is equal to the angle in the alternate segment.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a tangent $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{PT}}$ and a chord $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{PA}}$ at the point of contact T of a circle centered at O .
(ii) Measure $\angle \mathrm{APT}$ and note it.
(iii) Draw angle $\angle \mathrm{ABP}$ in the alternate segment and measure it.

You will see that $\angle \mathrm{APT}=\angle \mathrm{ABP}$

## Example:

In the figure, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$ is tangent to the circle of centre P .
(i) Express the length AP in terms of r .
(ii) What is measure of $\angle \mathrm{ABP}$ ? and why?
(iii) What is the radius of the circle?

## Solution:

(i) $\mathrm{AP}=\mathrm{AC}+\mathrm{PC}=(9+\mathrm{r}) \mathrm{cm}$
(ii) $\angle \mathrm{ABP}=90^{\circ}$ because tangent line and radial segment are perpendicular to each other.
(iii) ABP is right angled triangle, therefore using Pythagoras theorem, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (\mathrm{AP})^{2}=(\mathrm{AB})^{2}+(\mathrm{BP})^{2} & & \\
\Rightarrow & (9+\mathrm{r})^{2}=(15)^{2}+\mathrm{r}^{2} & \Rightarrow & 81+\mathrm{r}^{2}+18 \mathrm{r}=225+\mathrm{r}^{2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & 18 \mathrm{r}=225-81=144 & \Rightarrow & \mathrm{r}=144 \div 18=8
\end{aligned}
$$

$\therefore \quad$ Radius of the circle $=8 \mathrm{~cm}$

## Example:

In the figure, $\overline{\mathrm{OP}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{OQ}}$ are tangents to a circle centered at S . If $\angle \mathrm{POQ}=40^{\circ}$, then find:
(i) $\angle \mathrm{PSQ}$
(ii) $\angle S P Q$
(iii) $\angle \mathrm{OPQ}$

Solution:
(i) Join O and S .

As OPS is right angled triangle, therfore:
$\angle \mathrm{OPS}=90^{\circ}$

Also $\angle \mathrm{POS}=20^{\circ}$ (Half of $40^{\circ} . \overline{\mathrm{OS}}$ is angle bisector of $\angle \mathrm{POQ}$.)
$\therefore \angle \mathrm{PSO}=90^{\circ}-20^{\circ}=70^{\circ}$
Hence, $\angle \mathrm{PSQ}=\angle \mathrm{PSO}+\angle \mathrm{QSO}=70^{\circ}+70^{\circ}=140^{\circ} \quad(\angle \mathrm{PSO}=\angle \mathrm{QSO})$
(ii) In $\triangle \mathrm{PQS}, \mathrm{PS}=\mathrm{QS}$ (Radii of same circle)
$\therefore \angle \mathrm{SPQ}=\angle \mathrm{SQP}$ (Opposite angles of congruent sides of triangle)
Let $\angle \mathrm{SPQ}=\angle \mathrm{SQP}=x$
Then, $x+x+\angle \mathrm{PSQ}=180^{\circ} \quad \Rightarrow \quad 2 x+140^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$
$\Rightarrow \quad 2 x=180^{\circ}-140^{\circ}=40^{\circ} \quad \Rightarrow \quad x=20^{\circ}$
Hence, $\angle \mathrm{SPQ}=\angle \mathrm{SQP}=20^{\circ}$
(iii) $\angle \mathrm{OPQ}=\angle \mathrm{SPO}-\angle \mathrm{SPQ}=90^{\circ}-20^{\circ}=70^{\circ}$

Example: Find the measures of angles $a$ and $b$ in the adjoining figure.

## Solution:

As $\overline{\mathrm{OQ}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{OR}}$ are tangents, therefore:
$\angle \mathrm{ORP}=\angle \mathrm{OQP}=90^{\circ}$
Now OQPR is a kite.
$\therefore \quad 45^{\circ}+90^{\circ}+a+90^{\circ}=360^{\circ}$
$\Rightarrow a=360^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=135^{\circ}$
As $\overline{\mathrm{RS}}$ is a straight line and P lies on it.
$\therefore \quad a+\angle \mathrm{QPS}=180^{\circ} \Rightarrow 135^{\circ}+\angle \mathrm{QPS}=180^{\circ}$
$\Rightarrow \quad \angle \mathrm{QPS}=180^{\circ}-135^{\circ}=45^{\circ}$
In $\triangle \mathrm{PQS}, \mathrm{PQ}=\mathrm{PS} \quad$ (Radii of same circle)
$\therefore \angle \mathrm{PQS}=\angle \mathrm{PSQ} \quad$ (Opposite angles of congruent sides of triangle)
Then, $b+b+45^{\circ}=180^{\circ} \quad \Rightarrow \quad 2 b+45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$
$\Rightarrow \quad 2 b=180^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=135^{\circ} \quad \Rightarrow \quad b=67.5^{\circ}$
Example: Find the measures of angles $x, y$ and $z$ in the adjoining figure.

## Solution:

We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \angle B D C \\
\therefore \quad \therefore \quad y & =\angle B C A(\text { Theorem 10.6 }) \\
\therefore \quad & 60^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

In triangle BCD :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 56^{\circ}+y+z=180^{\circ} \\
\Rightarrow \quad 56^{\circ}+60^{\circ}+z & =180^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

$\Rightarrow z=180^{\circ}-56^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=64^{\circ}$
Now,
$x=\angle \mathrm{CBD}$ (Theorem 10.6)
$\Rightarrow \quad x=56^{\circ}$

topicTitle: 10.2 Angle in a Segment of a Circle
mdxBody:
## Segment of a Circle

A chord of a circle divides the circular region into two parts, called segments of the circle. The region between the chord and the minor arc is called the minor segment, and the region between the chord and the major arc is called the major segment.

## Angle in a Segment

An angle whose vertex is a point on the arc of a circle, and whose arms pass through the end points of a chord, is called the inscribed angle of the arc (the angle in the segment).

## Key Fact

The major segment is greater than a semi-circular region and always contains the centre of the circle, while the minor segment is smaller than a semi-circular region.

## Theorem 10.7

## Statement:

The measure of a central angle of a minor arc of a circle is double that of the angle subtended by the corresponding major arc.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a circle O and take points E, F and G on the same segment of the circle.
(ii) Measure angles E, F, G and the central angle $\angle$COD.
(iii) Check whether:

$$
2\angle E = 2\angle F = 2\angle G = \angle COD
$$

## Theorem 10.8

## Statement:

Any two angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a circle and a chord AB.
(ii) Take three points C, D and E on the same segment and join them with the end points of chord AB.
(iii) Measure $\angle C$, $\angle D$ and $\angle E$.

## Result:

Any number of angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.

## Theorem 10.9

## Statement:

The angle in a semi-circle is a right angle.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a semicircle with centre O.
(ii) Take a point P on the semicircle and draw AP and PB.
(iii) Measure $\angle$APB.

You will see that $\angle$APB is equal to $90^{\circ}$.

## Corollary:

If an arc of a circle subtends a right angle at any point of the remaining part of the circle, then the arc is a semi-circle.

## Theorem 10.10

## Statement:

The angle in a segment greater than a semi-circle is less than a right angle.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a circle O and a chord AB such that the centre lies in the major segment.
(ii) Take three points P, Q and R on the major segment and join them with the end points of chord AB.
(iii) Measure $\angle P$, $\angle Q$ and $\angle R$.

You will see that angles P, Q, R are all less than right angles (acute angles).

## Theorem 10.11

## Statement:

The angle in a segment less than a semi-circle is greater than a right angle.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a circle O and a chord AB such that the centre lies in the major segment.
(ii) Take three points P, Q and R on the minor segment and join them with the end points of chord AB.
(iii) Measure $\angle P$, $\angle Q$ and $\angle R$.

You will see that angles P, Q, R are all greater than a right angle (obtuse angles).

## Example:

In the figure, $\overline{OP}$ and $\overline{OQ}$ are tangents to a circle centred at S. If $\angle POQ = 36^{\circ}$, find (i) $\angle PSQ$ (ii) $\angle SQP$ (iii) $\angle PTQ$, where T is a point on the major arc.

## Solution:

(i) Join O and S. As OPS is a right-angled triangle, $\angle OPS = 90^{\circ}$. Also $\angle POS = 18^{\circ}$ (half of $36^{\circ}$, since $\overline{OS}$ bisects $\angle POQ$).

$$
\therefore \angle PSO = 90^{\circ} - 18^{\circ} = 72^{\circ}
$$

Hence, $\angle PSQ = \angle PSO + \angle QSO = 72^{\circ} + 72^{\circ} = 144^{\circ}$.

(ii) In $\triangle PQS$, $PS = QS$ (radii of the same circle), so $\angle SPQ = \angle SQP$ (angles opposite equal sides). Let $\angle SPQ = \angle SQP = x$. Then:

$$
2x + 144^{\circ} = 180^{\circ} \Rightarrow x = 18^{\circ}
$$

Hence $\angle SPQ = \angle SQP = 18^{\circ}$.

(iii) By Theorem 10.7, the central angle is double the angle subtended by the corresponding major arc:

$$
\angle PTQ = \frac{1}{2}\left(\angle PSQ\right) = \frac{1}{2} \times 144^{\circ} = 72^{\circ}
$$

mdxBody:
## Cyclic Quadrilateral

A quadrilateral inscribed in a circle is called a cyclic quadrilateral, that is, a quadrilateral whose vertices all lie on the circle. The four points on the circle are called concyclic points.

## Theorem 10.12

## Statement:

The opposite angles of any quadrilateral inscribed in a circle are supplementary. In other words, the sum of the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is $180^{\circ}$.

## Class Activity:

(i) Draw a circle O and inscribe a quadrilateral ABCD in the circle.
(ii) Measure the interior angles A, B, C and D of the quadrilateral.
(iii) Add $\angle A$ and $\angle C$. What is the sum? It is $180^{\circ}$.
(iv) Add $\angle B$ and $\angle D$. What is the sum? It is again $180^{\circ}$.

## Key Fact

A cyclic trapezium is isosceles, and its diagonals bisect each other.

## Example:

In the figure, A, B, C and D are points on a circle, with O the centre. If $\angle POQ = 100^{\circ}$ and $\angle QRS = 120^{\circ}$, and PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral, find $\angle SPQ$.

## Solution:

Since PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral, its opposite angles are supplementary:

$$
\angle SPQ + \angle SRQ = 180^{\circ}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow \angle SPQ + 120^{\circ} = 180^{\circ} \Rightarrow \angle SPQ = 60^{\circ}
$$

## Example:

In the figure, A, B, C, D and E lie on the circumference of a circle. If $\angle ABD = 46^{\circ}$, $\angle ACB = 70^{\circ}$ and $\angle EAB = 50^{\circ}$, find (i) $\angle DCA$ (ii) $\angle AEB$.

## Solution:

(i) Since angles in the same segment are equal, $\angle ADB = \angle ACB = 70^{\circ}$.

In $\triangle ABD$:

$$
\angle ABD + \angle ADB + \angle BAD = 180^{\circ}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow 46^{\circ} + 70^{\circ} + \angle BAD = 180^{\circ} \Rightarrow \angle BAD = 64^{\circ}
$$

Since ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, its opposite angles are supplementary:

$$
\angle BAD + \angle BCD = 180^{\circ}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow 64^{\circ} + \left(70^{\circ} + \angle DCA\right) = 180^{\circ} \Rightarrow \angle DCA = 46^{\circ}
$$

(ii) Since AEBC is a cyclic quadrilateral, its opposite angles are supplementary:

$$
\angle AEB + \angle ACB = 180^{\circ} \Rightarrow \angle AEB + 70^{\circ} = 180^{\circ} \Rightarrow \angle AEB = 110^{\circ}
$$
title: 10.3 Cyclic Quadrilateral

mdxBody:
## Practical Geometry of Circles

## After studying this unit students will be able to:

- Locate the centre of a given circle.
- Draw a circle passing through three given non-collinear points.
- Complete the circle (i) by finding its centre, (ii) without finding its centre, when a part of its circumference is given by
- Draw a tangent to a given arc, without using the centre, through a given point P when: (i) P is middle point of the arc (ii) P is at the end of arc (iii) P is outside the arc.
- Draw a tangent to a given circle from a point P when:
(i) P is on the circumference (ii) P is outside the circle.
- Draw two tangents to a circle meeting each other at a given angle.
- Draw (i) direct common tangents or external tangents (ii) transverse common tangents or internal tangents, to two equal/unequal circles.
- Draw a tangent to two unequal (i) touching circles (ii) intersecting circles.
- Apply concepts of practical geometry of circles to real life word problems such as athletic tracks, recreational parks, Ferris wheels and mechanical machines.

A circle is symmetric about its centre and any of its diameters. Architects often use the circle's symmetrical properties when designing athletic tracks, recreational parks, buildings, roundabouts, Ferris-wheels, etc. Artists and painters find the circle almost indispensable in their work. Circular cylinders are used to print newspapers. Engineers exploit the circle's symmetrical properties as seen by the use of the circle in making watches, clocks, bicycles, cars, trains, ships, aero-planes, radios, telephones, trolleys, wheel-barrows, air-conditioners, rockets etc. Civilizations have progressed dramatically because of the invention of the circular wheel.

## Construction of Circles

## To Locate the Centre of a Circle

Given: A circle without centre.
Required: To locate the center of circle.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Take three points $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and C on a circle.
(ii) Join these points to obtain a triangle $A B C$.
(iii) Draw right bisectors of sides $\mathrm{AB}, \mathrm{BC}$ and AC which
meet each other at point O .
O is required center of circle.

## To Draw a Circle Passing Through Three Non-Collinear Points

Given: Three non-collinear points A, B and C.
Required: To draw a circle passing through these points.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Take three non-collinear points $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and C on a paper.
(ii) Join these points to obtain a triangle $A B C$.
(iii) Draw right bisectors of sides BC and AC which meet each other at point O .
(iv) With center O , construct a circle of radius OA or OB .

To Complete the Circle when a Part of its Circumference is Given:

## (a) By finding the Centre (b) Without finding the Centre

(a) To Complete a Circle by Finding its Centre when Part of Circumference is Given

Given: A part of circle i.e. an arc.
Required: To complete the circle by finding its center.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Take three points $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and C on the given arc.
(ii) Join these points to obtain a triangle $A B C$.
(iii) Draw right bisectors of sides $\mathrm{AB}, \mathrm{BC}$ and AC which meet each other at point O .
(iv) With center O , construct a circle of radius OA or OB of which the given arc is a part.

## (b) To Complete a Circle without Finding its Centre when Part of Circumference is Given

Given: A part of circle i.e. an arc.
Required: To complete the circle without finding its center.

## First Method

## Steps of Construction:

(i) Take three points $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and C on the given arc such that $A B=B C$.
(We can also $\mathrm{AB} \neq \mathrm{BC}$.)
(ii) Join these points to obtain a triangle ABC .
(iii) Draw $\mathrm{BD}=\mathrm{AC}$ and $\mathrm{CD}=\mathrm{BC}$ to obtain a triangle BCD .
(iv) Again draw $\mathrm{CE}=\mathrm{BD}$ and $\mathrm{DE}=\mathrm{CD}$ to obtain a triangle CDE .
(v) Continue in this way and construct triangles DEF, EFG, FGH and GHA.
(vi) Join points C to $\mathrm{D}, \mathrm{D}$ to $\mathrm{E}, \mathrm{E}$ to $\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{F}$ to $\mathrm{G}, \mathrm{G}$ to H and H to A in circular path to obtain required circle.

## Second Method

## Steps of Construction:

(i) Draw a chord AB of suitable length on an arc PQ .
(ii) Construct an internal angle of measure $120^{\circ}$ at point B and draw BC equal to AB .
(iii) Again, construct an internal angle of measure $120^{\circ}$ at point C and draw CD equal to BC .
(iv) Continue this procedure to obtain points E and F .
(v) Draw arcs $\mathrm{BC}, \mathrm{CD}, \mathrm{DE}, \mathrm{EF}$ and FA carefully such that length of these arcs
is equal to the arc AB .
